QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Charges-in-CFT-.title: Charges in CFT for curved space-time
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Charges-in-CFT-.content:
In CFT in curved space-time we have redefined Noether charges to be topological and independent of the choice of quantization. We can refine that definition by noticing that the Noether currents of conformal symmetry are all particular combinations of the stress tensor.
Q^\epsilon(\Sigma) = -\int _\Sigma d S_\mu T^{\mu\nu}\epsilon_\nu(x)
where \epsilon is the infinitesimal variation of coordinates under the conformal transformation of which we are computing the charge.
From charges to algebra
What is the commutator between the charges and the stress tensor itself? It has to be translation invariant so:
[Q_\epsilon, T^{\mu\nu} (x)]=[Q_\epsilon, T^{\mu\nu} (0)]
Plus, since we are considering first order, the variation has to be linear in T and \epsilon; the variation needs to be in the same spin representation of T and has to be conserved. We get a few candidates:
(\partial \xi) T^{\mu\nu}
(\xi \cdot\partial)T^{\mu\nu}
\partial _\rho \xi ^\mu T^{\rho\nu}
\partial ^\mu \xi _\rho T^\rho _\nu
which we need to symmetrize:
\comm{Q_\epsilon}{T_{\mu\nu}(x)} = a_0 \epsilon ^\rho \partial _\rho T_{\mu\nu} + a_1 (\partial _\rho \epsilon ^\rho)T_{\mu\nu} +a_2 (\partial ^\rho \epsilon _\mu)T_{\rho\nu}+a_3(\partial _\mu \epsilon ^\rho) T_{\rho\nu}+\textrm{symmetrization}
We have to impose a few more conditions:

Tracelessness, which implies that

a_2 = -a_3

Conservation of dimension implies that:

a_0=a_1 = -a_2
We can do one more thing: we take [Q_\epsilon(\Sigma), T^{\mu\nu} (0)], multiply by another function \xi(x') and take the integral:
\int _{\Sigma'}[Q_\epsilon (\Sigma), T^{\mu\nu} (0)]\xi _\nu dS_\mu \sim -[Q_\epsilon (\Sigma),Q_\xi (\Sigma')]

If we assume that the Q_\epsilon (\Sigma) are a representation of the algebra, then we should get something like:
[Q_\epsilon (\Sigma),Q_\xi (\Sigma')] = Q_{?}(\Sigma^{\prime\prime})
It can be proven that:
? = [\epsilon, \xi] = (\epsilon\cdot\partial)\xi - (\xi\cdot\partial)\epsilon
where the parentheses above are the Lie brackets. If we take \epsilon,\xi to be the coordinate variations induced by conformal transformations, we can obtain the conformal algebra.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Charges-in-curv.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Charges in curved space-time.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Charges-in-curv.title: Charges in curved space-time
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Charges-in-curv.content:
Noether charges assume a particular quantization: we quantize the theory on time slices connected by the unitary time evolution. This may not be the best recipe for quantization if we want to consider curved space-time.
Starting from a Noether current j_\mu ^a, we define the topological charge:
j_\mu ^a \mapsto Q_\xi(\Sigma)\equiv -\int_{\partial B = \Sigma} dS_\mu j^{\mu,a}(x)\xi _a(x)
This charge is related to the variation of operators through the Schwinger–Dyson equations, in fact, by integrating over B and contracting with \xi both sides of:
\partial_\mu\corr{j^\mu_a(x)\phi_1(x_1)...\phi_n(x_n)} = i\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta ^{d}(x-x_i)\corr{\phi_1(x_1)... \delta_a \phi_i ...\phi_n(x_n)}
we find:
i\sum_{x_k\in B}\xi _a\left\langle \phi_1(x_1)...\delta^a\phi_k(x_k)...\phi(x_n)\right\rangle = \langle Q_\xi(\Sigma)\phi_1(x_1) ... \phi_n(x_n)\rangle
Connection with standard charges

Choosing a particular surface whose normal vector is parallel to the time direction, we can recover the usual commutation relation of charges and operators:
\left\langle Q_\xi \phi\right\rangle =\int d^{d-1}x\,\xi _a\left\langle[J^{0,a},\phi]\right\rangle = i \xi _a \langle \delta ^a\phi\rangle
which is similar to the standard:
[Q,\phi] \sim i \delta \phi

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Field.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Checklist/Field representation of conformal generators.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Field.title: Field representation of conformal generators
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Field.content:
We have
f'(x) = e^{iG}f(x)
and
x' = g(x)\Rightarrow x = g^{-1} (x')
so that
f' = f\circ g^{-1}
If g is a conformal transformation, how do the functions transform?
Translations
g(x) = x^\mu + \epsilon ^\mu = x'^\mu
\Rightarrow g^{-1} (x) = x^\mu - \epsilon ^\mu
f'(x) = f(g^{-1}(x)) = f(x - \epsilon)\simeq f(x) -\epsilon ^\mu \partial _\mu f(x)
e^{-iP_\mu \epsilon ^\mu}f(x) \simeq f(x) - iP_\mu \epsilon ^\mu f(x)
P_\mu = -i\partial_\mu
Rotations
g(x) = x^\mu + \omega^{\mu\nu}x_\nu = x'^\mu
\Rightarrow g^{-1} (x) = x^\mu - \omega ^{\mu\nu}x_\nu + O\left(\omega ^2\right)
In fact:
x'^\mu - \omega ^{\mu\nu}x'_\nu =x ^\mu +\omega ^{\mu\nu} (x_\nu - x'_\nu) = x^\mu + O\left(\omega^2\right)
Then:
f'(x) = f(g^{-1}(x)) \simeq f(x - \omega x)\simeq f(x) -\omega ^{\mu \nu}x _\nu \partial _\mu f(x)
e^{-\frac{i}{2}L_{\mu\nu} \omega ^{\mu\nu}}f(x) \simeq f(x) - \frac{i}{2}L_{\mu\nu} \omega ^{\mu\nu} f(x)
The \frac{1}{2} factor compensates the double counting due to contracting two antisymmetric tensors.
Taking only the antisymmetric part:
\frac{1}{2}L_{\mu\nu} \omega ^{\mu\nu} = -i\omega^{\mu\nu}x_\nu\partial _\mu = -\frac{i}{2}\omega^{\mu\nu}(x_\nu\partial _\mu - x_\mu \partial _\nu)
L_{\mu\nu} = -i(x_\nu\partial _\mu - x_\mu \partial _\nu)
Dilations
g(x) = x^\mu + \left(\lambda^2-1\right)x^\mu = x'^\mu
\Rightarrow g^{-1} (x) = x^\mu - \left(\lambda^2-1\right) x^\mu + O\left(\left(\lambda^2-1\right)^2\right)
f'(x) = f(g^{-1}(x)) \simeq f\left(x - \left(\lambda^2-1\right) x\right)\simeq f(x) -\left(\lambda^2-1\right)x^\mu\partial _\mu f(x)
e^{-iD\left(\lambda^2-1\right)}f(x) \simeq f(x) - i\left(\lambda^2-1\right)D f(x)
D= -ix^\mu\partial _\mu
SCT
g(x) \simeq x^\mu + \left(2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2\right) = x'^\mu
It’s more useful to start from:
\mathrm{SCT}_b = I\circ P_{-b}\circ I
\mathrm{SCT}_{-b} = I\circ P_{b}\circ I
\Rightarrow g^{-1} (x) \simeq x^\mu - \left(2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2\right)
f'(x) = f(g^{-1}(x)) \simeq f\left(x - \left(2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2\right)\right)\simeq f(x) -\left(2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2\right)\partial _\mu f(x)
e^{-iK_\mu b^\mu}f(x) \simeq f(x) - iK_\mu b^\mu f(x)
K_\mu b^\mu = -i \left(2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2\right)\partial _\mu
K_\mu = -i\left(2x_\mu (x\cdot\partial) - x^2\partial _\mu\right)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Unita.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Checklist/Unitarity bound for scalars - proof.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Unita.title: Unitarity bound for scalars - proof
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Unita.content:
For scalars, we have a bound on dimensionality given by:
\Delta \geq\frac{d-2}{2}
Proof
The results stems from imposing:
\matel{\Delta,l=0}{K^2 P^2}{\Delta, l=0}\succcurlyeq 0
which reproduces the positiveness of the internal product in euclidean theory (conjugation \leftrightarrow inversion).
In the following, equalities that are valid inside the inner product above will be denoted with \simeq. Basically, we want to exploit the fact that:
K\ket{\Delta, l=0} = M\ket{\Delta, l=0} = 0
and:
D\ket{\Delta, l=0} = -i\Delta\ket{\Delta, l=0}
Then, we have:
K^2P^2 \simeq [K^2,P^2] \simeq K_\mu [K^\mu, P^2]
where in the second equality we used:
\comm{AB}{C} = A\comm{B}{C} + \comm{A}{C}B
\comm{A}{BC} = B\comm{A}{C} + \comm{A}{B}C
Continuing our computation:
K^2P^2 \simeq K_\mu \left(P_\nu\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu} +\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu} P_\nu\right)
Now we employ:
\anticomm{A}{B} = 2AB - \comm{A}{B}
to obtain:
K^2P^2 \simeq K_\mu \left(2P_\nu\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu}-\comm{P_\nu}{\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu}}\right)
Let’s compute the second term; from the conformal algebra:
\begin{aligned}
& {\left[D, K_\mu\right]=-i K_\mu,} \\
& {\left[D, P_\mu\right]=i P_\mu,} \\
& {\left[K_\mu, P_\nu\right]=2 i\left(\eta_{\mu \nu} D-M_{\mu \nu}\right),} \\
& {\left[K_\mu, M_{\nu \rho}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\mu \nu} K_\rho-\eta_{\mu \rho} K_\nu\right),} \\
& {\left[P_\rho, M_{\mu \nu}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\rho \mu} P_\nu-\eta_{\rho \nu} P_\mu\right),} \\
& {\left[M_{\mu \nu}, M_{\rho \sigma}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\nu \rho} M_{\mu \sigma}+\eta_{\mu \sigma} M_{\nu \rho}-\eta_{\mu \rho} M_{\nu \sigma}-\eta_{\nu \sigma} M_{\mu \rho}\right),}
\end{aligned}
we get:
\comm{P_\nu}{\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu}} = -2(d-2)P^\mu
Then:
K_\mu\comm{P_\nu}{\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu}} = -4d(d-2)\Delta
Now on to the first term:
2P_\nu\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu}= 2iP_\nu\left(\eta^{\mu \nu} D-M^{\mu \nu}\right)\simeq 2 \Delta P^\mu
2K_\mu P_\nu\comm{K^\mu}{P^\nu} \simeq 4i \Delta\comm{K_\mu}{P^\mu} = 8\Delta^2d
Therefore, we need ot impose the condition:
8\Delta^2 d - 4\Delta d(d-2)\geq 0
which leads to:
\Delta\geq \frac{d-2}{2}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Vecto.title: Vector-scalars 3PF
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Checklist/Vecto.content:
We want to prove the relation:
\corr{\phi _{\Delta _1}(x_1)\phi _{\Delta _2}(x_2)v^{\mu}_{\Delta_v}(x_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\phi_1\phi_2v}Z^{\mu}_{123}}{X_{12}^{2h_{12v} +1}X_{23}^{2h_{2v1}-1}X_{13}^{2h_{1v2}-1}}
where:
h_{ijk} \coloneqq \frac{\Delta _i +\Delta _j - \Delta _k}{2}
Z^{\mu}_{ijk}\coloneqq \frac{X_{ik}^\mu}{X^2_{ik}}-\frac{X_{jk}^\mu}{X^2_{jk}}
Proof
Working in embedding space, given the condition for traceless antisymmetric tensors:
T:\left\{\begin{array}{l}
T^{A_1,...,A_l} \quad \textrm{TST of }SO(d+1,1)\\
T^{A_1,...,A_l} (\lambda P) = \frac{1}{\lambda ^{\Delta _t}}T^{A_1,...,A_l} (P)\\
\textrm{transversality: } P_{A_i}T^{A_1,...,A_l}(P) = 0 \quad\forall i=1,...,l\\
t^{\mu _1 ...\mu _l}(x) = \left. \left(\frac{\partial P _{A_1}}{\partial x_{\mu _1}}\right)...\left(\frac{\partial P _{A_l}}{\partial x_{\mu _l}}\right)T^{A_1,...,A_l}\right|_{P_{ps}}
\end{array}\right.
We can start from the ansatz:
\corr{\Phi _{\Delta _1}(P_1)\Phi _{\Delta _2}(P_2)V^{A}_{\Delta_v}(P_3)} = {T^A}f((P_1\cdot P_2),(P_2\cdot P_3),(P_1\cdot P_3))
\corr{\Phi _{\Delta _1}(P_1)\Phi _{\Delta _2}(P_2)V^{A}_{\Delta_v}(P_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\Phi_1\Phi_2O}T^A}{(P_1\cdot P_2)^{\alpha}(P_2\cdot P_3)^{\beta}(P_1\cdot P_3)^{\gamma}}
The most general form for T^A is:
T^A = aP_1^A(P_2\cdot P_3) +bP_2^A(P_1\cdot P_3) +cP_1^A(P_1\cdot P_3) +dP_2^A(P_2\cdot P_3) 
Terms proportional to P_3^A are killed by transversality automatically, which also imposes:
a=-b,\quad c=d=0
Gathering the scalar coefficient:
T^A =(P_1\cdot P_3)(P_2\cdot P_3)\left(\frac{P_1^A}{P_1\cdot P_3} - \frac{P_2^A}{P_2\cdot P_3}\right)
The scalars outside the parenthesis can be reabsorbed in f; then we define
Homogeneity fixes the form of f:
K^A \coloneqq\left(\frac{P_1^A}{P_1\cdot P_3} - \frac{P_2^A}{P_2\cdot P_3}\right)
\corr{\Phi _{\Delta _1}(P_1)\Phi _{\Delta _2}(P_2)V^{A}_{\Delta_v}(P_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\phi_1\phi_2v}K^A}{(P_1\cdot P_2)^{\alpha}(P_2\cdot P_3)^{\beta}(P_1\cdot P_3)^{\gamma}}
we can also fix the coefficient through homogeneity, we need to solve the system:
\left\{
\begin{array}{lll}
\alpha+\gamma = \Delta_1\\
\alpha + \beta = \Delta_2\\
\gamma+\beta-1 = \Delta_3
\end{array}
\right.
Now we just need to pull back from embedding space on the Poincaré section. We already know that:
P_i \cdot P_j\left.\vphantom{\sum}\right|_{ps} = -\frac{1}{2}(x_i-x_j)^2\coloneqq -\frac{1}{2}X_{ij}^2
We need to compute
k^{\mu}(x) = \left. \left(\frac{\partial P _{3,A}}{\partial x_{3,\mu}}\right)K^{A}\right|_{P_{3,ps}}
where:
\left(\frac{\partial P _{3,A}}{\partial x_{3,\mu}}\right) = \left(0,2x_3^\mu, \delta_\nu^\mu\right)
so that:
\left(\frac{\partial P _{3,A}}{\partial x_{3,\mu}}\right) P_i ^A = -x_3^\mu +x_i^\mu = X_{i3}^\mu
Then, reabsorbing the constants into \lambda, we arrive at:
\corr{\phi _{\Delta _1}(x_1)\phi _{\Delta _2}(x_2)v^{\mu}_{\Delta_v}(x_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\phi_1\phi_2v}\left(\frac{X_{13}^\mu}{X^2_{13}}-\frac{X_{23}^\mu}{X^2_{23}}\right)}{X_{12}^{2h_{12v} +1}X_{23}^{2h_{2v1}-1}X_{13}^{2h_{1v2}-1}}
which is exactly what we wanted

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-Algeb.title: Conformal Algebra
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-Algeb.content:
The conformal algebra is given by
\begin{aligned}
& {\left[D, K_\mu\right]=-i K_\mu,} \\
& {\left[D, P_\mu\right]=i P_\mu,} \\
& {\left[K_\mu, P_\nu\right]=2 i\left(\eta_{\mu \nu} D-M_{\mu \nu}\right),} \\
& {\left[K_\mu, M_{\nu \rho}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\mu \nu} K_\rho-\eta_{\mu \rho} K_\nu\right),} \\
& {\left[P_\rho, M_{\mu \nu}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\rho \mu} P_\nu-\eta_{\rho \nu} P_\mu\right),} \\
& {\left[M_{\mu \nu}, M_{\rho \sigma}\right]=i\left(\eta_{\nu \rho} M_{\mu \sigma}+\eta_{\mu \sigma} M_{\nu \rho}-\eta_{\mu \rho} M_{\nu \sigma}-\eta_{\nu \sigma} M_{\mu \rho}\right),}
\end{aligned}
With all other possible commutators being 0.

The dilation generator D and the Lorentz generator M_{\mu\nu} commute, so it’s possible to choose a common eigenbase for them.
In general the commutator of an operator with the Lorentz generator is proportional to the rotation of the operator in it representation:

\comm{M_{\mu\nu}}{O^I} = i\left[R^{(rappr_O)}(M_{\mu\nu})\right]^I_J O^J

Notice that P and K act as ladder operators on the eigenstates of dilation operator.

Alternative notation
We introduce the object:
\mathcal{J}^{AB}\sim\left(\begin{array}{c:c:c}M_{\mu\nu} & \frac{P+K}{2} & \frac{P-K}{2}\\ \hdashline
-\frac{P+K}{2}&0&D\\ \hdashline -\frac{P-K}{2}&-D&0\end{array}\right)
where A,B=1,...,d+2. This object is antisymmetric:
\mathcal{J}^{AB} = -\mathcal{J}^{BA}
We can summarize the conformal algebra by writing the commutation relations of \mathcal{J}^{AB}:
\comm{J_{AB}}{J_{CD}} = \eta_{BC}J_{AD}-\eta_{AC}J_{BD}-\eta_{BD}J_{AC}+\eta_{AD}J_{BC}
where:
\eta_{AB}\sim\left(\begin{array}{ccc|cc}
\\
&\eta _{\mu\nu}&&&\\
\\
\hline&&&1\\
&&&&-1\\
\end{array}\right)
this means that the conformal algebra is the same algebra for SO(d+1,1) in euclidean geometry or SO(d,2) in Minkowskian geometry.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-Killi.title: Conformal Killing equation
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-Killi.content:
Given
x^\mu \mapsto x^{\prime \mu} \simeq x^\mu +\epsilon ^\mu
Such a transformation that satisfies the metric transformation for the conformal group:
ds^2\mapsto\Omega^2(x)ds^2
exists if and only if \epsilon satisfies the Killing equation:
\partial _\mu\epsilon _\nu +\partial _\nu\epsilon _\mu =\frac{2}{d}\partial ^\rho \epsilon _\rho \eta_{\mu\nu}
In non-flat metric, using covariant derivatives:
\nabla _\mu\epsilon _\nu +\nabla _\nu\epsilon _\mu =\frac{2}{d} \nabla ^\rho \epsilon _\rho g_{\mu\nu} 


                  
                  Proof
                  
                

The equation that we need to satisfy is:
\mathcal{L}_{\epsilon}g = \lambda (x) g
Where \mathcal{L}_{\epsilon} is the Lie derivative w.r.t. the flow generated by \epsilon. Carrying out the computation:
\left(\mathcal{L}_{\epsilon}g\right)_{\mu\nu} = \epsilon ^\rho \nabla_\rho (g_{\mu\nu})+g_{\rho \nu}\nabla _\mu \epsilon ^\rho + g_{\mu\rho} \nabla _\nu \epsilon ^\rho
Using \nabla_\rho (g_{\mu\nu})=0 (we are using a metric-compatible and torsion-free connection check )  we obtain:
\nabla _\mu \epsilon _\nu + \nabla _\nu \epsilon _\mu = \lambda (x) g_{\mu\nu}
Taking the trace on both sides leads to
\lambda (x) = \frac{2}{d}\nabla_\rho \epsilon ^\rho
Which is the desired result.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-block.title: Conformal blocks

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-group.title: Conformal group
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conformal-group.content:
The conformal group is the group of coordinate transformations which act on the metric by introducing a proportionality factor which could depend on the coordinates:
ds^2\mapsto\Omega(x)ds^2
It’s basically an extension of the Poincaré group that also admits dilations and a specific type of transformation, called special conformal transformation (SCT) which is quadratic in the coordinates.
Infinitesimal transformations
The infinitesimal transformations associated to the conformal group can be derived from the conformal Killing equation, in the flat case:
\partial _\mu\epsilon _\nu +\partial _\nu\epsilon _\mu =\frac{2}{d}\partial ^\rho \epsilon _\rho \eta_{\mu\nu}
Translations
\epsilon^\mu = a^\mu
Lorentz
\epsilon ^\mu = \omega ^{\mu\nu} x_\nu
where \omega ^{\mu\nu} is antisymmetric.
Dilations
\epsilon ^\mu = (\lambda -1)x^\mu
Special Conformal Transformations
\epsilon ^\mu = 2 (b\cdot x) x^\mu - b^\mu x^2


                  
                  Finite SCT's I's and translations by b, P_b:
                  
                

x^\mu \overset{I}{\mapsto} \frac{x^\mu}{x^2}
\mathrm{SCT}_b = I\circ P_{-b}\circ I
This can be useful when considering finite transformations:
\mathrm{SCT}_{b} = [\mathrm{SCT}_{b/n}]^n


Generators
Since the group is not compact, there can’t be a finite-dimensional unitary representation. We can however find an infinite-dimensional one in field space, see Field representation of conformal generators for details.
From a given representation of generators we can derive the algebra.
Translations
The action of the group is given by
e^{-iP_\mu \epsilon ^\mu}
The representation on fields is:
P_\mu = -i\partial_\mu
Lorentz
The action of the group is given by
e^{-\frac{i}{2}L_{\mu\nu} \omega ^{\mu\nu}}f(x)
The representation on fields is:
L_{\mu\nu} = -i(x_\nu\partial _\mu - x_\mu \partial _\nu)
Dilations
The action of the group is given by
e^{-iD\left(\lambda^2-1\right)}
The representation on fields is:
D= -ix^\mu\partial _\mu
Special Conformal Transformations
The action of the group is given by
e^{-iK_\mu b^\mu}
The representation on fields is:
K_\mu = -i\left(2x_\mu (x\cdot\partial) - x^2\partial _\mu\right)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conserved-curre.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Conserved currents in GFT's.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conserved-curre.title: Conserved currents in GFT's
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Conserved-curre.content:
Take \ket{O_{\Delta, r}} a primary state with positive norm (if norm is 0 it corresponds to the identity)
Take first descendant P_\mu \ket{O_{\Delta, r}}, then
\norm{\xi ^\mu P_\mu \ket{O_{\Delta, r}}}^2\geq 0
translates to
\Delta \geq \Delta _{un} (d,r)
where \Delta _{un} (d,r) is determined by unitarity bounds.
When the inequality is saturated, the first descendant is a null state


                  
                  Null states 
                  
                

States whose operators, when put in a correlation function, return 0


\comm{P_\mu}{O_{\Delta, r}} = \textrm{null state}
note that from commutator we obtain one of the representations we get from l\otimes 1 = l+1\oplus l \oplus l-1, so only the last one corresponds to the saturation of the unitarity bound.


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Given a TST with \Delta = l+d-2, its first descendant:
\partial_\nu O ^{\nu\mu_1\mu_2...}
has dimensionality \Delta' = l+d-1 and is a null state.
\corr{\partial_\nu O ^{\nu\mu_1\mu_2...}X} = 0
In CFT, a local conserved currents of spin l must have dimension \Delta = l +d-2

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Correlation functions from embedding formalism - tensors.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.title: Correlation functions from embedding formalism - tensors
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.content:
Extending from Correlation functions from embedding formalism, we want to find the form of correlation functions for tensors.
Example: vector 2pt function
\langle v^\mu (x_1) v ^\nu (x_2)\rangle
Embed in higher dimensional space:
v^\mu (x) \mapsto V^A(P)
where
V^A(P) P_A =0 \quad\land\quad V^A(P)\sim V^A(P) +P^A
We then study
\langle V^A(P_1) V^B(P_2)\rangle
It needs to be a tensor of two indices
\langle V^A(P_1) V^B(P_2)\rangle = \eta ^{AB}f(P_1\cdot P_2)+ P_1^AP_2^Bg(P_1\cdot P_2)+ P_2^AP_1^Bh(P_1\cdot P_2)
imposing the homogeneity property fixes the scalars:
\langle V^A(P_1) V^B(P_2)\rangle = \frac{1}{(-2P_1\cdot P_2)^{\Delta _v}}\left(\eta ^{AB} +c _1 \frac{P_1^A P_2 ^B}{P_1\cdot P_2}+c _2 \frac{P_2^A P_1 ^B}{P_1\cdot P_2}\right)
Imposing transversality:
P_2 ^B +c_2 P_2 ^B =0\Rightarrow c_2= -1
Finally, the “gauge invariance” kills, meaning that it does not matter when projecting on the Poincaré section, the second term (the third term is not longitudinal), although sometimes it might be useful to keep it to make some symmetries clearer, so that:
\langle V^A(P_1) V^B(P_2)\rangle = \frac{1}{(-2P_1\cdot P_2)^{\Delta _v}}\left(\eta ^{AB}- \frac{P_2^A P_1 ^B}{P_1\cdot P_2}\right)
Then:
\langle v^\mu (x_1) v ^\nu (x_2)\rangle =\frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta_v}}\left(\eta^{\mu\nu} - \frac{2X_{12} ^\mu X_{12} ^\nu}{X_{12} ^2}\right)
Again, the 2PF is completely fixed in conformal theories. The term between the parentheses is called the inversion tensor:
I^{\mu\nu}(X_{12}) \equiv \left(\eta^{\mu\nu} - \frac{2X_{12} ^\mu X_{12} ^\nu}{X_{12} ^2}\right)
Tensor generalization
The construction above can be generalized to tensors
\corr{t_{\mu _1 ... \mu _l}(x_1)t_{\nu _1 ... \nu _l}(x_2)} = \frac{I _{\mu_1 \nu _1}...I _{\mu_l \nu _l}+\textrm{symmetrizations
}-\textrm{traces}}{(X_{12})^{2\Delta_t}}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Correlation functions from embedding formalism.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.title: Correlation functions from embedding formalism
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.content:
Using the embedding formalism, we denote fields lying in the embedding space as \Phi and fields lying in the original space as \phi. We require two properties for \Phi:
\Phi (P^A):\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\Phi (P^A _{ps} = (1,x^2,x^\mu)) = \phi (x^\mu)\\
\Phi (\lambda P^A) = \lambda ^{-\Delta _\phi}\Phi (P^A)
\end{array}\right.
We can now find the form of correlation functions, or n-point functions (nPF), for CFT’s. Here we derive them for scalars.
1 point functions
Scalars
\langle \Phi (P)\rangle
This needs to be a scalar. The only scalar of coordinates that we can construct using a single coordinate is the absolute value
\langle \Phi (P)\rangle = const?
Since the field has to scale according the second property defined above, we  only have two possibilities:
\langle \Phi (P)\rangle = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
0 &\textrm{if }\Delta_{\phi}\neq 0\\
1 &\textrm{if }\Delta_{\phi}= 0
\end{array}\right.
The only operator allowed to have dimension 0 is the identity.
2 point functions
Scalars
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\rangle
This too can only be a function of scalars
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\rangle = f(P_1\cdot P_2)
The second required property of the fields imposes that:
f((\lambda_1P_1)\cdot (\lambda_2P_2))=f(\lambda_1\lambda_2P_1\cdot P_2) = \frac{1}{\lambda_1 ^{\Delta_1}\lambda_2^{\Delta_2}}f(P_1\cdot P_2)
But since \lambda_1\lambda_2P_1\cdot P_2 is a single argument, \Delta _1 = \Delta _2 =\Delta, otherwise the function needs to be identically 0:
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\rangle= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\frac{\mathrm{const.}}{(-2P_1\cdot P_2)^\Delta} &\textrm{if }\Delta_1=\Delta_2 = \Delta\\
0 &\textrm{if }\Delta_1\neq \Delta _2
\end{array}\right.
On the Poincaré section, define:
P_{1,ps}\cdot P_{2,ps} = x_1 ^\mu x_{2 \,\mu} -\frac{1}{2}(x_1^2+x^2_2) = -\frac{1}{2}(x_1-x_2)^2\equiv-\frac{1}{2}X_{12}^2
so that, when \Delta _1 = \Delta _2 (reabsorbing the constant into the definition of fields):
\langle \phi _1(x_1)\phi _2(x_2)\rangle =\frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta_1}}
In a theory with scale symmetry but not conformal symmetry, one could have the 2PF \neq 0 when \Delta _1\neq\Delta _2.
From now on, assume that 2PF are “diagonal” in the space of operators (only non 0 2PF are those of an operator with itself).
3 point functions
Scalars
We have to consider all independent coordinate scalars
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\Phi _3(P_3)\rangle = f(P_1\cdot P_2,P_2\cdot P_3,P_1\cdot P_3)
Same tricks as before, we get
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\Phi _3(P_3)\rangle =\frac{\textrm{const. = }\lambda_{\Phi_1\Phi_2\Phi_3}}{(-2P_1\cdot P_2)^{h_{123}}(-2P_2\cdot P_3)^{h_{231}}(-2P_1\cdot P_3)^{h_{132}}}
where:
h_{ijk} \equiv \frac{\Delta _i +\Delta _j - \Delta _k}{2}
We already rescaled the fields to reabsorb the 2PF constant, so here the constant stays and depends on the theory. On the Poincaré section
-2(P_1\cdot P_2) = X_{12}^2
\langle \phi _1(x_1)\phi _2(x_2)\phi _3(x_3)\rangle =\frac{\lambda_{\phi_1\phi_2\phi_3}}{X_{12}^{2h_{123}}X_{23}^{2h_{231}}X_{13}^{2h_{132}}}
No free dependency on coordinates, only liberty is the constant depending on the theory.
Scalars-tensor
The 3PF of two scalars and and a tensor is given by:
\corr{\Phi _{\Delta _1}(x_1)\Phi _{\Delta _2}(x_2)O^{\mu_1...\mu_l}_{\Delta_3}(x_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\Phi_1\Phi_2O}(Z^{\mu_1}_{123}...Z^{\mu_l}_{123}-\mathrm{traces})}{X_{12}^{2h_{123} +l}X_{23}^{2h_{231}+l}X_{13}^{2h_{132}-l}}
Specifically for vectors, we get:
\corr{\phi _{\Delta _1}(x_1)\phi _{\Delta _2}(x_2)v^{\mu}_{\Delta_v}(x_3)} = \frac{\lambda_{\phi_1\phi_2v}Z^{\mu}_{123}}{X_{12}^{2h_{12v} +1}X_{23}^{2h_{2v1}-1}X_{13}^{2h_{1v2}-1}}
where:
Z^{\mu}_{ijk}\coloneqq \frac{X_{ik}^\mu}{X^2_{ik}}-\frac{X_{jk}^\mu}{X^2_{jk}}
A proof of this last result is provided in Vector-scalars 3PF.
4 pt functions
From 4PF’s and above, the correlations are not fixed
Consider the same field for simplicity
\langle \Phi (P_1)\Phi (P_2)\Phi (P_3)\Phi (P_4)\rangle =\frac{1}{(-2P_1\cdot P_2)^{\Delta _\Phi}(-2P_3\cdot P_4)^{\Delta _\Phi}}g(U,V)
where U,V are rotation invariant and conserve homogeneity. An example:
U=\frac{(P_1\cdot P_2)(P_3\cdot P_4)}{(P_1\cdot P_3)(P_2\cdot P_4)}
u\coloneqq \frac{X_{12} ^2X_{34} ^2}{X_{13} ^2X_{24} ^2}
V=\frac{(P_1\cdot P_4)(P_2\cdot P_3)}{(P_1\cdot P_3)(P_2\cdot P_4)}
v\coloneqq \frac{X_{14} ^2X_{23} ^2}{X_{13} ^2X_{24} ^2}
We can show that U,V are conformal invariants.
There are 3 independent combinations at any dimension.
This is the first correlator with actual dependency on coordinates.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.title: Correlation functions
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Correlation-fun.content:
Correlation functions for CFT can be found using the following methods:

Starting from ansatz and imposing covariance under conformal group (see below for sketch)
Exploiting Schwinger–Dyson equations (see below for sketch)
Using the embedding formalism, (see here).

Summary

























CorrelatorCFTQFT1 point0 if not identity\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\textrm{const} & \textrm{if scalar}\\ 0 & \textrm{otherwise}\end{array}\right.2 pointfixedtheory dependent (contains spectral info) TODO3 pointfixed up to a constant which is theory dependent but not coordinate dependent
Ansatz method
The ansatz is the following:
\corr{\Phi _1 (x_1)\Phi_2(x_2)} \equiv f(x_1,x_2)
basically we require the correlation function of two scalars to only be dependent on the coordinates. Now we impose covariance:

Invariance under translations:

f(x_1,x_2) = f(X_{12}\equiv x_1-x_2)

Invariance under Lorentz:

f(X_{12}) = f\left(X_{12}^2\right)

Covariance under dilations:

\corr{\Phi' _1 (x'_1)\Phi'_2(x'_2)} = f(X'_{12})
\corr{\Phi' _1 (x'_1)\Phi'_2(x'_2)} = \lambda ^{-\Delta _1}\lambda ^{-\Delta _2}\corr{\Phi _1 (\lambda ^{-1}x'_1)\Phi_2(\lambda ^{-1}x'_2)} = \lambda ^{-(\Delta _1  + \Delta _2)}f\left(\lambda ^{-1}X'_{12}\right)
f(y/\lambda) = \lambda ^{\Delta _1 + \Delta _2}f(y)
Putting these 3 together:
f(X_{12}) = \frac{\mathrm{const}}{\abs{X_{12}}^{\Delta_1+\Delta _2}}

SCT’s are combinations of translations and inversions, so we can also impose invariance under inversions ⇒ The two energy dimensions need to be the same for the constant to be non 0.
when \Delta _1 = \Delta _2:
\langle \Phi _1(x_1)\Phi _2(x_2)\rangle =\frac{const}{X_{12}^{2\Delta_1}}
The constant can be reabsorbed into the definition of fields. From now on, assume that 2PF’s are “diagonal” in the space of operators (only non 0 2PF are those of an operator with itself).
\corr{O_I O_J} = \frac{\delta _{IJ}}{X_{12}^{2\Delta_I}}
The 2 point function is completely fixed in conformal theories

Schwinger-Dyson method

Schwinger-Dyson equations impose covariance at infinitesimal level. Consider the n point correlator:
\corr{O_1 ... O_n}
and define a charge on a surface that does not surround the points (see picture above):
Q^\epsilon(\Sigma) = -\int _\Sigma d S_\mu T^{\mu\nu}\xi_\nu(x)
\langle Q_\xi(\Sigma)O_1 ... O_n\rangle = 0
but the surface can also be expanded to infinity so that it encompasses each point:
0 =\sum_{x_k\in B}\xi _a\left\langle O_1(x_1)...\delta^aO_k(x_k)...O(x_n)\right\rangle
Then, we can define a linear differential operator that encodes these variations:
\mathcal{D}(x_i,\partial _i)\corr{O_1 ... O_n} =0
Solving these differential equations leads to the correct form of correlators.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Crossing-symmet.title: Crossing symmetry
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Crossing-symmet.content:
The conformal block formalism leads to a graph representation (contributions to a 4PF are given by sum over irreps):
\corr{\phi (x_1)\phi (x_2)\phi (x_3)\phi (x_4)} = \frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta _\phi}}\frac{1}{X_{34}^{2\Delta _\phi}}\sum _{\Delta,l} \lambda ^2_{\Delta ,l} g _{\Delta ,l}(u,v) 
u\coloneqq \frac{X_{12} ^2X_{34} ^2}{X_{13} ^2X_{24} ^2}
v\coloneqq \frac{X_{14} ^2X_{23} ^2}{X_{13} ^2X_{24} ^2}

Our expansion is only one possible choice, diagram varies with the choice of OPE.

Only the dependence on coordinates changes.
Taking two kinds of expansions (for example those in the picture) and subtracting them:
\sum _{\Delta ,l}\lambda^2{\Delta,l} \left(u^{-\Delta _\phi}g_{\Delta,l}(u,v)-v^{-\Delta _\phi}g_{\Delta,l}(v,u)\right) = 0
If the sums converge (OPE’s have finite rays of convergence), the equation above should hold for any u,v.
We find that each term in the parentheses is non 0. The equation above is called the crossing symmetry (the equation relates to the CFT data, which is the set of coefficients \left\{\{\Delta,l\},\lambda_{\Delta ,l}\right\})
Casimir trick
The conformal blocks seem to be very important, so there is a huge amount of literature dedicated to computing them. It was found that conformal blocks satisfy a second order differential equation that in a sense defines them, which can be found through Casimir operators.
For the conformal algebra we have two Casimir’s; the quadratic one is:
C_2 = J_{AB}J^{AB}=...
Which acts the same way on a given irrep:
C_2(\Delta,l)\coloneqq C_2 \ket{\Delta, l} = (l (l+d-2)+ \Delta(\Delta-d))\ket{\Delta, l}
Inside a 4PF we can insert the sum over the projectors over irreps:
\id = \sum _{\Delta, l } P_{\Delta,l}
P_{\Delta,l} \equiv \sum _{\alpha \beta} g _{\alpha\beta} ^{-1} \op{\alpha}{\beta}
\alpha,\beta = \mathcal{O},P\mathcal{O},PP\mathcal{O},...
where g is the g is the Gram matrix:
g_{\alpha\beta} = \ip{\alpha}{\beta}
The 4PF becomes:
\corr{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)\id\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)}
=
\sum _{\Delta ,l} \matel{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}{P_{\Delta,l}}{\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)}
The correlation also admits a conformal block expansion
W_{\Delta ,l}(x_i)\coloneqq \matel{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}{P_{\Delta,l}}{\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)} = \frac{\lambda _{\Delta , l }^2}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}g_{\Delta, l}(u,v)
Now we insert the Casimir:
\matel{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}{P_{\Delta,l}C_2}{\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)}
=
C_2(\Delta,l)\matel{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}{P_{\Delta,l}}{\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)} = C_2(\Delta,l) W_{\Delta ,l}(x_i)
I can also work on the left-hand side, replacing C_2 = J_{AB}J^{AB} and performing the commutators of J with the field operators
\comm{J_{AB}J^{AB}}{\phi(x_3)\phi (x_4)} = \comm{J_{AB}}{\comm{J^{AB}}{\phi(x_3)\phi(x_4)}}
Generally, the commutator will be a differential operator:
\comm{J^{AB}}{\phi (x_k)} \equiv \mathcal{D}_{x_k}\phi (x_k)
Iterating, we get a second order differential equation:
\mathcal{D}^{(2)}_{x_3x_4}W_{\Delta ,l}(x_i) = ...=\frac{\lambda _{\Delta , l }^2}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}\tilde{\mathcal{D}}^{(2)} _{u,v}g_{\Delta,l}(u,v)
\Rightarrow\tilde{\mathcal{D}}^{(2)} _{u,v}g_{\Delta,l}(u,v)= C_2(\Delta,l) g_{\Delta,l}(u,v)
This equation defines g and the constraints are given by the OPE limit (X_{12}, X_{34} very small). In even dimension, it has been shown that the equation is not too hard.
In even dimension we have a solution using the variables
u=z\bar{z}
v=(1-z)(1-\bar{z})
In d=2
g_{\Delta,l} (z,\bar{z}) = K_{\Delta+l}(z)K_{\Delta-l}(\bar{z}) + \textrm {switch }(z,\bar{z})
K_\beta(x) \coloneqq x^{\beta/2} {}_2F_1(\beta/2,\beta/2,\beta/2,x)
With F being the hypergeometric function
In d=4:
g_{\Delta,l} (z,\bar{z}) = \frac{z\bar{z}}{z-\bar{z}}\left(K_{\Delta+l}(z)K_{\Delta-l-2}(\bar{z}) + \textrm {switch }(z,\bar{z})\right)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Cotangent fields
Cotangent manifolds
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Similarly to tangent manifolds, taking the union of all cotangent spaces \mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M} of a manifold \mathcal{M} we get the cotangent manifold of \mathcal{M}:
\mathcal{T}^*\mathcal{M} \coloneqq \bigcup_{p\in\mathcal{M}} \mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Cotangent spaces
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Cotangent spaces \mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M} to a manifold \mathcal{M} at a point p are a complementary notion to the one of tangent spaces \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}, which send vectors into scalars:
\omega_p \in\mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M}
\omega_p:\mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathbb{R}
They represent the space of a linear functions acting on \mathcal{T}_p \mathcal{M}:
V_p,W_p \in \mathcal{T} _p \mathcal{M},\qquad \lambda \in \mathbb{R},
\omega_p(V_p+W_p) = \omega_p (V_p)+\omega_p(W_p)
\omega_p(\lambda V_p) = \lambda\omega_p(V_p)
\omega_p is either called cotangent vector, dual vector or one-form.
By linearity we get that:
V_p = V^\mu e_\mu
\omega_p (V_p) = V^\mu \omega_p (e_\mu)
Considering that the \omega_p (e_\mu) \coloneqq \omega_\mu shold be the components of \omega_p, we can define the basis of the dual space:
\omega_p = \omega _\mu dx^\mu\qquad dx^\mu (e_\nu) \coloneqq \delta_\nu^\mu
so that:
\omega_p (V_p) = V^\mu \omega_\mu
How do dual vectors transform under change of basis?


                  
                  Change of basis 
                  
                

Assume that the dual basis transforms according to some \tensor{M}{{^\mu}{_\nu}}:
dx'^\mu \coloneqq\tensor{M}{{^\mu}{_\nu}}dx^\nu
then, consider the transformation rules for the vector basis:
e'_\mu = \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'_\mu}e_\nu
we then take the Kronecker delta and apply the previous identities:
\tensor{\delta}{{^\mu}{_\nu}} = dx'^\mu (e'_\nu) = \frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}\tensor{M}{{^\mu}{_\sigma}}dx^\sigma(e_\rho) = \frac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\nu}\tensor{M}{{^\mu}{_\rho}}
Therefore:
\tensor{M}{{^\mu}{_\rho}} = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\rho}


dx'^\mu = \frac{\partial x'^\mu}{\partial x^\nu}dx^\nu
which makes sense if we understand the dx^\mu as differentials.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Differentiable curves
Differentiable manifolds
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
An object \mathcal{M} is an m-dimensional differentiable manifold if:

\mathcal{M} is a topological space
\mathcal{M} has a family (called atlas) of pairs (called charts) \left\{(u_A,\varphi _A)\right\}_A such that:

Each u_A (called neighborhoods) is an open subset of \mathcal{M} and their union covers the entire \mathcal{M}:
u_A\subset \mathcal{M}, \qquad \bigcup_{A}\, u_A = \mathcal{M}

The \varphi _A (called coordinate functions) are homeomorphisms which map a subset u_A into a subset of \mathbb{R}^m:
\varphi_A :u_A\mapsto u'_A\subset\mathbb{R}^m

If the intersection of two neighborhoods is not empty, then there exist differentiable maps that bring the coordinate maps applied on the intersection into one another:
\begin{gather}
u_A\cap u_B\neq0\\
\Downarrow\\
\exists\, \psi _{AB}:\varphi_B(u_A\cap u_B)\mapsto\varphi_A(u_A\cap u_B),\quad\psi_{AB}\in C^1
\end{gather}
these maps are changes of coordinates.
x = \varphi_A(p),\, y = \varphi_B(p)\Rightarrow x(y) =\psi_{AB} (y)




Differentiable structures
If an atlas encompasses all compatible charts, it becomes a differentiable structure of \mathcal{M}.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Differentiable maps
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Given a map between manifolds
f:\mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathcal{N}
we say that f is differentiable if, for each p\in\mathcal{M} mapped into f(p)\in\mathcal{N} and charts:
(u,\varphi) \textrm{ of }\mathcal{M}: p\in u,
(u',\varphi ') \textrm{ of }\mathcal{N}: f(p)\in u',
then:
\varphi'\circ f\circ\varphi^{-1}\in C^1.
This means that, given the coordinates:
x^\mu \coloneqq (\varphi (p))^\mu, \qquad \mu = 1,...,m,
y^\alpha \coloneqq (\varphi' (p))^\alpha, \qquad \alpha = 1,...,n,
We have the mapping:
y(x) = \varphi '\circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}(x)
These differentiable maps f‘s are sometimes called smooth
Diffeomorphisms
If m=n and \exists f^{-1} then the f‘s are called diffeomorphisms. Two manifold are called diffeomorphic if there exists a diffeomorphism connecting them
Change of bases

If \mathcal{M}=\mathcal{N} and f is the identity transformation, we are encoding a local change of basis, which is differentiable as seen in Differentiable manifolds:
y(x) = \varphi '\circ\varphi ^{-1}(x)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Differential geometry/Differentiable scalar functions.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Differentiable scalar functions
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
We say that a function f which maps a point on a manifold \mathcal{M}, with a chart (u,\varphi), to a scalar,
f:\mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathbb{R},
is differentiable if:
f\circ\varphi ^{-1}\in C^1.
By abuse of notation, usually f\circ \varphi^{-1} (x) \sim f(x) which works conceptually locally once a chart is specified.
Space of scalar functions
We denote the space of scalar differentiable functions:
\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}] \coloneqq\left\{f:\mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, f\textrm{ differentiable}\right\}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Exponential maps
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
We can summarize the action and the properties of the flow by redefining it in a smart way. First, we notice that:
\sigma ^\mu (t,x_0) = \sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}\left.\frac{1}{n!}\frac{d^n}{ds^n}\sigma(s,x_0)\right|_{s=0} t^n = \left.\exp\left[t\frac{d}{ds}\right]\sigma(s,x_0)\right|_{s=0}
Since the derivative of the flow is the vector field V that defines it, we could try and redefine the flow as:
\sigma^\mu (t,x_0) \coloneqq \exp\left[tV\right]x_0^\mu
We need to verify that this definitions satisfies the right equations and boundary conditions:
\left.\vphantom{\sum}\exp\left[tV\right]x_0^\mu\right|_{t=0} = x_0^\mu\qquad \exp\left[0\cdot V\right] = \id
\frac{d}{dt} \exp\left[tV\right]x_0^\mu = V\left(\exp\left[tV\right]x_0^\mu\right)
we also verify the composition property:
\exp\left[(t+s)V\right]x_0^\mu = \exp\left[tV\right]\circ\exp\left[sV\right]x_0^\mu

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Exterior product
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
We introduce the exterior (wedge) product \wedge operation which acts on elements of the dual basis:
dx^{\mu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _p} \coloneqq \frac{1}{p!} \sum _{\Pi} (-1)^{\mathrm{sign}(\Pi)} dx^{\Pi (\mu_1)}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\Pi (\mu_p)}
where the \Pi‘s are permutations. By definition, the wedge product is anticommutative under permutation of two elements:
 ...\wedge dx^{\mu _l}\wedge dx^{\mu _{l+1}}\wedge ... = - ...\wedge dx^{\mu _{l+1}}\wedge dx^{\mu _{l}}\wedge ...
Exterior product of forms
We can define the wedge product of two forms:
\omega\in \Omega^r[\mathcal{M}] \quad \xi\in \Omega^s[\mathcal{M}]
\bullet\wedge\bullet :\Omega^r[\mathcal{M}]\times \Omega^s[\mathcal{M}]\mapsto\Omega^{r+s}[\mathcal{M}]
\zeta \equiv \omega\wedge\xi = \frac{1}{r!s!} \omega_{\mu_1...\mu_r}\xi_{\nu_1...\nu_s}dx^{\mu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _r}\wedge dx^{\nu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _s}
Since:
\zeta \equiv \frac{1}{(r+s)!}\zeta_{\mu_1...\mu_r\nu_1...\nu_{s}}dx^{\mu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _r}\wedge dx^{\nu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _s}
we have that:
\zeta_{\mu_1...\mu_r\nu_1...\nu_{s}} = \frac{(r+s)!}{r!s!}\omega_{[\mu_1...\mu_r}\xi_{\nu_1...\nu_s]}
See here for notation details.
We also find that:
\omega\wedge\xi = (-1)^{rs}\xi\wedge\omega

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Forms
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Forms, or q-forms if we are specifying their type, are fully antisymmetric (0,q) tensors which are defined through the wedge product:
\omega\in \mathcal{T}_p^{(0,q)}\mathcal{M} 
\omega\coloneqq \omega_{\mu_1 ...\mu_q} (dx^{\mu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _q})
Of course, we could also expand the definition of forms to tensor fields:
\omega\in \Omega^q[\mathcal{M} ]
\omega\coloneqq \omega_{\mu_1 ...\mu_q} (dx^{\mu _1}\wedge ...\wedge dx^{\mu _q})
The action of forms on elements of the tangent basis is:
\omega (e_{\mu_1},...,e_{\mu_q}) =  \frac{\omega_{\mu_1,...,\mu_q}}{p!} \sum _{\Pi} (-1)^{\mathrm{sign}(\Pi)} dx^{\Pi (\mu_1)}(e_{\mu_1})\otimes...\otimes dx^{\Pi (\mu_q)}(e_{\mu_1})
\omega (e_{\mu_1},...,e_{\mu_q}) = \frac{\omega_{\mu_1,...,\mu_q}}{p!} \sum _{\Pi} (-1)^{\mathrm{sign}(\Pi)} \delta^{\Pi (\mu_1)}_{\mu_1}\times ...\times \delta^{\Pi (\mu_q)}_{\mu_q}
Since the form is antisymmetric:
\omega (e_{\mu_1},...,e_{\mu_q}) =\omega_{\mu_1,...,\mu_q}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Homeomorphisms
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content: A homeomorphism is a bijective and continuous function between topological spaces that has a continuous inverse function.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Inner products
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
We can define an inner product on a manifold by applying a one-form \omega_p to a vector V_p (the inner product is local):
\corr{\,\bullet, \bullet\,}:\mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathbb{R}
\corr{\omega_p, V_p}\coloneqq \omega_p (V_p)
which reduces to the usual contraction of components:
\corr{\omega_p, V_p} = \omega_\mu V^\mu
Extension to tensors
We could expand the definition of inner product to admit any possible contractions of (0,q) and (q,0) tensors or tensor fields:
\omega \in\mathcal{T}_p^{(0,q)}\mathcal{M} , \quad V\in \mathcal{T}_p^{(q,0)}\mathcal{M},
\corr{\omega,V} = \omega_{\mu_1,...,\mu_q}V^{\mu_1,...,\mu_q}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Integral curves
Lie derivatives
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Take two tangent fields V,W\in \mathfrak{X}[\mathcal{M}] of a manifold \mathcal{M}, which map to the elements V_p, W_p of the tangent spaces \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M} at a point p; then, consider the flow \sigma_t generated by V. We define the Lie derivative of W with respect to V computed at point p.
\mathcal{L}: \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}
\left.\vphantom{\sum}\mathcal{L}_V W\right|_{x =\varphi(p)} \coloneqq \lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0^+} \frac{1}{\epsilon}\left(\left.\vphantom{\sum}\left(\sigma _{-\epsilon}\right)_* W\right|_{\sigma_\epsilon(x)} - \left.\vphantom{\sum}W\right|_{x}\right)
where \left(\sigma _{-\epsilon}\right)_* is the pushforward map defined by the flow at fixed time and (u,\varphi) is a valid chart at point p.
The action on the elements of W can be obtained by expanding each term at first order:


                  
                  Computations 
                  
                

For small \epsilon:
\sigma ^\mu (\epsilon,x) \simeq \sigma ^\mu (0,x) + \epsilon \left.\frac{d}{dt}\sigma ^\mu (t,x)\right|_{t=0} = x^\mu +\epsilon V^\mu
x'^\mu \simeq x^\mu +\epsilon V^\mu
The basis of the tangent space changes according to:
e'_\mu = \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'^\mu}e_\nu \simeq \left(\delta^\nu_\mu - \epsilon\partial _\mu V^\nu\right)e_\nu
The vector W at x' is:
\left.\vphantom{\sum}W\right|_{x'} \simeq \left.\vphantom{\sum}W^\mu \right|_{x+\epsilon V}  e'_\mu \simeq \left(W^\mu +\epsilon V^\nu\partial _\nu W^\mu\right)\left(\delta^\rho_\mu - \epsilon\partial _\mu V^\rho\right)e_\rho
\left.\vphantom{\sum}W\right|_{x'} \simeq W^\mu e_\mu + \epsilon\left(V^\nu \partial _\nu W^\mu e_\mu - W^\mu\partial _\mu V^\nu e_\nu\right)


\left.\vphantom{\sum}\mathcal{L}_V W\right|_{x} =\left(V^\nu\partial_\nu W^\mu - W^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu\right)e_\mu 
Lie brackets
We can denote a Lie derivative using Lie brackets:
\left[\,\bullet,\bullet\,\right]: \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}
[X,Y] \coloneqq X\circ Y - Y\circ X
In general, for a function f\in\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}], X(Y(f)) does not act as an element of the tangent space as the operation involves second derivatives; however, expanding the Lie brackets we find that they reduce to Lie derivatives:
[X,Y] (f) = [\mathcal{L}_X Y] (f)
[X,Y] = \mathcal{L}_X Y
Properties
Lie brackets satisfy the following properties:

Antisymmetry:
[V,W] = - [W,V]

Bilinearity, take \lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\mathbb{R}:
[V,\lambda_1W_1+\lambda_2W_2] = \lambda_1[V,W_1] +\lambda_2 [V,W_2]
[\lambda_1 V_1 + \lambda_2 V_2 ,W] = \lambda_1[V_1,W] + \lambda _2 [V_2,W]

Take f\in\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}]:
[V,fW] = V(f)W +[V,W]
\mathcal{L}_V(fW) = V(f) W +\mathcal{L}_V W

Bianchi identity:
[[V,W],Z]+[[W,Z],V]+[[Z,V],W]=0


Geometric interpretation
TODO add drawing
The Lie derivative encodes the non-commutativity of two flows; stopping at second order:
\sigma ^\mu (t,x) \simeq x^\mu + tV^\mu +\frac{t^2}{2}V^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu
\tau ^\mu (t,x) = x^\mu + tW^\mu+\frac{t^2}{2}W^\nu\partial _\nu W^\mu
Note that first order and non-mixed second order terms are going to cancel out during computation:
\begin{split}
\tau ^\mu (\delta,\sigma(\epsilon ,x)) \simeq \hphantom{\sum}& \left(x^\mu + \epsilon V^\mu +\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}V^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu\right)\\
+&\left(\delta W^\mu+\delta\epsilon V^\nu\partial _\nu W^\mu +\frac{\delta^2}{2} W^\nu\partial _\nu W^\mu\right)
\end{split}
\begin{split}
\sigma ^\mu (\epsilon,\tau(\delta ,x)) \simeq \hphantom{\sum}& \left(x^\mu + \delta W^\mu +\frac{\delta^2}{2}W^\nu\partial _\nu W^\mu\right)\\
+&\left(\epsilon V^\mu+\delta\epsilon W^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu +\frac{\epsilon^2}{2} V^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu\right)
\end{split}
Therefore:
\tau ^\mu (\delta,\sigma(\epsilon ,x))- \sigma ^\mu (\epsilon,\tau(\delta ,x)) = \delta\epsilon[V,W]^\mu
\tau ^\mu (\delta,\sigma(\epsilon ,x))- \sigma ^\mu (\epsilon,\tau(\delta ,x)) = \delta\epsilon(\mathcal{L}_VW)^\mu
Extensions to other objects
Action on vector basis
Starting from
\mathcal{L}_V W =\left(V^\nu\partial_\nu W^\mu - W^\nu\partial _\nu V^\mu\right)e_\mu 
We try to find the action of the Lie derivative on the elements of the vector basis by considering its action on the vector with components W^\nu = 1 if \nu =\mu and 0 elsewhere:
\mathcal{L}_V e_\mu = -\partial _\mu V^\rho e_\rho
(\mathcal{L}_V e_\mu)^\rho = -\partial _\mu V^\rho
Extension to functions
Take f\in\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}]; we define its Lie derivative as
\mathcal{L}_Vf \coloneqq V(f)
Which somewhat agrees with \mathcal{L}_V(fW) = V(f) W +\mathcal{L}_V W
Extension to forms
The inner product defined on fields is basically a scalar function; following this notion, we try to extend the Lie derivative to one-forms starting from:
\mathcal{L}_V\corr{\omega,W} = V\left(\vphantom{\sum}\corr{\omega,W}\vphantom{\sum}\right)
Then we define the chain rule:
\mathcal{L}_V\corr{\omega,W} = (\mathcal{L}_V \omega)_\mu W^\mu  +\omega _\mu (\mathcal{L}_V W)^\mu
Then, gathering the correct terms:
(\mathcal{L}_V \omega)_\mu= \omega_\nu \partial _\mu V^\nu +V^\nu\partial _\nu \omega_\mu
\mathcal{L}_V \omega= (\omega_\nu \partial _\mu V^\nu +V^\nu\partial _\nu \omega_\mu)dx^\mu
Action on dual basis
Taking \omega_\nu =1 if \nu =\mu and 0 elsewhere, we get the action of the Lie derivative on the dual basis:
\mathcal{L}_V dx^\mu= (\partial _\rho V^\mu)dx^\rho
(\mathcal{L}_V dx^\mu)_\rho= \partial _\rho V^\mu
Extension to tensors
We can derive the action of the Lie derivative on any tensor by applying the chain rule to any product and tensor product: in fact, any tensor is basically the product of a function with the tensor product of the bases of the tangent and cotangent spaces
T = \tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}
Then, the Lie derivative on T acts as follows:
\begin{split}
\mathcal{L}_VT = &\hphantom{+} (\mathcal{L}_V\tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}})\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}\\
&+ \tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,(\mathcal{L}_Ve_{\mu_1})\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}\\
&+... \\
&+ \tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes (\mathcal{L}_Ve_{\mu_q})\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}\\
&+\tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes (\mathcal{L}_Vdx^{\nu_1})\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}\\
&+...\\
&+\tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes (\mathcal{L}_Vdx^{\nu_r})
\end{split}
Example: metrics
Take the tensor:
h = h_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu\otimes dx^\nu
Applying the chain rule we obtain:
\mathcal{L}_Vh = \left(V^\rho \partial _\rho h_{\mu\nu} +h_{\rho\nu}\partial _\mu V^\rho +h_{\mu\rho}\partial _\nu V^\rho\right)dx^\mu\otimes dx ^\nu

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Pullback map
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Let f:\mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathcal{N} be a differentiable map; we can define the differentiable pullback map f^* which maps the cotangent space of the manifold \mathcal{N} at f(p) to the cotangent space of \mathcal{M} at p:
f^* : \mathcal{T}^*_{f(p)}\mathcal{N}\mapsto\mathcal{T}_p ^* \mathcal{M}
The pullback map acts on dual vectors according to the following relation of inner products, which uses the concept of pushforward maps f_*:
\corr{f^*\omega_{f(p)},V_p} \coloneqq\corr{\omega_{f(p)},f_* V_p}
So that the components of the pulled-back dual vector are:
[f^*\omega_{f(p)}]_\mu = \frac{\partial y^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}\omega_\alpha
Invertibility
Since if f is not a diffeomorphism the transformation \frac{\partial y^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu} cannot be inverted, vectors can only be pushed-forward and dual vectors can only be pulled-back.
Composition rules
(g\circ f)^* = f^*\circ g^*

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Pushforward maps
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Let f:\mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathcal{N} be a differentiable map; we can define the differentiable pushforward map f_* which maps the tangent space of the manifold \mathcal{M} at p to the tangent space of \mathcal{N} at f(p):
f_* :\mathcal{T}_{p}\mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathcal{T}_{f(p)}\mathcal{N}
Given a function g:\mathcal{N}\mapsto\mathbb{R}, pushforward maps act on vectors as follows:
[f_*V_p] (g) = V_{p}(g\circ f)
Note that [f_*V_p] is a vector acting f(p) in the tangent space \mathcal{T}_{f(p)}\mathcal{N}.
How do the vector elements change? We take the charts:
(u,\varphi)\qquad \varphi(p) \coloneqq x
(u',\varphi')\qquad \varphi'(f(p)) \coloneqq y
then, using:
\varphi'\circ f\circ \varphi ^{-1} (x) = y(x)
and:
V_p[g\circ f] = V^\mu\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}(g\circ\varphi'^{-1}(y(x)))= (f_* V_p) ^\alpha\frac{\partial}{\partial y^\alpha} g(\varphi'^{-1}(y))
we obtain:
(f_* V_p) ^\alpha = \frac{\partial y^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu}V^\mu
This notion can easily be extended to tensors in \mathcal{T}_p ^{(q,0)}\mathcal{M}
Invertibility
Since if f is not a diffeomorphism the transformation \frac{\partial y^\alpha}{\partial x^\mu} cannot be inverted, vectors can only be pushed-forward and dual vectors can only be pulled-back.
Composition rules
(g\circ f)_* = g_*\circ f_*

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Tangent fields
Tangent manifolds
Tangent spaces
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
The tangent space to a manifold \mathcal{M} at a point p is denoted by \mathcal{T}_p \mathcal{M}.
We define it by defining the properties of its elements V_p\in\mathcal{T}_p \mathcal{M}; take two differentiable scalar functions f,g,\in\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}], then:
V_p:\mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}]\mapsto \mathbb{R}
has the following properties:

Chain rule:
V_p(f\cdot g) = V_p(f)\cdot g(p) + f(p)\cdot V_p(g)

Linearity:
V_p(f+g) = V_p(f) + V_p(g)
    V_p(\lambda f) = \lambda V_p (f)\quad \lambda\in\mathbb{R}


These are the same properties satisfied by derivatives.
Take a chart (u,\varphi) so that \varphi (p) = x^\mu; then, we get a basis for the tangent space:
\left\{e_\mu\right\}_\mu \coloneqq \left\{\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}\right|_{p=\varphi^{-1}(x)}\right\}_\mu
So that any local vector can be defined as:
V_p = V^\mu e_\mu,\qquad V^\mu\in \mathbb{R},\,\forall\mu
These vectors act on scalar functions as:
V_p(f) = V^\mu \left.\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{-1}(x)\right)}{\partial x^\mu}\right|_{p=\varphi^{-1}(x)}
Change of basis
In the presence of two charts (u,\varphi), (u',\varphi ') such that:
p\in u\cap u',
see change of bases, then a vector V_p\in \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M} can be expressed in two bases:
V_p(f) = V^\mu \left.\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{-1}(x)\right)}{\partial x^\mu}\right|_{p}= V^{\prime\mu}\left.\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{\prime-1}(x')\right)}{\partial x^{\prime\mu}}\right|_{p}
Using x'(x) = \varphi'\circ\varphi^{-1}(x):
V^{\prime\mu}\left.\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{\prime-1}(x')\right)}{\partial x^{\prime\mu}}\right|_{p} = V^{\prime\mu}\left.\frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x^{\prime \mu}}\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{-1}(x)\right)}{\partial x^{\nu}}\right|_{p} = V^\mu \left.\frac{\partial f\left(\varphi^{-1}(x)\right)}{\partial x^\mu}\right|_{p}
we find that the vector components transform as a traditional vector:
V^{\prime\mu} = \frac{\partial x^{\prime\mu}}{\partial x^\nu}V^\nu
Equivalently, the vector basis transforms according to:
e'_\mu = \frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'_\mu}e_\nu
Alternative definition
We could also define tangent spaces as the equivalence class of all directional derivatives \frac{d}{dt} for a given curve C(t) passing through p at t=0, so that:
\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = \left.V^\mu \frac{\partial}{\partial x ^\mu}\right|_{p}\qquad p =C(0)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Tensor fields
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Similarly to tangent fields, tensor fields T map a manifold into the corresponding tensor manifold:
T: \mathcal{M}\mapsto \mathcal{T}^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M}
We can define the set of all tensor fields:
\mathfrak{X}^{(q,r)}[\mathcal{M}] \coloneqq\left\{T: \mathcal{M}\mapsto\mathcal{T}^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M}\right\}
Note that:

\mathfrak{X}^{(1,0)}[\mathcal{M}]= \mathfrak{X}[\mathcal{M}] are the tangent fields
\mathfrak{X}^{(0,1)}[\mathcal{M}] = \Omega^1[\mathcal{M}] are the cotangent fields
\mathfrak{X}^{(0,0)}[\mathcal{M}] = \mathfrak{F}[\mathcal{M}] are the scalar fields

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Tensor manifolds
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
Tensor manifolds for a manifold \mathcal{M} at a point p are an extension of the tangent manifolds to the tensor case:
\mathcal{T}^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M}\coloneqq\bigcup_{p\in\mathcal{M}}\mathcal{T}_p^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.title: Tensor spaces
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Differential-ge.content:
We introduce a (q,r)-type tensor T_P in a tensor space \mathcal{T}_p^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M}, defined at a point p of a manifold \mathcal{M}, as an element of a specific tensor product of tangent spaces and cotangent spaces:
T_P\in\mathcal{T}_p^{(q,r)}\mathcal{M} =\left(\bigotimes_{q\textrm{ times}} \mathcal{T}_p\mathcal{M}\right)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{r\textrm{ times}} \mathcal{T}^*_p\mathcal{M}\right)
T_P = \tensor{T}{{^{\mu_1...\mu_q}}{_{\nu_1...\nu_r}}}\,\,e_{\mu_1}\otimes...\otimes e_{\mu_q}\otimes dx^{\nu_1}\otimes...\otimes dx^{\nu_r}
The pair (q,r) is called rank of the tensor.

Taking q=1,r=0 we get tangent spaces
Taking q=0,r=1 we get cotangent spaces
Taking q=0,r=0 we get scalars

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Dilation-eigenv.title: Dilation eigenvalue
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Dilation-eigenv.content:
The eigenvalue of the dilation generator:
\comm{D}{\phi _\alpha (0)} = i\Delta _\phi \phi _\alpha (0)
is the energy dimension of the field. In fact, taking the dilation transformation:
x^\mu \mapsto \lambda x^\mu \simeq (1+\epsilon)x^\mu
\epsilon \simeq \lambda -1
When acting on operators:
O^I\mapsto O^{\prime I} = e^{i (\lambda-1)D}O^Ie^{-i (\lambda-1)D}\simeq O^I +i\epsilon \comm{D}{O^I}\simeq O^I -\epsilon \Delta _O O^I
Now, to first order, this is equivalent to the expansion of:
\lambda ^{-\Delta _O} O
So the \Delta _O is the dimension in inverse length (i.e. energy, see Energy dimensions)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Embedding-forma.title: Embedding formalism
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Embedding-forma.content:
The conformal group is isomorphic to SO(d+1,1) in euclidean metric, see here for details, the embedding space is:
\mathbb{R} ^{d+1,1}\supset\mathbb{R} ^{d}
By looking at the conformal transformations on the embedding space, which should look like Lorentz transformation, and then only considering the relevant subspace, we should be able to reduce the complexity of studying the conformal representations.
Coordinates in the embedding space are denoted by:
P^A\in\mathbb{R} ^{d+1,1}
x^\mu\in\mathbb{R} ^{d}
Define lightcone coordinates:
P^A = P^A_{lc} \equiv (P^+,P^-,P^\mu)
P^\pm \equiv P^{d+2} \pm P^{d+1}
ds^2 = dP^\mu dP_\mu - dP^+dP^-
The associated metric is:
\eta _{lc}\sim\left(\begin{array}{c|c}
\begin{array}{cc}0 & -\frac{1}{2}\\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{array}&0\\
\hline
0&\begin{array}{ccc}1 &&\\ &\ddots&\\ &&1\end{array}
\end{array}\right)
So that:
P_1\cdot P_2 = P_{1 \,\mu}P^\mu _2 - \frac{1}{2} (P_1^+ P_2^- + P_1^- P_2^+)
Now, SO(d+1,1) acts trivially on P^A:
P^A\mapsto P^{\prime A} =  R^A_BP^B
we want to find the transformation rules for x from this relation. In order to do so, we need to identify the correct relevant subspace of the embedding space. This subspace is d-dimensional and needs to be invariant under rotations (otherwise these transformations would potentially send a point of the subspace into another point outside of it).

Consider the null hyperbole:
I \equiv \left\{P^A\in \mathbb{R}^{d+1,1}: P^2 = 0\right\}
This subspace is clearly left invariant by rotations. Then, consider the rays on the hyperbole (projective space):
\lambda P^A\quad \lambda \neq 0\land P^A \in I
Call this class \lambda, then we suppose we can identify our target subspace \mathbb{R}^d with basically any “section” in the hyperbole (see Quotient set):
\mathbb{R} ^d \leftrightarrow I_{/\lambda}
We choose a representative for the class by fixing the first element and last d elements; the remaining element is fixed by lying on the hyperbole:
P^A_{ps} = (1,x^2,x^\mu)
The set of points in this form is called Poincaré section (red in the image).
Under rotations, a point in the Poincaré section might end up outside of it, but then we can rescale (thanks to focusing on equivalence classes) to return inside the section.
P^A _{ps}\overset{R\in SO(d+1,1)}{\mapsto} P^{\prime A}=\tensor{R}{{^A}{_B}}P^B_{ps}
Rescaling:
P^{\prime A}_{ps} = \frac{P^{\prime A}}{P^{\prime +}} = (1, x'^2,x^{\prime \mu})
Now we claim that:
x^{ \mu} \mapsto x^{\prime \mu}
is a conformal transformation.
Extension to fields
Scalars
Denote fields lying in the embedding space as \Phi and fields lying in the original space as \phi. We require two properties for \Phi:
\Phi (P^A):\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\Phi (P^A _{ps} = (1,x^2,x^\mu)) = \phi (x^\mu)\\
\Phi (\lambda P^A) = \lambda ^{-\Delta _\phi}\Phi (P^A)
\end{array}\right.
Tensors
Consider a class of tensors present in any dimensions: Traceless Symmetric Tensors (TST)
t^{\mu _1 ...\mu _l}\quad\textrm{rank-}l \,\textrm { TST of }\, SO(d)
symmetrized and traceless.
We want to associate t to a T defined in the embedding space on the projective null hyperboloid.
T:\left\{\begin{array}{l}
T^{A_1,...,A_l} \quad \textrm{TST of }SO(d+1,1)\\
T^{A_1,...,A_l} (\lambda P) = \frac{1}{\lambda ^{\Delta _t}}T^{A_1,...,A_l} (P)\\
\textrm{transversality: } P_{A_i}T^{A_1,...,A_l}(P) = 0 \quad\forall i=1,...,l\\
t^{\mu _1 ...\mu _l}(x) = \left. \left(\frac{\partial P _{A_1}}{\partial x_{\mu _1}}\right)...\left(\frac{\partial P _{A_l}}{\partial x_{\mu _l}}\right)T^{A_1,...,A_l}\right|_{P_{ps}}
\end{array}\right.
The transversality property ensures we’re encoding a field living in the tangent space to the projective lightcone; note that:
\left(\frac{\partial P _{A}}{\partial x_{\mu }}\right)_{P_{ps}} = (0,2x^\mu,\delta ^\mu _\nu)
so that:
\left. P^A\left(\frac{\partial P _{A}}{\partial x_{\mu }}\right)\right|_{P_{ps}} = 0
This induces a sort of gauge invariace, killing longitudinal polarizations (see Index Notation):
T^{A_1,...,A_l} \sim T^{A_1,...,A_l} + P^{(A_1}Q^{A_2,...,A_l)}
The extra terms are killed by transversality.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/General-Relativ.content:

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Generalized-Fre.title: Generalized Free Theories
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Generalized-Fre.content:
Free theories
Consider the simplest free CFT:
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2}\phi \square\phi
where \phi is a primary operator whose dimension is \Delta _\phi = \frac{d-2}{2}, which implies that the theory has a unitary representation in Minkowskian signature (but does not necessarily means that the theory is unitary).
Since we have conformal symmetry, we can fix some correlation functions, up to the 3PF (constants aside):
\corr{\phi(x_1)} =0
\corr{\phi(x_1)\phi (x_2)} =\frac{1}{X_{12} ^{2\Delta _\phi}}
\corr{\phi(x_1)\phi (x_2)\phi (x_3)} =0
Operators
We want to define operators organized in terms of primaries and descendants.
First, we introduce normal ordering:
\normalorder{\theta(x)} \equiv \theta (x) - \corr{\theta (x)}
which, in terms of ladder operators, corresponds to bringing all the annihilators on the right and all the creators on the left.
Then, we can construct operators in the form of powers of normal ordered operators:
\theta ^{(n)} (x) \sim \normalorder{\phi ^n (x)}
We can also construct derivatives of operators; we need to be careful here because we may end up in a descendant, while for now we are only working on primaries. For instance, take a local current:
\normalorder{\phi (x) \partial _\mu \phi (x)} = \frac{1}{2}\partial _\mu (\normalorder{\phi(x)^2})
$$This is a descendant.
>[!note]
> 
>In general, total derivatives of operators are descendants.

We can try combinations of spin-2 candidates to obtain a primary operator:

\phi \partial _\mu\partial _\nu\phi

\partial _\mu\phi \partial _\nu\phi

\eta _{\mu\nu}\phi 
It turns out that the corresponding primary is the [[Stress tensor|stress tensor]].
#### OPE
Take the [[Operator Product Expansion|OPE]]:
\phi 1(P_1)\phi 2(P_2)\sim\sum{\phi_k}C ^{\phi_k}{\phi _1,\phi 2}(X{12},\partial _2)\phi_k (x_2)
The operator $C$ is completely determined in CFT up to a certain constant. For a free theory this holds at operator level, not just inside correlation functions
\begin{split}
\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2) &= \normalorder{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)} + \frac{1}{X_{12} ^{2\Delta \phi}}\id \
&= \frac{1}{X{12} ^{2\Delta \phi}}\id +\sum{n}\frac{1}{n!}X_{12}^{\mu 1}…X{12}^{\mu _n}\normalorder{\phi (x_1)\partial _{\mu_1}…\partial _{\mu_n}\phi(x_1)}
\end{split}
we can kind of see the OPE structure emerging. There can only be traceless symmetric tensor inside the expansion. We also note that an operator $O$ appears in the OPE of $\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)$ if and only if their 3PF is non zero:
O(y)\subset\mathrm{OPE}\left[\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)\right]\Leftrightarrow\corr{O(y)\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}\neq 0
All the rest is computed employing [[Wick's theorem]]
E.G.
\corr{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)\normalorder{\frac{\phi^2(x_3)}{\sqrt{2}}}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{X_{13}^{2\Delta}X_{23}^{2\Delta}}

\corr{\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)\normalorder{\frac{\phi^2(x_3)}{\sqrt{2}}}} = \frac{\lambda_{\phi\phi\phi^2}}{X_{12}^{2h_{123} }X_{23}^{2h_{231}}X_{13}^{2h_{132}}}
This allows us to determine the coefficient $\lambda$.
## Generalized Free Theories (GFT's)
GFT's are built up starting from a [[Primary operators|primary]] elementary field $O_{\Delta, r} ^I$:
\comm{K_\mu}{O_{\Delta, r} ^I(0)} = 0

\Downarrow

\corr{O_{\Delta, r} ^I(x_1) O_{\Delta, r} ^J(x_2)} = \frac{T^{IJ}(X_{12})}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}}\overset{\textrm{scalars}}{\longrightarrow}\frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}}
where we impose diagonal [[Correlation functions from embedding formalism#2-point-functions|2PF]]'s and that 1PF's are 0.
Normal free theories have a fixed dimensionality which saturates the [[Unitarity bounds|unitarity bound]].
\Delta = \Delta_{min} = \frac{d-2}{2}
For bigger dimensionalities, we cannot associate the theory to free bosons but it will still contain a unitary representation of conformal symmetries; these are the GFT's. We compute [[Correlation functions|correlation functions]] using [[Wick's theorem|Wick's contractions]]; for $n$ operators:
\corr{O_{\Delta,r}(x_1)O_{\Delta,r}(x_2)…O_{\Delta,r}(x_n)}
If $n$ is odd:
![[WickContraction0.svg]]
For $n$ even the contraction will be non 0. ==This also implies that the theory does not present interactions==.
EG $n=4$, $r= 0$ (scalars):
\corr{O_{\Delta}(x_1)O_{\Delta}(x_2)O_{\Delta}(x_3)O_{\Delta}(x_4)}
We have to perform the Wick contractions:
![[WickScalar4pf.svg]]
So that:
\corr{O_{\Delta}(x_1)O_{\Delta}(x_2)O_{\Delta}(x_3)O_{\Delta}(x_4)} = \frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}\left(
1

\frac{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}{X_{13}^{2\Delta}X_{24}^{2\Delta}} + \frac{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}{X_{14}^{2\Delta}X_{23}^{2\Delta}}
\right)

We define this as:
\corr{O_{\Delta}(x_1)O_{\Delta}(x_2)O_{\Delta}(x_3)O_{\Delta}(x_4)} = \frac{1}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{34}^{2\Delta}}g(u,v)
where:
g(u,v) \equiv \left(1+u^\Delta +\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)^\Delta\right)

u \equiv \left(\frac{X_{12}X_{34}}{X_{13}X_{24}}\right)

v \equiv \left(\frac{X_{14}X_{23}}{X_{13}X_{24}}\right)
### Multi-trace operators
Composing elementary fields, we can produce so-called ==multi-trace (or multi-twist) operators== obtained by taking normal order of products of elementary fields with derivatives inserted somewhere, of the form:
\tilde{O}{\Delta’, r’} \sim\normalorder{O{\Delta, r} (x) \partial _{\mu _1}…\partial _{\mu l}\square ^n O{\Delta, r} (x) (x)}
this needs to be normal ordered (so that the 1PF is 0), an [[Irreducible representations|irrep]] of $SO(d)$ (TST) and a primary operator.
The dimensionality of these objects is given by
\Delta ’ = 2\Delta +l +2n
so that if $r=0$ (scalar) then $r'=l$.
### Correlation functions
We can compute correlation functions of mixtures of elements and composite elements, again by Wick contractions. Note that normal ordered products are already Wick contracted, so the contraction has to be done with elements outside the normal ordering. EG:
\corr{O_{\Delta} (x_1)O_{\Delta} (x_2)\normalorder{\frac{O_{\Delta} ^2(x_3)}{\sqrt{2}}}}
is contracted like this: 
![[Wickmixed.svg]]
And we get:
\corr{O_{\Delta} (x_1)O_{\Delta} (x_2)\normalorder{\frac{O_{\Delta} ^2(x_3)}{\sqrt{2}}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\times 2 \times \frac{1}{X_{12} ^{2\Delta}X_{23} ^{2\Delta}}
note that this means:
\corr{O_{\Delta} (x_1)O_{\Delta} (x_2)\normalorder{\frac{O_{\Delta} ^n(x_3)}{\sqrt{2}}}} = 0 \quad n>2
which [[Operator Product Expansion#properties|implies]]:
O_{\Delta} (x_1)\times O_{\Delta} (x_2)\supset\normalorder{O^2},\normalorder{O\partial^l \square^n O}

O_{\Delta} (x_1)\times O_{\Delta} (x_2)\nsupseteq\normalorder{O^n}
another example (each element needs to be selected twice)
\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\corr{\normalorder{O_{\Delta} ^2(x_1)}\normalorder{O_{\Delta} ^2(x_2)}\normalorder{O_{\Delta} ^2(x_3)}}\propto \frac{6}{X_{12}^{2\Delta}X_{23}^{2\Delta}X_{13}^{2\Delta}} \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}
and another
\corr{\normalorder{O^2}\normalorder{O^2}\normalorder{O^4}}\neq 0 \Rightarrow \normalorder{O^2}\times\normalorder{O^2}\supset\normalorder{O^4},\normalorder{O^2}
### Non locality
GFT's are inherently non-local, as explained [[Non locality of GFT's|here]].

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Highest-weight-.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Highest weight representations of the conformal group.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Highest-weight-.title: Highest weight representations of the conformal group
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Highest-weight-.content:
Highest weight representations for the conformal group are those where there exists a primary state \ket{\Delta} such that:
K^\mu \ket{\Delta} =0
D\ket{\Delta} = \Delta \ket{\Delta}
The other eigenstates are constructed applying the ladder operator P_\mu to the primary states; this adds a Lorentz index, which generally adds or reduces the spin by 1 (can’t be lower then 0). Non primary states are called descendants.

These representations of the conformal group are unitary in Lorentzian metric.
Since the conformal group is non compact, if the representation is unitary we won’t be able to find a state \ket{\Delta '} which gets annihilated by P_\mu:
\nexists \ket{\Delta '} : P_\mu\ket{\Delta '} = 0

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Index-Notation.title: Index Notation
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Index-Notation.content:
Types of indices

Greek indices for spacetime indices (tensor indices)
Lower-case latin indices for

spacelike components
local Lorentz components
group components (for gauge indexes)


Upper case latin indexes for spinor indexes
Dotted upper case latin indices for conjugate spinor indexes. Generally speaking, dotted indexes indicate complex conjugate indexes.
Upper index : Denotes the components of a vector, or a basis of dual vectors. Example : V^{\mu} is the components of a vector, d x^{\mu} is a basis of dual vectors, T_{\mu} d x^{\mu} is a dual vector.
Lower index : Denotes the components of a dual vector, or a basis of vectors. Example : T_{\mu} is the components of a dual vector, \partial x_{\mu} is a basis of vectors, V^{\mu} \partial x_{\mu} is a vector.

Operations on indices

Parenthesis : Denotes the symmetrization of a tensor with respect to those indices. That is, for n indices,
T_{\left(\right. \alpha \beta \gamma . . . \left.\right)} = \frac{1}{n !} \underset{p \in p e r m u t a t i o n s}{\sum} T_{p \left(\right. \alpha \beta \gamma . . . \left.\right)} .
Examples : T_{\left(\right. \alpha \beta \left.\right)} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\right. T_{\alpha \beta} + T_{\beta \gamma} \left.\right), p^{\left(\right. i} q^{j \left.\right)} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\right. p^{i} q^{j} + p^{j} q^{i} \left.\right). Note, in particular, that the parenthesis notation can span indices over multiple tensors.
Brackets : Denotes the antisymmetrization of a tensor with respect to those indices. That is, for n indices,
T_{\left[\right. \alpha \beta \gamma . . . \left]\right.} = \frac{1}{n !} \underset{p \in p e r m u t a t i o n s}{\sum} \left(-1\right)^{n_{p}} T_{p \left(\right. \alpha \beta \gamma . . . \left.\right)}
where n_{p} indicates the number of single permutations of p. Example :
T_{\left[\right. \alpha \beta \gamma \left]\right.} = \frac{1}{6} \left(\right. T_{\alpha \beta \gamma} - T_{\gamma \beta \alpha} + T_{\beta \gamma \alpha} - T_{\alpha \gamma \beta} + T_{\gamma \alpha \beta} - T_{\beta \alpha \gamma} \left.\right)
Like the parenthesis notation, it can span over multiple tensors. Example : f_{\left[\right. \alpha} g_{\beta \left]\right.} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\right. f_{\alpha} g_{\beta} - f_{\beta} g_{\alpha} \left.\right)
Comma : Denotes the partial derivative with respect to this component. Example : V^{\alpha}{}_{, \beta} = \partial_{\beta} V^{\alpha}
Semicolon : Denotes the covariant derivative with respect to this component. Example : V^{\alpha}{}_{; \beta} = \partial_{\beta} V^{\alpha} + \Gamma^{\alpha}{}_{\beta \gamma} V^{\gamma}

Less common

Pipe : Denotes the covariant derivative with respect to local Lorentz indices. Example : V^{a}{}_{\left|\right. i} = \partial_{i} V^{a} + \omega^{a}{}_{b i} V^{b}
Colon : Denotes the covariant derivative with the Levi-Civita connection. Example :
V^{\alpha}{}_{: \beta} =\sum_{\alpha , \beta , \gamma} \left(\right. \partial_{\alpha} V^{\alpha} + \left\{\right._{\beta \gamma}^{\alpha} \left.\right\} V^{\gamma} \left.\right)

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Non-locality-of.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Non locality of GFT's.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Non-locality-of.title: Non locality of GFT's
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Non-locality-of.content:
Example
Defining operators in Fourier space and going back, we define the Lagrangian:
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2} \phi \square^{1-p}\phi\quad p>0
By dimensional analysis, we demand:
[\mathcal{L}] = d
so:
2\Delta _\phi + 2(1-p) = d
\Delta _\phi  = \frac{d-2}{2} +p
Going to Fourier and back, we see that the fields are defined at different points → non locality.
We see here some correlation between non locality and the unitarity bounds not being saturated.
GFT’s
In GFT’s, we find a non local stress tensor. The most intuitive candidate would be:
\normalorder{O_\Delta \partial _{\mu }\partial _{\nu}O_\Delta}\sim t_{\mu\nu}
but it doesn’t have the right dimension d, in fact on the left-hand side, using the example above we get
2\Delta +2 = d+2p
This also means that the stress tensor does not enter in any OPE. In fact, the OPE of local operators only contains local operators ⇒ this stress tensor is disconnected from local operators.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Operator-Produc.title: Operator Product Expansion
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Operator-Produc.content:
The Operator Product Expansion (OPE) is a technique used in CFT inside a correlator to expand the product of two operators into a convergent sum of local operators applied to primaries.
O ^{I_1} _1(x_1)\overset{OPE}{\times}O^{I_2}_2(x_2)\overset{\textrm{inside corr.}}{\sim} \sum_{O_k \textrm{ primaries}}C ^{I_1 I_2}_{12;J}(X_{12},X_{23},\partial_3)O_k ^J(x_3)
Or, more conveniently for computations:
O ^{I_1} _1(x_1)\overset{OPE}{\times}O^{I_2}_2(x_2)\overset{\textrm{inside corr.}}{\sim} \sum_{O_k \textrm{ primaries}}C ^{I_1 I_2}_{12;J}(X_{12},\partial_2)O_k ^J(x_2)
The first equation is important as it shows that it is possible to perform OPE every time there exists a ball encapsulating x_1,x_2 and separates the corresponding operators from all the others.
Using the state-operator correspondence, this can be translated into:
\ket{\theta_1 \theta_2} = \sum _{\ket{\phi}\in\mathcal{H}}C_{\theta_1\theta_2\phi}(x)\ket{\phi} = \sum _{\textrm{primaries }\theta_k}\sum _{\textrm{desc } n}C(x)^{\mu_1,...\mu_n;IJ}_{\theta_1,\theta_2\theta _k}P_{\mu_1}...P_{\mu_n}\ket{\theta_k}
Properties

Convergent with finite radius
Valid inside path integral
The operator C is completely determined in CFTs up to some constant (see below)
An operator O appears in the OPE of \phi(x_1)\phi(x_2) if and only if their 3PF is non zero:

O(y)\subset\mathrm{OPE}\left[\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)\right]\Leftrightarrow\corr{O(y)\phi(x_1)\phi(x_2)}\neq 0

Only TST’s with even spin can have a non zero 3PF with two scalars:

\corr{\phi\phi O^{\mu_1...\mu_l}}\neq 0 \Leftrightarrow O \textrm{ is TST and } l\textrm{ is even}
Example
Consider the 3PF:
\langle \Phi _1(P_1)\Phi _2(P_2)\Phi _3(P_3)\rangle =\frac{\lambda_{\Phi_1\Phi_2\Phi_3}}{X_{12}^{2h_{123}}X_{23}^{2h_{231}}X_{13}^{2h_{132}}}
We can take the OPE on the first two operators
\phi _1(P_1)\phi _2(P_2)\sim\sum_{\phi_k}C ^{\phi_k}_{\phi _1,\phi _2}(X_{12},\partial _2)\phi_k (x_2)
So that:
\begin{split}
\langle \phi _1(x_1)\phi _2(x_2)\phi _3(x_3)\rangle &=\sum_{\theta_k}C ^{\theta_k}_{\phi _1,\phi _2}(X_{12},\partial _2)\langle \theta_k (x_2)\phi _3(x_3)\rangle
\end{split}
Since 2PF’s are diagonal:
\begin{split}
\langle \phi _1(x_1)\phi _2(x_2)\phi _3(x_3)\rangle &=\sum_{\theta_k}C ^{\theta_k}_{\phi _1,\phi _2}(X_{12},\partial _2)\langle \theta_k (x_2)\phi _3(x_3)\rangle\\
& =C ^{\phi_3}_{\phi _1,\phi _2}(X_{12},\partial _2)\frac{1}{X_{23}^{2\Delta _3}}
\end{split}
The coefficient C can be found by expanding for X_{12}<<X_{13},X_{23} and matching powers. We have done it to second order in OPE for 3PF.
