QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Primary-operato.title: Primary operators
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Primary-operato.content:
QFT representations 
                  
                

When we think of field operators in QFT, usually these are combinations of ladder operators acting on the vacuum. This means that taking the commutators of these operators with the commuting generators (i.e. those that define the quantum numbers of the theory) of an algebra, the resulting variation corresponds to the transformation of the operator in the representation given by the quantum numbers of the created state.


We want to build field representations of the conformal group.
Recalling that M,D commute (common eigenbase), we can define the action of the algebra on the fields defined at the origin in the highest weight representation:
\comm{P_\mu}{\phi _\alpha (0)} = i\partial_\mu \phi _\alpha (0)
\comm{M_{\mu\nu}}{\phi _\alpha (0)} = iR^{(r_\phi)}(M_{\mu\nu}) \phi _\alpha (0)
\comm{D}{\phi _\alpha (0)} = i\Delta _\phi \phi _\alpha (0)
\comm{K_{\mu}}{\phi _\alpha (0)} = 0
Operators that satisfy these commutation laws (particularly the last one) are called primary operators.
The field at coordinate \neq 0 is not a primary operator:
\phi _\alpha (x) = e^{ipx}\phi _\alpha (0)e^{-ipx} = \phi _\alpha (0) - i[P,\phi]x+...
P ascends the ladder, so it’s not primary. States not annihilated by K are called descendants.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Quantization-in.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Quantization in conformal symmetry.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Quantization-in.title: Quantization in conformal symmetry
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Quantization-in.content:
Usually, when we quantize a theory, we select a direction of time and identify manifolds which are always orthogonal to the time direction (so they are space-like, admitting delta t =0) where we perform the quantization. Different layers are connected through time evolution.
In conformal symmetry this is not convenient, as the generator of time evolution is the hamiltonian, i.e. the 0 component of the momentum, which does not commute with dilation operator D and SCT operator K^\mu, so time evolution would not preserve quantum numbers.
Radial quantization

An alternative quantization identifies time as the radial direction, so that the manifolds on which we are going to quantize are gonna be spheres, and the generator of “time” evolution is going to be the dilation D (this is also coherent with the notion that D eigenstates are acted upon by ladder operators).
This will produce a theory that generates radially ordered correlation function (instead of path ordered ones):
\matel{\phi _f}{e^{-\lambda D}}{\phi _i}\rightarrow \int _{\substack{\phi (r_i) = \phi_i\\\phi (r_f) = \phi_f}}\mathcal{D} [\phi] e^{-S_E(\phi)}
The radial coordinates are defined by the metric:
ds^2 = d r^2 +r^2 d\Omega _{d-1} ^2
In this picture, we can define the Hilbert space \mathcal{H} on the sphere S_{d-1}\coloneqq r^2 d\Omega _{d-1} ^2. Given the fact that in conformal symmetry we have defined charges to be topological, we can act by a generator Q of the symmetry on \mathcal{H} by inserting the surface operator Q\left(S_{d-1}\right) into the path integral.
We can also define the radially ordered integral w.r.t. different points (just as we could define the time ordered integral in different reference frames in QFT). The radial ordering prescription is consistent because operators at the same radius but different angles on the sphere commute, just as spacelike-separated operators commute in the usual quantization.
Cylindrical picture

Define a new coordinate:
\tau = \log r
so that the metric becomes:
ds^2 = e^{2\tau}\left(d\tau ^2 +d\Omega ^2 _{d-1}\right)
This is a cylindrical metric (surface of the cylinder) times r^2, r\in [0,\infty):
\mathbb{R}\times S_{d-1}
When two metrics are connected through a multiplicative factor, they are said to be conformally equivalent, so the cylindrical metric is conformally equivalent to the flat space (although this change of coordinates is not a conformal transformation).
The cylindrical picture is easier to understand than radial one because it’s just like conventional quantization restricted to a succession of circles, however the two quantizations are equivalent.
CFT in radial quantization is equivalent to euclidean QFT at finite volume (on the cylinder). QFT’s on compact spaces have discrete spectra TODO so that’s what we expect here.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Reflection-posi.title: Reflection positivity
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Reflection-posi.content:
Reflection positivity means that a theory, whose observables are O_i(x_i), given a reflection transformation \Theta, satisfy:
\corr{O_1(x_1)...O_n(x_n)\Theta(O_1(x_1))...\Theta(O_n(x_n))}>0
The operator \Theta can be whatever, an example can be a reflection along an axis.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/State-operator-.title: State-operator correspondence
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/State-operator-.content:
Working in radial quantization, we want to understand how operators and states are related in conformally symmetric theories.
The main result we want to prove is the following:


                  
                  State-operator correspondence 
                  
                

In CFT, states are defined on the surface of a sphere and are generated by operators inside the sphere corresponding to the state. The statement can be summarized by:
\theta (0) \leftrightarrow \theta(0)\ket{0}\coloneqq \ket{\theta}


State ← operator
Performing the path integral on an empty sphere produces the vacuum state \ket{0}.
On the surface of the sphere, we have a Hilbert space spanned by the states  \ket{\phi _{\partial B}} which correspond to a field configuration \phi _{\partial B}(\mathbf{n}) on {\partial B}, so that a generic state \ket{\psi} can be written as:
\int\mathcal{D}\phi _{\partial B} \ip{\phi _{\partial B}}{\psi}\ket{\phi _{\partial B}}
The coefficients \ip{\phi _{\partial B}}{\psi} are given by the path integral over the interior of the sphere B. Consider the case \ket{\psi}=\ket{0} and assume R to be the radius of B. Then:
\ip{\phi _{\partial B}}{0} = \int_{\substack{r<R\\ \phi (R,\mathbf{n}) = \phi_{\partial B}(\mathbf{n})}}\mathcal{D}\phi (r,\mathbf{n})e^{-S[\phi]}
We can perform the same steps inserting an operator \theta (x), where x can be anywhere inside the sphere:
\matel{\phi _{\partial B}}{\theta(x)}{0} = \int_{\substack{r<R\\ \phi (R,\mathbf{n}) = \phi_{\partial B}(\mathbf{n})}}\mathcal{D}\phi (r,\mathbf{n})\theta(x)e^{-S[\phi]}
This defines the state {\theta(x)}\ket{0}. We conclude that operators inside the sphere generate states on the surface of the sphere.
State → operator

Take \ket{\theta_i} eigenstates of the dilation operator D defined on the surfaces \partial B_i of the spheres B_i.
We can convert these states into operators by “cutting holes” corresponding to the B_i and “glueing in” the states on the borders. This generates the same correlator we would obtain by considering operators inside the spheres:
\corr{...\theta_i(x_i)...} = \int \mathcal{D}\phi _{\partial B_i}\ip{\phi_{\partial B_i}}{\theta _i}\int_{\substack{\phi(x\in \partial B_i) = \phi _{\partial B_i}\\x\notin B_i}} \mathcal{D} \phi (x)e^{-S[{\phi}]}
This implies that states on the surfaces of the spheres correspond to operators inside the spheres.
State ←> operator
We define a local operator as an eigenstate of D in radial quantization. This provides us with the correspondence:
\mathcal{O}(0) \leftrightarrow \mathcal{O}(0)\ket{0}\coloneqq \ket{\mathcal{O}}
TODO check signs
\begin{aligned}
{\left[K_\mu, \mathcal{O}(0)\right] } & =0 & & \longleftrightarrow & K_\mu|\mathcal{O}\rangle & =0 \\
{[D, \mathcal{O}(0)] } & =-i\Delta \mathcal{O}(0) & & \longleftrightarrow & D|\mathcal{O}\rangle & =-i\Delta|\mathcal{O}\rangle \\
{\left[M_{\mu \nu}, \mathcal{O}(0)\right] } & =-i\mathcal{S}_{\mu \nu} \mathcal{O}(0) & & \longleftrightarrow & M_{\mu \nu}|\mathcal{O}\rangle & =-i\mathcal{S}_{\mu \nu}|\mathcal{O}\rangle
\end{aligned}

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Transformation-.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/QFT in Curved Space-Time/Transformation of fields under conformal symmetries.md
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Transformation-.title: Transformation of fields under conformal symmetries
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Transformation-.content:
We want to find out how fields
\phi _\alpha (x)
transform under conformal transformations. The first thing to notice is that it is sufficient to study the transformation of \phi (0), in fact:
\phi _\alpha (x) = e^{iPx}\phi _\alpha (0)e^{-iPx}
then, the commutator of \phi _\alpha (x) with an operator \mathcal{G} becomes:
\comm{\mathcal{G}}{\phi _\alpha (x)} = e^{ipx}\comm{\tilde{\mathcal{G}}}{\phi _\alpha (0)}e^{-ipx}
where we used the BCH formula to derive:
\tilde{\mathcal{G}} \equiv e^{-iPx}\mathcal{G}e^{iPx}=\sum _n \frac{(-i)^n}{n!}x_{\mu _1}x_{\mu _2} ...x_{\mu _n} \comm{P^{\mu_1}}{\comm{P^{\mu_2}}{\comm{...}{\comm{P^{\mu_n}}{\mathcal{G}}}...}}
Once one of these commutators is proportional to P, every higher order commutator vanishes, e.g.:
\tilde{D} = D -i x_\mu \comm{P^\mu}{D} + 0 = D +x\cdot P
This leads us to the identities:
\tilde{D} = D +x\cdot P
\tilde{M}_{\mu\nu} = M_{\mu\nu} -x_\nu P_\mu -x_\mu P_\nu
\tilde{K}_\mu = K_\mu +2x_\mu D + 2 x^\rho M_{\rho\mu}+ 2 x_\mu(x\cdot P)- (x\cdot x) P_\mu
This construction is useful as it implies that primary operators are all that’s needed to understand the field representations of conformal symmetries.
Finite transformations
Consider the conformal transformations
x{\mapsto} x'(x)
Which induce a transformation on the metric:
g_{\mu\nu} \mapsto g^\prime _{\mu\nu} = \Omega ^2 (x) g_{\mu\nu}

\Omega ^2 (x) =1 Poincare
\Omega ^2 (x) = \Omega ^2 dilations
\Omega (x) = (1-2b\cdot x + b^2 x^2) for SCT
The most general transformation that achieves this is:
\frac{\partial x^{\prime \mu}}{\partial x^\nu} = \Omega(x) \Lambda ^\mu \,_\nu
where \Lambda ^\mu \,_\nu is a Lorentz transformation.
The most general finite conformal transformation acting on an operator \phi _\alpha (x), belonging to a representation r_\phi of the Lorentz group, is:
\phi _\alpha (x) \mapsto \phi '_\alpha (x') = F_\alpha \,^\beta\phi _\beta (x(x'))
F_\alpha \,^\beta = \frac{1}{\Omega ^{\Delta_\phi}(x)}R^{(r_\phi)}\,_\alpha \,^\beta(\Lambda)
where \Delta_\phi is the energy dimension of the field and R^{(r_\phi)}\,_\alpha \,^\beta(\Lambda) is the matrix representation of the Lorentz transformation \Lambda.
These transformation rules are very restricting, as they need to be reproduced by correlation functions too.

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Unitarity-bound.title: Unitarity bounds
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Unitarity-bound.content:
Consider the first scalar descendant:
P^\mu \ket{\Delta, l=0}
Its correlation function with its inverted state is:
\matel{\Delta,l=0}{(IP^\nu I)P^\mu}{\Delta, l=0}
But the P operator under inversion is the K operator:
=\matel{\Delta,l=0}{K^\nu P^\mu}{\Delta, l=0}\succcurlyeq 0
We can exchange {K^\nu P^\mu} with the corresponding commutator:
\comm{K^\nu}{P^\mu} = 2 \left(\eta ^{\mu\nu}D - M^{\mu\nu}\right)
so that for scalars:
\matel{\Delta,l=0}{\eta ^{\mu\nu}D}{\Delta, l=0}\succcurlyeq 0\Rightarrow \Delta >0
We can do the same for second descendants:
P_\mu P^\mu \ket{\Delta, l=0}
obtaining (see proof here):
\Delta \geq\frac{d-2}{2}
which is saturated as the right-hand side is the dimension of free scalar fields.
For vector states l=1, and we should find that:
\Delta \geq d-1
Saturated because it’s the dimension of free currents.
Generically, we can always find that
\Delta \geq \Delta _{min}
where \Delta _{min} depends on the spin representation.
For traceless symmetric tensors of spin l:
\Delta _{min} = d+l-2\quad \forall l>0
For d=4, representations of SO(4) can be labelled by spinorial indices j_1 , j_2 = j_1 +p:
\Delta \geq j_1 +\frac{p}{2}+2\quad j_1\neq 0
\Delta \geq \frac{p}{2}+1\quad j_1 = 0
Substituting:
(0,0) (scalars), we get \Delta_{min} = 1
(0,1) (fermions), we get \Delta_{min} = 3/2
(j,j) (TST), we get \Delta_{min} = j +2
(0,2) (antisymmetric tensor F_{\mu\nu}), we get \Delta_{min} = 2

QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Unitarity-of-CF.title: Unitarity of CFT
QFT-in-Curved-Space-Time/Unitarity-of-CF.content:
In CFT, we are working on infinite dimensional representations of the conformal group, as this group is not compact and therefore can’t admit finite unitary representations.
Working in euclidian signature SO(d+1,1), the claim is that highest weight representations in this signature become unitary representations of SO(d,2). Note that they can’t both be unitary. Think of it this way:
t_E = -it_M
in order to preserve rotation invariance in scalars, the rotation needs to change accordingly. The unitarity in Minkowski signature is guaranteed by the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction theorem, reported here too:


                  
                  Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction theorem 
                  
                

Transclude of Osterwalder-Schrader-reconstruction-theorem


We define a reflection \Theta in our euclidian theory in the cylindrical picture.
We select the reflection to be the \tau inversion:

In the corresponding radial picture, we are sending r\mapsto 1/r.
So, in order to have a unitary theory in Minkowski, we need that, in Euclidean signature, the following is satisfied:
\corr{I(\psi),\psi}>0\quad \forall \psi
How do we verify that this condition is consistent with conformal algebra? Take a primary state \ket{\psi _P}, then:

Assume that \corr{I(\psi_P ),\psi_P}>0
We verify that the first descendant satisfies the condition

\corr{I(P_\mu\psi_P ),P_\nu\psi_P}\succcurlyeq 0
here the condition is in the sense of positive semi-definiteness. This tool can be used to impose bounds on the dimensionality of primaries.


                  
                  Info
                  
                

We are basically redefining the dual states. In normal quantum mechanics, those are the ‘dagger’ states, while here we need to perform the radial inversion.


Representation theory approach
Basically we want to compare
SO(d+1,1)\quad\textrm{vs} \quad SO(d,2) 
Let us use the encoding through the object J_{AB}:
\comm{J_{AB}}{J_{CD}} = \eta_{AC}J_{BD}-\eta_{BC}J_{AD}-\eta_{AD}J_{BC}+\eta_{AC}J_{BD}
where the flat metric is:
\eta_{AB} = \left(
\begin{array}{ccccc}
-1 & & & & \\
& -1 & & & \\
& & 1 & & \\
& & & \ddots & \\
& & & & 1
\end{array}
\right)
with: A,B,C,D = -1,0,...,d and greek letters going from 0 to d-1, which identify the Lorentz group:

In Minkowski unitarity implies:
[J_{AB}]^\dagger = \pm J_{AB}
with the identification:
M_{\mu\nu} = J_{\mu\nu}
D = J_{-1,d}
\frac{P_\mu - K_\mu}{2} = J_{\mu,d}
\frac{P_\mu + K_\mu}{2} = J_{\mu,-1}
In order to get to Euclidean, we need to analytically continue the (0,0) component; in Euclidean, we have:
A,B,... = -1,0,...,d
a,b,... = 1,...,d
The rotations (corresponding to Lorentz) act on the a,b indices:

So that the euclidean rotations are a mixture of rotations, sct’s and momenta from Minkowski
M^E_{ab} = J_{ab} \leftarrow\textrm{mixture of } SO(d-1)\textrm{ rotations in Mink. and } P,K
while the dilation operator becomes:
D^E = iJ_{-1,0}\leftarrow P_0+K_0
this is sometimes called conformal hamiltonian. Momenta and sct’s become:
P_a ^E = J_{a,-1}+iJ_{a,0}
K_a ^E = J_{a,-1}+iJ_{a,0}
The claim is that these Euclidean generators satisfy the conformal algebra.
Now P,K behave like ladder operators
P^{E^\dagger} = K^E
This is the behavior we expect from inversion in cylindrical picture.

The cylinder is \mathbb{R}\times S_{d-1}. In order to pass from euclidian to Minkowski we need to perform a Wick rotation of \tau. When we do that (see Covering space) we end up in:
\textrm{covering space}\left[S_1\times S_{d-1}\right] = \mathbb{R}^{d-1,1}
In particular, the dilation operator is sent to P_0+K_0 check.
See Tasi lectures on CFT in Lorentzian (Simmons-Duffin).
Representation of conformal group in 1D
Here, the conformal group basically reduces to the group of linear transformations.
SO(2,1)\quad\textrm{vs} \quad SO(1,2) 
No rotations, 3 generators P,K,D
\comm{D}{P} = P
\comm{D}{K} = -K
\comm{K}{P} = 2D
The quadratic Casimir is:
C_2 = \frac{1}{2} M_{\mu\nu} M^{\mu\nu} +\frac{1}{2} \left(P_\mu K^\mu +K_\mu P^\mu\right)- D^2 \overset{d=1}{=}D(1-D)+PK
A generic transformation in Euclidean is written as:
e^{\frac{1}{2} \theta ^{AB} J_{AB}}
So, unitarity in Euclidean means:
[J_{AB}]^\dagger = -J_{AB}
We also have the “Minkowski-inherited” unitarity condition we found earlier (i.e. what guarantees unitarity once we go back to minkowski), which would be
K^\dagger = P
Both need to be satisfied. Let’s discuss the first, introduce the operators:
L_0\coloneqq iJ_{-1,0} = -\frac{i}{2}(P+K)
L_\pm\coloneqq -\frac{i}{2}(P-K) \mp D
Their algebra is:
\comm{L_0}{L_\pm} = \pm L_\pm
\comm{L_-}{L_+} = 2L_0
L_- ^\dagger = L_+
Let us consider an irrep and the action of the quadratic Casimir on its states.
Define a \Delta\in\mathbb{C} so that it satisfies.
C_2\ket{\psi} = {\Delta(1-\Delta)}\ket{\psi}
Note that {\Delta(1-\Delta)} must be real.
We build the representation starting from a state \ket{\Delta,n} s.t.:
L_0\ket{\Delta,n} = n\ket{\Delta,n}
L_+\ket{\Delta,n} = (\Delta +n)\ket{\Delta,n+1}
L_-\ket{\Delta,n} = (n-\Delta)\ket{\Delta,n-1}
Iterating, one the following must happen:

\Delta\in\mathbb{Z} → the iteration will truncate, we either get

Highest weight representations, \Delta\in\mathbb{Z}^+
Lowest weight representations, \Delta\in\mathbb{Z}^-


Otherwise, iteration goes on forever
Now we impose unitarity:

\ip{\Delta,n}{\Delta,n} \geq 0
L_+ ^\dagger = L_- \Leftrightarrow \matel{\Delta,n}{L_-}{\Delta,n+1} = \matel{\Delta,n+1}{L_+}{\Delta,n}^*
Consider the ratio of norms
\frac{\ip{\Delta,n+1}{\Delta,n+1}}{\ip{\Delta,n}{\Delta,n}} = \frac{n+\bar{\Delta}}{n+\Delta ^*}\coloneqq\lambda _n
with \bar{\Delta}\coloneqq (1-\Delta).


                  
                  Proof
                  
                

You need to use the following:
L_- \ket{\Delta,n+1} = (n+\bar{\Delta})\ket{\Delta,n}
\left(L_+ \ket{\Delta,n}\right)^\dagger = \bra{\Delta,n} L_- = \left(n+\Delta\right)^* \bra{\Delta,n+1}
Substitute the first into the denominator and the second into the numerator


We want that
\lambda _n\in \mathbb{R}\quad\land\quad\lambda _n\geq 0\quad \forall n
We get that:
\lambda _n\in \mathbb{R}\Leftarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\Delta\in\mathbb{R}\\
\lor\\
\Delta = \frac{1}{2} +i\mu
\end{array}\right.
The last part is proven by dividing \Delta in real and imaginary part:
\frac{n+\bar{\Delta}}{n+\Delta ^*} = \frac{n +(1-\Delta _\Re-i\Delta_\Im)}{n+\Delta _\Re-i\Delta_\Im}
L_0 is the generator of SO(2)\in SO(1,2) so n is real. Then, in order to have real \lambda _n, \Delta_\Re =1/2 or \Delta real.


                  
                  Principal series 
                  
                

\Delta = \frac{1}{2} +i\mu
We always get \lambda _n =1, so unitarity is guaranteed.




                  
                  Complementary series 
                  
                

If \Delta \in \mathbb{R}, how do we guarantee that \lambda _n >0?
\lambda _n = \frac{n+\bar{\Delta}}{n+\Delta ^*} = \frac{\left(n+1/2\right)^2-\left(\Delta+1/2\right)^2}{(n+\Delta)}
the sequence grows with n, set n=0, then:
0\leq \Delta \leq 1




                  
                  Discrete series 
                  
                

For \Delta \in\mathbb{Z}^+ we get two irreps:
\left\{\begin{array}{lll}


n\geq 0 &\mathcal{D}^+\Delta &\textrm{lowest weight representation}\
n\leq -\Delta &\mathcal{D}^-\Delta &\textrm{highest weight representation}
\end{array}\right.



For \Delta \in\mathbb{Z}^- we have a finite dimensional representation of a non-compact group → non unitary
For \Delta =0 we have a trivial representation.

How can we see that these representations are not the highest weight representations that we are used to?

Quantum-Information/Distances/Bures-dist.title: Bures distance
Quantum-Information/Distances/Bures-dist.content:
The Bures distance is a distance derived from the notion of Fidelity
D_{B} (\rho_1,\rho _2) \equiv \sqrt{2} \sqrt{1-\sqrt{F(\rho_1,\rho _2) }}
see Holevo’s book, page 200 for further details.
The Bures distance is considered useful in the context of quantum metrology.

Quantum-Information/Distances/Fidelity-a.title: Fidelity and Trace Distance connection

Quantum-Information/Distances/Fidelity.title: Fidelity
Quantum-Information/Distances/Fidelity.content:
Fidelity is kind of like the opposite of distance; the fidelity between two states \rho _1,\rho_2 is often defined by:
F(\rho_1,\rho _2) \equiv \norm{\sqrt{\rho _1}\sqrt{\rho _2}}^2 _1
or by its square root (not used here). The \norm{\cdot}_1 is the Trace norm operation.
F(\rho_1,\rho _2) =\left(\tr\sqrt{\sqrt{\rho _1}\rho _2\sqrt{\rho _2}}\right)^2
Properties

Since
\norm{\theta}_1 = \norm{\theta ^\dagger}_1
The fidelity is symmetrical in its inputs

F(\rho_1,\rho _2) =F(\rho_2,\rho _1)

The fidelity hits its maximum when the two states are identical

F(\rho,\rho) = 1

If \rho _1 \rho _2 = \rho _2 \rho _1 = 0, then the fidelity is null.
Under Quantum channels, the fidelity is monotonous non-decreasing:
F(\rho_1,\rho _2) \leq F(\Phi (\rho_1),\Phi(\rho _2))
This makes sense as LCPT maps add noise to the system, making it less distinguishable. Unitary maps saturate the relation above.

Fidelity with pure state
If one of the states, e.g. \rho _1, is a pure state:
\rho _1 = \op{\psi}{\psi}
Then the fidelity reduces to
F(\op{\psi }{\psi },\rho ) = \ev{\psi}{\rho}
see fidelity on Holevo’s book.

Quantum-Information/Distances/Kolmogorov.title: Kolmogorov distance
Quantum-Information/Distances/Kolmogorov.content:
The Kolmogorov distance measures how much two probability distribution differ from each other; given the probability distributions
\{p_x\}_x,\{q_x\}_x
the Kolmogorov is defined as:
D_K \left(\{p\}\{q\}\right) \equiv \frac{1}{2}\sum _x\abs{p_x-q_x}

Quantum-Information/Distances/Qubit-dist.title: Qubit distance

Quantum-Information/Distances/Trace-Dist.title: Trace Distance
Quantum-Information/Distances/Trace-Dist.content:
The trace distance draws from the Trace norm to define a notion of distance; given two Density matrix operators \rho_1,\rho_2, their trace distance is defined as:
D(\rho _1,\rho _2) \equiv \frac{1}{2}\norm{\rho _1-\rho _2}_1
where \norm{\cdot}_1 is the trace norm.
The trace distance is considered useful for dealing with decision problems (e.g. discriminating between two states)
Alternative form
An alternative form for the trace distance, useful in many proofs, is:
D(\rho _1,\rho _2) = \max_\Pi\tr\left(\Pi (\rho _1-\rho _2)\right)
where \Pi indicates projectors.
Proof

Parallelism with Kolmogorov distance
In the special case of commuting operators:
[\rho _1,\rho _2] = 0
The trace distance reduces to the Kolmogorov distance, which can be proven by direct computation in the common eigenbasis of the two operators.
This allows us to kind of think of statistical mechanics as the abelian quantum statistical mechanics.
POVM’s
Another connection with the Kolmogorov distance arises from the POVM formalism. Operationally, if we build an appropriate measurement device, the trace distance reduces to the Kolmogorov distance.
Given two density matrices \rho _1,\rho _2 and a POVM \{E_n\} describing a measurement device, two probability distributions arise from the measurements:
p_n ^{(1)} = \tr(E_n \rho _1)\rightarrow \{p_n ^{(1)}\}_n
p_n ^{(2)} = \tr(E_n \rho _2)\rightarrow \{p_n ^{(2)}\}_n
we can define a concept of distance between states given the measurement device, which is the Kolmogorov distance between the probability distributions defined above:
D_{\{E_n\}_n}(\rho _1,\rho_2) = D_K\left(\{p_n ^{(1)}\}_n,\{p_n ^{(2)}\}_n\right)
It turns out that, if we select the optimal measurement device, this distance reduces to the trace distance:
\max_{\{E_n\}_n}D_{\{E_n\}_n}(\rho _1,\rho_2) = D(\rho _1,\rho _2)
Proof

Properties

The trace distance is non-negative and is 0 only when the operators are the same:

D(\rho _1,\rho _2)\geq 0\qquad D(\rho _1,\rho _2) = 0\Leftrightarrow \rho _1 = \rho _2

The trace distance of orthogonal states is 1:

\rho_1\rho _2= \rho _2\rho _1 = 0\Rightarrow D(\rho _1,\rho _2) =1

The trace distance is commutative

D(\rho _1,\rho _2) = D(\rho _2,\rho _1)

The trace distance satisfies the triangular inequality
D(\rho _1,\rho _2) \leq D(\rho _1,\rho _3)+D(\rho _3,\rho _2)
which can be proven using the projection form for the trace distance
Under unitary channels \mathcal{V}, the trace distance is constant
D(\mathcal{V}(\rho _1),\mathcal{V}(\rho _2)) = D(\rho _1,\rho _2)
Generally, however, quantum channels \Phi contract the trace distance
D(\Phi(\rho _1),\Phi(\rho _2)) \leq D(\rho _1,\rho _2)
this can be proven following the same formalism as the one used for the proof of the alternative form of the trace distance:

\rho _1-\rho _2 \equiv A-B
D(\rho _1,\rho _2) = \max_{\Pi} \tr (\Pi (\rho _1 -\rho _2)) = \tr (A)
\begin{split}D(\Phi(\rho _1),\Phi(\rho _2)) & = \max_{\Pi} \tr (\Pi \Phi(\rho _1 -\rho _2)) \\ &\leq \max_{\Pi} \tr (\Pi \Phi(A))\leq\tr ( \Phi(A))\leq \tr (A)\end{split}

Given two joint states \rho _{AB}, \sigma _{AB} such that their reduced density matrices are \rho _A = \tr _B\rho _{AB}, \sigma _A = \tr _B\sigma _{AB}:
D(\rho _{AB},\sigma _{AB}) \geq D(\rho _A,\sigma _A)
which makes sense as in the partial trace operation we are losing information on the system B. This property can be proven using the previous property and selecting the channel
\Phi: \rho _{AB}\overset{\Phi}{\mapsto}\rho _A\otimes \ket{0}_B\bra{0}
or using the fact that the partial trace is a proper quantum channel

Helstrom theorem
There is an operational connection from the trace distance definition to the “real world” through the Helstrom’s theorem. In fact, in the case where we work in an ensemble of 2 states on which we have no information regarding the associated probability distribution, we suppose that the two states are chaotically created (50% rate) and the minimum probability of error for distinguishing them becomes:
\min P_{error} = \frac{1}{2} \left(1-\frac{1}{2} \norm{\rho _1 - \rho _2}_1\right) =\frac{1}{2} \left(1-D(\rho _1,\rho _2)\right)

Quantum-Information/Distances/Uhlmann-th.title: Uhlmann theorem
Quantum-Information/Distances/Uhlmann-th.content:
Uhlmann theorem connects the notions of Fidelity and Purification.
Suppose we have two states \rho _1,\rho _2 in the system S, and suppose we purify them using a reference system R.
\rho _1 \mapsto \ket{\psi _1}_{SR}
\rho _2 \mapsto \ket{\psi _2}_{SR}
Then, the fidelity between the two states is:
F(\rho_1,\rho _2) = \max_{ \ket{\psi _1}_{SR}, \ket{\psi _2}_{SR}} \abs{\prescript{}{SR}{\ip{\psi _1}{\psi _2}} _{SR}}^2= \max_{ \ket{\psi _1}_{SR}} \abs{\prescript{}{SR}{\ip{\psi _1}{\psi _2}} _{SR}}^2
where the max means the maximum w.r.t. all possible purifications of the state(s).
Proof
Used: Schmidt decomposition and Orthogonality relation for unitaries

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Bell-st.title: Bell states
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Bell-st.content:
The notion of Bell states can be defined for any dimension d; specifically, it can be shown that the maximally entangled state \ket{\psi}_{AB}\bra{\psi} for a pair of qudits is:
\ket{\psi}_{AB}\bra{\psi} \textrm{ maximally entangled}\Leftrightarrow\ket{\psi}_{AB}=\left(\mathrm{Id}\otimes U\right)\ket{\varphi _d}_{AB} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\mathrm{vec}(U),
\ket{\varphi _d}_{AB} \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\ket{j}_A\ket{j}_B,
where \mathrm{vec} indicates the vectorization of an operator. The unitaries U are the Heisenberg-Weyl operators W_{a,b}, which are basically a generalization of the Pauli operators to d-dimensional spaces.
\ket{\psi _{a,b}}=\left(\mathrm{Id}\otimes W_{a,b}\right)\ket{\varphi _d}
\ket{\psi _{a,b}}_{AB}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum _{k=0}^{d-1} e^{2\pi i (k+b)a/d}\ket{[k+b]_d}_A\ket{k}_B
These states form a basis for the Hilbert space \mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B.
Qubit case
The Bell basis for Qubits is usually denoted by:
\ket{\Psi ^+ } = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\ket{00} + \ket{11}\right)
\ket{\Psi ^- } = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\ket{00} - \ket{11}\right)
\ket{\Phi ^+ } = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\ket{10} + \ket{01}\right)
\ket{\Phi ^- } = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\ket{10} - \ket{01}\right)
Bell state creation

Using the CNOT gate and the Hadamard Gate, qubit Bell states can be created, take the state \ket{\Psi ^+}_{AB} as an example:
\left(CNOT\circ H_A\right)\ket{0}_A\ket{0}_B = \ket{\Psi ^+}_{AB}

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Bell's-.title: Bell's theorem
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Bell's-.content: Bell’s theorem states that hidden variable theories are inconsistent with quantum mechanics, if we exclude the possibility of giving up locality.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/CHSH-in.title: CHSH inequality
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/CHSH-in.content:
The CHSH inequality, named after the authors Clauser, Horne, Shimony, and Holt, is used to experimentally prove Bell’s theorem.
Consider a bipartite system and 4 binary observables, A,A' for one of the subsystems, and B,B' for the other. Then build the observable
C\equiv A(B+B^\prime)+ A^\prime (B-B^\prime)
Since the outcome of the single observables must be \pm 1, then:
\abs{\langle C \rangle} = \abs{\langle AB\rangle +\langle A^\prime B\rangle +\langle AB^\prime\rangle - \langle A^\prime B^\prime\rangle}\leq 2
which is the CHSH inequality. Hidden variable theories state that there exists a probability distribution under a variable \lambda for any observable, so that
\langle AB\rangle= \sum _{AB}\int d\lambda p(\lambda) AB\, P(A|\lambda)P(B|\lambda)
Quantum mechanics violates the CHSH inequality: choose the observables:
A\mapsto \hat{\sigma}_{\vec{a}} = \vec{a}\cdot\vec{\sigma}
B\mapsto \hat{\sigma}_{\vec{b}} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{\sigma}
where the \vec{\sigma} are the Pauli operators and \norm{a}\leq 1, \norm{b}\leq 1.
Now, if the composite system is in the Bell state
\ket{\Psi ^- } = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\ket{00} - \ket{11}\right)
then
\bra{\Psi _-}\hat{\sigma}_{\vec{a}}\otimes\hat{\sigma}_{\vec{b}}\ket{\Psi_-} = -(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})
Finally, we can choose the 4 a,b,a’,b’ vectors to be at a relative angle of \pi/4 to each other (in that order), if we do so, we find:
\langle C\rangle _{\psi_-}=2\sqrt{2}>2

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Choi-st.title: Choi state

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Complet.title: Completely chaotic state

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Concurr.title: Concurrence

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entangled states
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
As seen in Density matrix operators in the subsection regarding joint states, entangled states are all the states which cannot be expressed as Convex combinations of factorized states (separable states):
\rho_{AB} \neq\sum _i p_i \rho ^{(i)} _A\otimes\tau^{(i)} _B

Convex combinations of entangled states are not necessarily entangled, e.g. the combination of the Bell states with equal probability returns an operator proportional to the identity.
Volume of separable states is much smaller (but not 0 measure) than that of entangled states
Bell states are the states which maximally violate CHSH inequality, while separable states obey the inequality.
Generally, determining whether a state is entangled or not is a NP hard problem, however there are a few criteria which may be useful.
The local knowledge of an entangled state carries more information than the knowledge of the corresponding global state. In fact, it can be shown that for a pure state on the bipartite system AB, the state is entangled if and only if the Conditional entropy of B given A is smaller than 0:

S(B|A) <0,
S(A,B)<S(A).

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement cost
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
Alice and Bob share infinite copies of Bell states and can perform LOCC’s; they have to generate a target state \rho _{AB}^{\otimes M} using N pairs of these copies. Separable states have 0 cost. Define the rate
R=\frac{N}{M}
which vanishes for separable states (A and B don’t need to use any Bell state copy) and maximizes at 1 for Bell states. Then, we define the entanglement cost by taking the limit of the minimum (over LOCC’s) of this rate
E_C\left(\rho _{AB}\right) =\lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}\min R
We don’t necessarily need to have exact Bell states, but they need to be “close enough”

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement criteria
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
PPT criterion
Majorization criterion
Entanglement witness techinques
Other criteria rely on local transformations which are positive but not completely positive (see Quantum channel representations). There is a theorem that states:
if \rho_{AB} entangled, then \exists \Lambda P but not CP that allows to identify entanglement

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement distillation
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
Suppose Alice and Bob share N (which will go to infinity) copies of a state \rho _{AB}. They want to produce (distill) M copies of maximally entangled states.
R=\frac{M}{N}
This R is the rate of distillation for a fixed LOCC. Now, we take the limit of this rate maximizing over LOCC’s, obtaining the entanglement distillation
E_D(\rho_{AB}) =\lim \max R
We don’t necessarily need to have exact Bell states, but they need to be “close enough”
For some entangled states, this functional evaluates to 0 (some entangled states are too weak to produce Bell states, e.g. entangled states whose Partial transpose is positive, see PPT criterion). Distillation is not exactly the inverse of cost, there is some sort of arrow of time.
E_D(\rho _{AB}) \leq E_C(\rho_{AB})
For qb-qb (Qubits) systems, entanglement is always distillable.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement measures
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
In order to define a sound entanglement measure E, we need a number of properties:

E:\sigma\left(\mathcal{H}_{AB}\right)\mapsto\mathbb{R}^+
E(\rho_{AB}^{sep})=0
Sometimes E(\rho _{AB} ^{ent})>0
Invariance under local unitaries E(\rho _{AB}) = E\left(U_AV_B\rho_{AB}U_A^\dagger V_B^\dagger\right). Invariance under global unitaries is impossible because those transformations can generate (and destroy) entanglement
\Phi LOCC, then E(\Phi(\rho _{AB}))\leq E(\rho _{AB})
We can find these functionals, namely:


Relative entropy of entanglement
Concurrence
Entanglement of formation (number of Bell copies necessary to produce a target state)
Entanglement cost (limit of ratio between Bell copies and copies of a target state to be produced)
Entanglement distillation (limit of ratio of target number of Bell states and copies of available state)
Distillation is bigger than cost, meaning that there exists a kind of arrow of time for entanglement

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement of formation
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
The entanglement of formation quantifies the number of maximally entangled states necessary to generate a target state through LOCC protocols.
This turns out to be not a precise definition but still a good entanglement measure.
Define ensemble so that:
\rho _{AB} =\sum_i p_i \ket{\psi_i}_{AB}\bra{\psi_i}
Focus on the Pure states first; find the Schmidt decomposition:
\ket{\psi}_{AB} =\sum _l \lambda _l \ket{\phi _l}_A\ket{\varphi _l}_B
\rho _A = \sum_l \lambda_l ^2\op{\phi_l}{\phi_l}
Then, we define the entanglement of formation by:
E_F(\rho _{AB})\equiv\min _{\textrm{ensembles}}\left(\sum_i p_i S\left(\rho _A ^{(i)}\right)\right)
\rho _A ^{(i)} \equiv \tr _B(\ket{\psi _i}_{AB}\bra{\psi _i})
where S is the Von Neumann entropy.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.title: Entanglement witness techinques
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Entangl.content:
Methods to avoid tomography. Definition of entanglement witness: \theta observable s.t.:
\tr\left( \theta \rho _{AB} ^{sep}\right)\geq 0\quad \forall \rho _{AB} ^{sep}
\theta must contain negative eigenvalues so that \exists \rho _{AB} s.t. \tr\left( \theta \rho _{AB} \right)< 0.
The condition \tr(\theta\rho) = 0 identifies a hyperplane on the space of bipartite states that divides the space into 2 regions, one of which contains the separable states but also some entangled states, while the other only contains entangled states.
There is also the issue of the optimality of the hyperplane (whether it is tangent to separable states or not) + possible rotations in the hyperspace.
An example of witness is given by a modified version of the operator defined in CHSH inequality
C = A\otimes (B+B^\prime) +A^\prime\otimes(B-B^\prime)
\rho _{AB}^{(sep)} =\sum_lp_l\rho ^{(l)} _A \rho _B ^{(l)}
\langle C\rangle _{sep} =\sum_l p_l \left(\langle A\rangle _l(\langle B\rangle _l+\langle B^\prime\rangle _l) +\langle A ^\prime\rangle _l(\langle B\rangle _l-\langle B^\prime\rangle _l)\right)\leq 2
\langle A\rangle _l \equiv \tr\left(A\rho _A ^{(l)}\right)
Therefore, we define the witness
\theta = 2\mathrm{Id} - C

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/GHZ-sta.title: GHZ states
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/GHZ-sta.content:
Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger states were proposed to translate the Bell test in multipartite systems
Take the entangled state
\ket{GHZ} = \frac{\ket{000}+\ket{111}}{2}
tracing over a single subsystem
\frac{1}{2}\left(\op{00}{00}+\op{11}{11}\right)
which is a separable state. Now consider the measurement X_AY_BY_C,
X_AY_BY_C\ket{GHZ}=-\ket{GHZ}
so the outcome of the associated measurement is \pm1.
Swapping the measures X,Y on two subsystems bears the same result. In hidden variable theory, we can associate a quantity m=\pm1 to each measurement, so that
m_A^Xm_B^Ym_C^Y=-1
m_A^Ym_B^Xm_C^Y=-1
m_A^Ym_B^Ym_C^X=-1
Problem is that multiplying all these identities together yields
m_A^Xm_B^Xm_C^X=-1
Going back to quantum theory
X_AX_BX_C\ket{GHZ}=\ket{GHZ}
This incompatibility is measurable with just 3 measurement

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.title: Bell telephone
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.content:
The idea behind the Bell telephone is to exploit the entanglement in a Bell states to send classical information (bits) without using a classical communication line and without transmission delay, which would violate causality.
The protocol would work as follows:

Alice and Bob share a qubit Bell state, say \ket{\psi ^+}_{AB}
Alice can choose to perform a projective measurement on A either on the Z basis or on the X basis (see Pauli operators)
Bob performs the same type of measurement immediately after on B, hoping to read some kind of information
Call the type of measurement that Alice and Bob perform A,B, while the measurement output is a,b. We don’t have communication if we can verify that, whatever Alice does on her system, Bob won’t notice (see also Popescu-Rohrlich box, where the same condition for non-signaling theories is found):

P(b|A,B) = P(b|A^\prime, B)
P(b|A,B) = \sum_a P(a,b|A,B)
In terms of Density matrix operators, the reduced density matrix on Bob’s system will always be the completely chaotic state.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.title: Classical teleportation machine
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.content:
We want to send a quantum state using a single copy of it from Alice to Bob; schematically:

You could build a Quantum cloner out of it. It is possible to prove that quantum cloners and classical teleportation are the same
Classical teleportation → Quantum cloner

Quantum cloner → Classical teleportation
We need to employ Quantum state tomography.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/Quantum Information/Entanglement/Impossible machines/Joint measurement of incompatible observables.md
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.title: Joint measurement of incompatible observables
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.content:
Incompatible observables means [A,B]\neq 0.
The goal of this protocol is to find:
P_\psi(a,b|A\&B)
Problems arise from some conditions (here, \overset{\cdot}{=} signifies imposing a condition):

Marginal on measures on A reproduces measure on A

P_\psi(a|A\&B)=\sum_bP_\psi(a,b|A\&B)\overset{\cdot}{=}P_\psi(a|A)

Same for B

P_\psi(b|A\&B)=\sum_aP_\psi(a,b|A\&B)\overset{\cdot}{=}P_\psi(b|B)
These two conditions taken together are incompatible. If such a machine is possible, then so is the Bell telephone ([X,Z]\neq 0).
Proof through Bell test
Consider the same setting of measures for the CHSH inequality, with the further assumption that Bob has a machine for joint measurement of B,B’ and that [B,B^\prime]\neq 0. Message is encoded in the type measurement chosen by Alice. On Bob’s side, the communication protocol dictates:
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
b=b^\prime \Rightarrow A\\
b=-b^\prime \Rightarrow A^\prime
\end{array}\right.
Compute the probability of success of the protocol:

P(A) = P(A') = \frac{1}{2}
P(b=b'|A) = \sum_{a,b,b^\prime} P(a,b,b^\prime|A,B\&B^\prime)\frac{\abs{b+b^\prime}\abs{a}}{2}
\abs{b+b^\prime}=2 if b=b', 0 otherwise.
P(b=-b'|A') = \sum_{a',b,b^\prime} P(a,b,b^\prime|A',B\&B^\prime)\frac{\abs{b'-b}\abs{a'}}{2}
P_{succ} =\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a,b,b^\prime} P(a,b,b^\prime|A,B \& B^\prime)\frac{\abs{b+b^\prime}\abs{a}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a',b,b^\prime}P(a,b,b^\prime|A,B\&B^\prime)\frac{\abs{b-b^\prime}\abs{a'}}{2}
We only need to prove P_{succ}\geq \frac{1}{2}. If this is the case, then we could build a Bell telephone, which we know to be impossible. Removing abs val on a,a^\prime creates lower bound. Carry out the sum employing marginal of joint incompatible measurement machine (conditions above). One of the terms is
\sum_{a,b,b^\prime} P(a,b,b^\prime|A,B\&B^\prime)\frac{(b+b')a}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}P(a,b|A,B)ab+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab'}P(a,b^\prime|A,B^\prime)ab^\prime
Do the same for the other.
Now, notice that we have a sum of expectation values, for example:
\sum_{ab}P(a,b|A,B)ab = \langle AB\rangle
So that
P_{succ}\geq\frac{1}{4}\left(\langle AB\rangle+\langle AB^\prime\rangle+\langle A^\prime B\rangle-\langle A^\prime B^\prime\rangle\right)=\langle C\rangle/4
Therefore:
P_{succ}\geq\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}> \frac{1}{2}

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.title: Quantum cloner
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.content:
We show that, were a quantum cloner possible, then so must be the Bell telephone.
In a Bell telephone setting, suppose Bob has a quantum cloner; then, after a measurement from Alice, he copies his state n times, so that he has n copies of the same state ⇒ He can decode alice’s choice of measurement, as he would have one of the following Ensembles.
\mathcal{E} = \left\{\frac{1}{2};\ket{0}^{\otimes n},\ket{1}^{\otimes n}\right\}
\mathcal{E} = \left\{\frac{1}{2};\ket{+}^{\otimes n},\ket{-}^{\otimes n}\right\}
These two configurations are distinguishable.
Direct proof of impossibility
The map representing a quantum cloner can be written as
\Phi _{cloner} (\op{\psi}{\psi}\,\op{0}{0}) = \op{\psi}{\psi}\,\op{\psi}{\psi}
In Stinespring representation:
\Phi _{cloner} (\op{\psi}{\psi}\,\op{0}{0}) = \tr_E \left(U_{SE} (\op{\psi}{\psi}\,\op{0}{0})\,\ket{0}_E\bra{0})U_{SE}^\dagger\right)
Everything is pure, so the problem is equivalent to:
U_{SE} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_S\ket{0}_E = \ket{\psi}_S\ket{\psi}_S\ket{\chi_\psi}_E \quad\forall\psi
This is impossible though, in fact we can take the inner product
\ip{\psi}{\phi} =\abs{\ip{\psi}{\phi}}^2\ip{\chi_\psi}{\chi_\phi}
This can be satisfied for orthogonal states (classical copier), otherwise it only works on a single vector. A quantum cloner does not work even for just two non-orthogonal vectors, which is exactly the setting for bell telephones.

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.title: Universal NOT gate
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Impossi.content:
Universal NOT means flipping any state on the Bloch sphere:
\ket{\psi}\overset{UNOT}{\mapsto}\ket{\psi ^\perp}\quad\forall \psi.
If this was possible ⇒ Quantum cloner
Approximate UNOT
Approximate UNOT means that:
\forall\epsilon, \exists ? \Phi \textrm{ LCPT s.t.} \quad F\left(\Phi(\op{\psi}{\psi}), \op{\psi^\perp}{\psi^\perp}\right)\geq 1-\epsilon \quad\forall\psi 
The Depolarizing channel:
\Phi _p (\rho) =p\rho +(1-p)\mathrm{Id}/2
can be defined as a map even for some negative p. What happens then is that the output state is kind of a UNOT as it lies on the opposite side of the line in the Bloch sphere, however the line is shorter (not pure).

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Majoriz.title: Majorization criterion

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/PPT-cri.title: PPT criterion
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/PPT-cri.content:
The partial transpose criterion is based upon the Partial transpose operation. When the partial transpose is applied to separable states, it does not cause any problem as it maps separable states into separable states.
When the partial transpose is applied to entangled states, it could happen that the result is non positive.
\rho _{AB} ^{T_A} \not\geq 0\Rightarrow \rho _{AB} ^{T_A} \textrm{ is entangled}
Not the other way around (unless we are considering qubit-qubit and qutrit-qubit cases).

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Popescu.title: Popescu-Rohrlich box
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Popescu.content:
The PR box violates the Tsirelson’s bound without communication between parties, how does it work?
x,y are selected by Alice and Bob to select the type of measurement to perform on the box (A,A’ …), while a,b are the measurement outcomes.
Joint conditional prob distribution:
P(a,b|x,y) = \left\{\begin{array}{l} 1/2 \quad a\mathrm{XOR}b = x\mathrm{AND} y\\ 0 \quad otherwise\end{array}\right.
which leads to a truth table:

It might look like that Alice and Bob are actually coordinating, and that communication might be hidden somewhere, is that actually the case?
Being non signaling means that whatever Alice does, Bob cannot detect that action and viceversa ⇒ marginal probability distribution on Alice’s side
P(a|x,y) = \sum_b P(a,b|x,y)
if theory is non signaling
P(a|x,y) = P(a|x, y^\prime)\quad \forall y,y^\prime
this is exactly what happens.
In the real world there must exist a hidden communication line for the box to work, but once it is built, from Alice and Bob’s perspective there is no communication.
The pr box has \langle C\rangle = 4

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Relativ.title: Relative entropy of entanglement
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Relativ.content:
It is a geometric measure of entanglement, represented by the distance between the state and the separable states:
E(\rho_{AB}) \equiv \min _{\rho _{AB}^{sep}}D\left(\rho_{AB},\rho_{AB}^{sep}\right)

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Tsirels.title: Tsirelson's bound
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Tsirels.content:
Tsirelson’s bound dictates a constraint on the correlations measured with the CHSH inequality. Using the same notation:
C^2 = 4\mathrm{Id}+[A,A^\prime]\otimes[B,B^\prime]
Then we take the Operator norm and employ the triangular inequality
\norm{C^2}_\infty\leq4+\norm{[A,A^\prime]}_\infty\norm{[B,B^\prime]}_\infty
All the A,A’,B,B’ have norm 1. We can employ this and apply the triangular inequality to the norm of the commutators.
\norm{[A,A^\prime]}_\infty\leq \norm{AA^\prime}_\infty+\norm{A^\prime A}_\infty\leq 2\norm{A}_\infty\norm{A^\prime}_\infty=2
\norm{C^2}_\infty\leq 8
\norm{C}_\infty=\sqrt{\norm{C^2}_\infty} \leq 2\sqrt{2}
Bell states are the states that saturate this bound, as seen in CHSH inequality.
Tsirelson’s bound violations
In principle, a theory which is not quantum mechanics could permit \langle C\rangle =4. Can we imagine such theories?
Yes, e.g. Alice and Bob coordinate their measures. To do so you need some kind of communication between A and B.
There are also theories that do not allow communication between parties yet still violate Tsirelson’s bound, e.g. Popescu-Rohrlich box

Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Werner-.title: Werner states
Quantum-Information/Entanglement/Werner-.content:
Werner states are qubit-qubit states defined by:
\rho _{AB} (p) = p\op{\psi _-}{\psi _-} +(1-p) \mathbb{1}/4
so, \exists p_0: Werner state is on the border that divides separable and entangled states. This p_0 can be found through PPT (qubit-qubit case is 1/3)
There exist Entanglement measures which are monotonous non increasing under LOCC transformation, then if a state is not a Werner state it can be transformed into one following a LOCC map; if the resulting Werner state is entangled, then so must be the original state.

Quantum-Information/Entropies/Shannon-en.title: Shannon entropy
Quantum-Information/Entropies/Shannon-en.content:
Given a probability distribution \{\lambda\}, we can define the Shannon entropy
H(\lambda_k) = -\sum _i \lambda _i \logbit \lambda _i
Decision tree splits
In the context of decision trees, given the node t with classes j,
H(t) = -\sum _j p(j|t) \logbit p(j|t)
we can also define the information gain
\mathrm{GAIN}_{split} (t) \equiv H(t) - \sum _j\frac{n_j}{n_t}H(j)
where n_k is the number of records at node k.
A decision tree based on the minimization of entropy tends to prefer a large number of partitions. Solution: consider only binary split or modify the information gain:
\mathrm{GainRatio}_{split}(t) \equiv \frac{\mathrm{GAIN}_{split}(t)}{\mathrm{SplitInfo}(t)}
\mathrm{SplitInfo} (t)\equiv- \sum _j \frac{n_j}{n_t}\logbit\frac{n_j}{n_t}

Quantum-Information/Entropies/Von-Neuman.title: Von Neumann entropy
Quantum-Information/Entropies/Von-Neuman.content:
Given a state \rho, we can define its Von Neumann entropy:
S(\rho) \equiv -\tr(\rho\logbit\rho)
If we find the spectral decomposition of \rho, so that \lambda_k are its eigenvalues, the Von Neumann entropy reduces to the Shannon entropy for the probability distribution \{\lambda\}:
S(\rho) = H(\lambda_k) = -\sum _i \lambda _i \logbit \lambda _i

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Closed-s.title: Closed systems
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Closed-s.content: Closed systems are physical systems that evolve following Schrödinger’s equation, meaning that evolutions are unitary and invertible. Physically, this means that the system has no interactions with an external system.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Composit.title: Composite systems
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Composit.content:
Given two Hilbert spaces \mathcal{H}_A and \mathcal{H}_B, a composite system can be constructed out of the two:
\mathcal{H}_{AB} = \mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B
and vectors in \mathcal{H}_{AB} assume the form
\ket{\psi}_{AB} = \sum_{ij} \alpha _{ij}\ket{i}_A\otimes\ket{\varphi _j}_B
where \{\ket{i}_A\}_i and  \{\ket{\varphi _j}_B\}_j are bases for \mathcal{H}_A and \mathcal{H}_B respectively.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Convex-c.title: Convex combinations
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Convex-c.content:
Given elements \vec{v}_i of a vector space, we can build the convex combination of the \vec{v}_i from a probability distribution \{\lambda _i\}_i:
\sum_i \lambda_i \vec{v}_i

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Density-.title: Density matrix operators
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Density-.content:
Density matrix operators are a generalization of Pure states, where the presence of noise (or external perturbation) is admitted in the system, see Open systems. A generic density matrix operator \rho needs to satisfy the following properties:

\rho is a hermitian operator:

\rho = \rho ^\dagger

In order to satisfy the probabilistic interpretation of quantum mechanics:

\tr \rho = 1

Generally
\tr\rho ^2\leq 1
when the inequality is saturated, the state is said to be pure, otherwise it is said to be mixed. Mixed state are associated with the presence of classical noise in the system (see Ensembles).
\rho is positive semidefinite
\rho\geq 0
which means it can always be cast in the form
\rho = \sum_k p_k\op{\psi_k}{\psi _k}
from this form (called spectral decomposition), it is clear that any mixed state can be expressed as a convex combination of pure states; this has an immediate connection to Ensembles.

Space of density operators
\sigma(\mathcal{H}) = \left\{\rho: \rho\textrm{ is a density matrix operator}\right\}
\sigma(\mathcal{H}) is a convex space, meaning that it is closed under Convex combinations:
\sum _j p_j\rho _j\in \sigma(\mathcal{H})
The border (vertices and curve lines) of \sigma(\mathcal{H}) represent pure states.
Open systems
Consider an open system \mathcal{H}_S interacting with an environment \mathcal{H}_E; the state of the total system is
\rho _{SE} \in \sigma\left(\mathcal{H}_{SE}\right)
it is possible to recover the information of the state of the system S from \rho _{SE} by performing a Partial trace operation:
\rho _S=\tr _E \rho _{SE}
this operator is called reduced density matrix.
Types of joint states
States in a composite system \mathcal{H}_{AB} = \mathcal{H_A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_B, called joint states, can be categorized as follows:

Factorized states, which can be cast in the form
\rho_{AB} = \rho _A\otimes\tau _B
where \rho _A\in \sigma(\mathcal{H}_A) and \tau _B\in \sigma(\mathcal{H}_B).
Separable states, which are Convex combinations of factorized states:
\rho_{AB} =\sum _i p_i \rho ^{(i)} _A\otimes\tau^{(i)} _B
where \rho _A^{(i)}\in \sigma(\mathcal{H}_A) and \tau _B^{(i)}\in \sigma(\mathcal{H}_B)
Entangled states (or non separable), which cannot be expressed as convex combinations of factorized states. Entangled state represent states whose correlations between the reduced density matrices of the composite system are not just classical (as is the case for separable states).

Pure states
Pure composite states are either factorized
\ket{\psi} _{AB} = \ket{\psi}_A\ket{\phi}_B
or entangled (not factorized). These two cases can be distinguished through the Schmidt decomposition.
The convex combination of factorized states only works in the density matrix operator framework.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Ensemble.title: Ensembles
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Ensemble.content:
State ensembles are statistical collections of pure states. It is useful to define them through a real-world scenario: suppose that we have a machine capable of preparing pure states (state preparation device), however the machine is not perfect, leading to the creation of a set of states \{\ket{\psi}_i\}_i, whose rate follows a probability distribution p_i. Then, the ensemble is given by this set of states and the associated probability distribution.
\varepsilon\equiv \left\{\ket{\psi _i}\in\mathcal{H}, \quad p_i\textrm{ probabilty distribution}\right\}_i
Ensembles and density operators
Multiple ensembles can be associated with the same density operator, so that they are functionally (i.e. from a measurement perspective) the same.
How are different ensembles with the same density operator linked together?
Consider two ensembles
\varepsilon = \left\{\ket{\psi _i},p_i\right\}_i\qquad\varepsilon ' = \left\{\ket{\phi _i},q_i\right\}_i
Generally, the indices can span different ranges, however those can be brought to the same range by adding states with null weight.
Denote the equivalence relation between ensembles with \varepsilon \sim\varepsilon ', meaning that they can be described by the same density operator \rho, then
\varepsilon \sim\varepsilon '\Leftrightarrow \exists \,\mathcal{U} \textrm{ unitary}:\sqrt{p_i}\ket{\psi_i}=\mathcal{U}_{ij}\sqrt{q_j}\ket{\phi_j}
where \mathcal{U}_{ij} are the matrix elements of the unitary \mathcal{U}.
Proof
\Leftarrow
Remember the Orthogonality relation for unitaries:
\sum _l \mathcal{U}_{il}\mathcal{U}^*_{jl} = \delta _{ij}
\sum _l \mathcal{U}^*_{li}\mathcal{U}_{lj} = \delta _{ij}
Construct the density operators associated with the two ensembles
\rho = \sum_i p_i\op{\psi_i}{\psi _i}
\rho ' = \sum_i q_i\op{\phi_i}{\phi _i}
Using the orthogonality relations and
\sqrt{p_i}\ket{\psi_i}=\mathcal{U}_{ij}\sqrt{q_j}\ket{\phi_j}
direct computation shows that \rho = \rho ^\prime
\Rightarrow
Consider two purifications of \rho, (whose system we denote with S, so \rho \rightarrow \rho _S), \ket{\psi}_{SR},\ket{\psi '}_{SR}
\ket{\psi}_{SR} \equiv \sum _i \sqrt{p_i}\ket{\psi_i}_S\ket{i}_R
\ket{\psi '}_{SR} \equiv \sum _i \sqrt{q_i}\ket{\phi_i}_S\ket{i}_R
Different purifications are linked by a local unitary U_R:
\ket{\psi '}_{SR} = \left(\id_S\otimes U_R\right)\ket{\psi}_{SR}
By computing \prescript{}{R}{\ip{i}{\psi'}}_{SR}  on both sides of the relation above, we arrive at
\sqrt{p_i}\ket{\psi_i}=\mathcal{U}_{ij}\sqrt{q_j}\ket{\phi_j}
where we define \mathcal{U}_{ij} \equiv \matel{i}{U_R}{j}.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Euler-ro.title: Euler rotations
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Euler-ro.content:
Given a rotation of \theta around a 3-dimensional axis \hat{n}, \exists\,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3 such that:
U_{\hat{n}} (\theta) = U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha_1)U_{\hat{x}}(\alpha_2)U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha _3)
There exists a generalized version of this theorem, relying on rotations around two arbitrary, non necessarily orthogonal, axes. The number of rotations required depends on “how orthogonal” the two axes are.
Generalized Euler rotations

Using:
U^\dagger_{\hat{n}}(\theta)\sigma _i U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)= \sum_j\left(R(\theta)_{\hat{n}}\right)_{ij}\sigma_j
We find the action of a rotation unitary upon another rotation unitary:
\begin{split}U^\dagger_{\hat{n}}(\theta)U_{\hat{m}}(\phi) U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)& = \exp\left[-\frac{i}{2}\sum_i m_iU^\dagger_{\hat{n}}(\theta)\sigma_i U_{\hat{n}}(\theta) \phi\right]\\&= \exp\left[-\frac{i}{2}\sum_{ij} m_i\left(R(\theta)_{\hat{n}}\right)_{ij}\sigma_j \phi\right]\\ &= U_{R_{\hat{n}}(-\theta){\hat{m}}}(\phi)\end{split}
Basically, given the possibility of performing rotations around two non-orthogonal vectors, rotations around all the vectors obtained by rotating the original vectors around one another are also possible. Using this trick, it is possible to generate at least a pair of orthogonal vectors, from which we return to the original Euler rotations.
Lemma for unitaries
Statement
We can prove that, given a unitary U\in SU(2):
U = (\textrm{global phase}) AXBXC
where A,B,C are unitaries such that ABC=\mathrm{Id}.
Proof
Starting from Euler’ theorem we have:
U = (\textrm{global phase}) U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha)U_{\hat{y}}(\beta)U_{\hat{z}}(\delta)
Using XYX = -Y:
XU_{\hat{y}}(\beta)X = U_{\hat{y}}(-\beta)
same thing for Z:
XU_{\hat{z}}(\beta)X = U_{\hat{z}}(-\beta)
so that:
U = (\textrm{global phase}) U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha)U_{\hat{y}}(\beta/2)XU_{\hat{y}}(-\beta/2) XU_{\hat{z}}(\delta)
U = (\textrm{global phase}) U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha)U_{\hat{y}}(\beta/2)XU_{\hat{y}}(-\beta/2) XXU_{\hat{z}}\left(-\frac{\delta+\alpha}{2}\right)XU_{\hat{z}}\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right)
U = (\textrm{global phase}) U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha)U_{\hat{y}}(\beta/2)XU_{\hat{y}}(-\beta/2) U_{\hat{z}}\left(-\frac{\delta+\alpha}{2}\right)XU_{\hat{z}}\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right)
Now we can claim
A \equiv U_{\hat{z}}(\alpha)U_{\hat{y}}(\beta/2)
B\equiv U_{\hat{y}}(-\beta/2) U_{\hat{z}}\left(-\frac{\delta+\alpha}{2}\right)
C \equiv U_{\hat{z}}\left(\frac{\delta-\alpha}{2}\right)
and
ABC = \mathrm{Id}

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Heisenbe.title: Heisenberg-Weyl operators

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Open-sys.title: Open systems
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Open-sys.content:
Open quantum systems describe physical systems that present interactions with an external system (conventionally called environment) over which we assume to have no control (can’t perform measurements etc.). Let us call the Hilbert space of the system that we control \mathcal{H}_S and \mathcal{H}_E the Hilbert space associated to the environment; then, the composite (total) system is denoted by
\mathcal{H}_{SE} = \mathcal{H} _S\otimes\mathcal{H}_E
We can always assume \mathcal{H}_{SE} to be a closed system, so that its states evolve following unitary transformations.
When we discard the system of the environment, its action lingers on the system \mathcal{H}_S in the form of noise ⇒ classical noise is the result of the interaction with the system with an external inaccessible environment (see Purification).

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Operator.title: Operator norm
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Operator.content:
Given an operator
\theta \in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H})
the operator norm is defined by
\norm{\theta}_\infty \equiv \sup _{\norm{\ket{v}}=1}\norm{\theta\ket{v}}
where \ket{v} is a vector of the Hilbert space

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Orthogon.title: Orthogonality relation for unitaries

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Partial-.title: Partial trace
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Partial-.content:
Given an operator \theta_{AB} lying in a composite system \mathcal{H}_{AB}:
\theta_{AB} \in \mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{H}_{AB}\right)
the partial trace operation can be performed on the operator, where a trace is performed only on the elements of one of the systems composing \mathcal{H}_{AB}:
\begin{split}
\theta _B=\tr _A \theta _{AB} &\equiv \sum _i\prescript{}{A}{\bra{\phi_i}}\theta_{AB}\ket{\phi_i}_{A},\\
\theta _A=\tr _B \theta _{AB} &\equiv \sum _i
\prescript{}{B}{\bra{\psi_i}}\theta_{AB}\ket{\psi_i}_{B},
\end{split}
where \{\ket{\phi _i}_A\}_i and \{\ket{\psi _j}_B\}_j are bases for the systems composing \mathcal{H}_{AB}.
It can be proven that the partial trace operation is a LCPT map.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Partial-.title: Partial transpose

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Pauli-op.title: Pauli operators
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Pauli-op.content:
The Pauli operators are the elements of the \mathrm{su}(2) algebra. In quantum computation, they are usually denoted by X,Y,Z:
X \sim \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}
Y \sim \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}
Z \sim \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}
They are hermitian and trace-less operators.
Pauli algebra
Denote a the Pauli matrices with:
\sigma_1 = X\quad\sigma_2 = Y\quad \sigma_3 = Z
The algebra of the group is:
\left[\sigma_i,\sigma_j\right]=2\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k
The anticommutator relation is:
\left\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\right\}=2\delta_{ij}
A useful relation to remember is:
\sigma_i\sigma_j =\delta_{ij} +i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k
Square root of Pauli’s
For reference, here are the square roots of the Pauli matrices: wip
\sqrt{X} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i &1-i\\1-i & 1+i\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\left((1+i)\id + (1-i) X\right)
Pauli group for n qubits
We can consider the action of Pauli operators P_i =\mathrm{Id},X,Y,Z acting on n qubits. This is a representation of the Pauli Group:
\mathcal{P}_n\equiv \left\{\omega \bigotimes_{i=0}^{n-1}P_i: \omega \in\left\{1,-1,i,-i\right\}\right\}

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Polar-de.title: Polar decomposition

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Pure-sta.title: Pure states

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Purifica.title: Purification
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Purifica.content:
Given a mixed state (see Density matrix operators) \rho _A\in\sigma(\mathcal{H}_A), it is always possible to introduce an auxiliary system R such that the state of the composite system AR is pure and the Partial trace over the auxiliary system returns the original state.
\forall \rho _A\in\sigma(\mathcal{H}_A), \exists \mathcal{H}_R:
\rho_{AR}\in\sigma(\mathcal{H}_{AR}) \textrm{ is pure and }\tr_R\rho_{AR} = \rho _A 
Proof
We can build the purified state directly for a generic \rho _A:
\rho _A = \sum _i p_i \ket{\psi_i}_A\bra{\psi_i}
we can always choose the dimension of the reference system and we pick an orthonormal basis for it \{\ket{i}_R\}_i; then we build the pure state:
\ket{\psi}_{AB} \equiv \sum _i \sqrt{p_i}\ket{\psi_i}_A\ket{i}_B
we can verify by direct computation that this state is correctly normalized and the partial trace over B satisfies the requirement.
Different purifications
The purification process is not unique and different purifications can be found. Given \rho _A and its purification \ket{\psi}_{AR}, we have:
\ket{\psi}_{AR},\ket{\psi '}_{AR} \,\textrm{ are two different purifications of }\rho _A
\Updownarrow
\exists U_R \textrm{ local unitary on } R:\ket{\psi '}_{AR} = \left(\mathrm{Id}_A\otimes U_R\right)\ket{\psi}_{AR}
\Uparrow
This is easy, just perform the partial trace on R.
\Downarrow
Apply the Schmidt decomposition:
\ket{\psi ^{\prime}}_{AR} = \sum _k \lambda _k \ket{\phi ^{(k)}}_A \ket{\varphi ^{\prime(k)}}_R
\ket{\psi }_{AR} = \sum _k \lambda _k \ket{\phi ^{(k)}}_A\ket{\varphi  ^{(k)}}_R
Given that \ket{\varphi  ^{(k)}}_R and \ket{\varphi  '^{(k)}}_R form a basis for R, they must be linked by a unitary transformation, we call it U_R, proving the theorem.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Qubits.title: Qubits
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Qubits.content:
Qubits are usually considered the information units of quantum information. Mathematically speaking, they are states of the density matrix space of a 2 dimensional Hilbert space, whose basis is generally chosen from the eigenvectors of the Pauli operators.
\rho \in \sigma(\mathcal{H}_2)
\rho \sim \begin{pmatrix}p & \gamma \\ \gamma ^* & 1-p\end{pmatrix}
where 0\leq p \leq 1 and
\abs{\gamma} \leq \sqrt{p(1-p)}
This relation is saturated by pure states.
Bloch sphere

An insightful representation for these objects is given by the Bloch sphere, depicted above.
Any linear operator acting on \mathcal{H}_2 can be expressed as a linear combination of Pauli operators and the identity:
\theta\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_2)
\theta = \sum _\mu \alpha _\mu\sigma _\mu
\sigma _\mu \equiv (1,\vec{\sigma})
In the case of density matrix operators \rho, the constraints on the operators themselves translate into constraints on the a_\mu:

\rho = \rho ^\dagger\Rightarrow \alpha_\mu \in\mathbb{R} \quad\forall \mu
\tr \rho =1\Rightarrow \alpha _0 = 1/2
\rho \geq 0\Rightarrow \norm{\vec{\alpha}}\leq 1/2,\qquad \alpha _\mu \alpha ^\mu \geq 0
We define the Bloch vector (v in the picture, r here) as \vec{r} \equiv 2\vec{\alpha}, so that:

\rho =\frac{1}{2}\left(\id + \vec{r}\cdot\vec{\sigma}\right)
\norm{\vec{r}}\leq 1
Pure states saturate the last inequality.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Schmidt-.title: Schmidt decomposition
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Schmidt-.content:
The Schmidt decomposition theorem allows to distinguish entangled states from separable states (see Density matrix operators) when the state of the composite system is pure
Theorem
Given a pure joint state \ket{\psi }_{AB}\in\mathcal{H}_{AB} and orthonormal bases for the composing systems A,B, \{\ket{i}_A\}_i , \{\ket{j}_B\}_j,
\ket{\psi}_{AB} = \sum_{ij}\alpha _{ij} \ket{i}_A\ket{j}_B
\alpha _{ij} \equiv \prescript{}{A}{\bra{i}}\prescript{}{B}{\bra{j}}\,\ket{\psi}_{AB}\qquad\sum_{ij}\abs{\alpha _{ij}}^2 =1
The Schmidt decomposition theorem states that \exists \{\ket{\phi ^{(i)}}_A\}_i, \{\ket{\varphi ^{(j)}}_B\}_j  bases for the composing systems A,B, and \exists \{\lambda _k\}_k, \lambda _k\geq 0\in \mathbb{R}, \sum_k \lambda _k ^2 =1 such that:
\ket{\psi } _{AB} = \sum _{k=1} ^r \lambda _k \ket{\phi ^{(k)}}_A\ket{\varphi ^{(k)}}_B
where r is called the Schmidt rank of the state,
r\leq \min \{\dim\mathcal{H}_A,\dim\mathcal{H}_B\}
Proof
\ket{\psi}_{AB} = \sum_{ij}\alpha _{ij} \ket{i}_A\ket{j}_B
\alpha _{ij} is generally a rectangular matrix, however it can always be cast into a square matrix by filling the shorter side with 0 entries. Assume it is square then, without loss of generality. The SVD can be applied to it:
\alpha _{ij} = \sum _{l} U_{il}D_{ll} V_{lj}
Substituting into the expression of the joint state:
\ket{\psi}_{AB} = \sum_{ij}\sum _{l} U_{il}D_{ll} V_{lj} \ket{i}_A\ket{j}_B
Unitary transformations send a basis into another basis; define the two new bases:
\ket{\phi ^{(l)}}_A\equiv \sum_i U_{il}\ket{i}_A
\ket{\varphi ^{(l)}}_B\equiv \sum_j U_{jl}\ket{j}_B
Initially we have sent A into a higher dimensional space; is the new basis actually a basis for the original A? In order to have an \alpha which presents the 0’s in the correct spots, those 0’s need to be in the same positions in U, so everything works. The joint state becomes
\ket{\psi}_{AB} = \sum _{l} D_{ll}\ket{\phi ^{(l)}}_A\ket{\varphi ^{(l)}}_B
The D_{ll} are non negative, is the sum of their squares =1?
\tr D^2 = \tr UDDU^\dagger = \tr UDVV^\dagger DU^\dagger = \tr \alpha ^\dagger\alpha = 1
therefore the D_{ll} are exactly the \lambda _l of the theorem.
r corresponds to the rank of D
\mathrm{rank} D =\mathrm{rank}\sqrt{\alpha ^\dagger\alpha} \leq \min \{\dim\mathcal{H}_A,\dim\mathcal{H}_B\}
Implications
After performing a Schmidt decomposition, if we apply the Partial trace to the joint state it becomes clear that the \lambda ^2 _k are the eigenvalues of the reduced density matrix, with one of the bases \{\ket{\phi ^{(i)}}_A\}_i, \{\ket{\varphi ^{(j)}}_B\}_j being composed of the eigenvectors of the operator. This means that the reduced density matrices of a joint pure state are isospectral.
Furthermore, if the joint state is separable, we know automatically that r=1, so that entangled pure states share the property r\neq 1.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Singular.title: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Singular.content:
It is a generalization of diagonalization for non-hermitian operators.
\forall \theta \in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}), \exists U,V \textrm{ unitaries}, D\textrm{ diagonal}, D\geq 0 : \theta = UDV
Proof
The proof relies on the Polar decomposition of \theta:
\theta = KU = VDV^\dagger U \equiv VDU_1
where U_1 is still unitary
Spectrum
By construction, the SVD eigenvalues (i.e. the eigenvalues of D) are the same as those of the operators K,J in the polar decomposition.

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Superope.title: Superoperators

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Trace-no.title: Trace norm
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Trace-no.content:
The trace norm for an operator \theta is defined as follows
\norm{\theta}_1 \equiv \tr \sqrt{\theta ^\dagger \theta}
Properties

The trace norm of an operator is the same as the trace norm of its hermitian,
\norm{\theta}_1 = \norm{\theta ^\dagger}_1
which can be proven thanks to the Polar decomposition:
\theta = KU = UJ
where K,J have the same spectrum

\tr \sqrt{\theta ^\dagger \theta} = \tr \sqrt{J ^\dagger J}

Quantum-Information/Foundations/Vectoriz.title: Vectorization
Quantum-Information/Foundations/Vectoriz.content:
Given a matrix
M_{B\leftarrow A}=\sum_{ij}m_{ij}\ket{i}_B\bra{j}_A,
then its vectorization is given by:
\ketvec{M_{B\leftarrow A}}\equiv\mathrm{vec}\left(M_{B\leftarrow A}\right) = \sum_{ij}m_{ij}\ket{j}_A\ket{i}_B

Quantum-Information/Measurements/Born-ru.title: Born rule
Quantum-Information/Measurements/Born-ru.content:
Given a state \ket{\psi}\in \mathcal{H} and a projective measurement device, characterized by the observable \theta =\sum _j\lambda _j \op{j}{j}, the Born rule predicts the rate of a given measurement outcome j
P_j(\ket{\psi}) = \abs{\ip{j}{\psi}}^2
Born rule for ensambles
Suppose that a projective measurement \theta =\sum _j\lambda _j \op{j}{j} is performed on an ensemble generated by a state preparation device \varepsilon
\varepsilon\equiv \left\{\ket{\psi}_i\in\mathcal{H}, \quad p_i\textrm{ probabilty distribution}\right\}
then, the Born rule in this context becomes
P_j (\varepsilon) = \sum _k p_k \abs{\ip{j}{\psi _k}}^2
Born rule for density matrices
Using Density matrix operators
\rho = \sum_k p_k\op{\psi_k}{\psi _k}
The Born rule becomes
P_j(\rho) = \ev{j}{\rho}

Quantum-Information/Measurements/Helstro.title: Helstrom's theorem
Quantum-Information/Measurements/Helstro.content:
Helstrom’s theorem provides a lower bound on the error associated with a POVM built to discriminate the two states composing a given ensemble.
\varepsilon = \left\{\rho _1,\rho _2;p_1,p_2=1-p_1\right\}
Denote the POVM as
\{E_1,E_2\}
P_i(\rho _j) = \tr(E_i\rho_j)
We define the error probability by summing the probabilities all possible sources of error
P_{error} = p_1P_2(\rho _1)+ p_2P_1(\rho _2)
Statement
\min P_{error} = \frac{1}{2} \left(1-\norm{p_1\rho _1 - p _2 \rho _2}_1\right)
where \norm{\cdot}_1 is the Trace norm.

\min P_{error} \leq \frac{1}{2}
If \rho _1, \rho _2 are orthogonal:
\rho _1\rho _2 = \rho _1 \rho _2 = 0
then \min P_{error}=0.

Proof

Quantum-Information/Measurements/Naimark.title: Naimark's theorem
Quantum-Information/Measurements/Naimark.content:
Naimark’s dilation theorem guarantees that a POVM set identifies at least one measurement apparatus (parallelism with ensemble equivalence).
Statement
Given a system S in the state \rho _S and a set of operators satisfying

E_j \geq 0\qquad \forall j
\sum _j E_j = \id
Then we can always choose a system R in the state \tau _R and a measurement unitary V_{SR} such that

P_j(\rho) = \tr (E_j \rho)
Proof
We construct the measurement unitary and the reference system given a certain POVM set; we choose the dimension of R to match the number of possible measurement outcomes. Then, we specify the action of the unitary on the states \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R:
V_{SR} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R\equiv\sum _j \left(V_j ^{(S)}\sqrt{E_j ^{(S)}}\ket{\psi} _S\right)\ket{j}_R
Where V_j ^{(S)} is a generic local unitary. Is the scalar product conserved on the states \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R?
\prescript{}{R}{\bra{0}}\prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R =\prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}} \ket{\psi}_S =\prescript{}{R}{\bra{0}}\prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}}V^\dagger_{SR}V_{SR} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R
\prescript{}{R}{\bra{0}}\prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}}V^\dagger_{SR}V_{SR} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R = \sum _j\prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}}E_j\ket{\psi}_S = \prescript{}{S}{\bra{\phi}} \ket{\psi}_S
The unitary can be extended to all the other subspaces. Finally, performing a projective measurement on the reference system (the process is linear so we can focus on the special case where \rho is a pure state)
\rho _S = \ket{\psi}_S\bra{\psi}
P_j (\rho) = \tr_S\left( \,\prescript{}{R}{\matel{j}{V_{SR}}{0}}_R \,\ket{\psi}_S\bra{\psi}\,\prescript{}{R}{\matel{0}{V_{SR}^\dagger }{j}}_R\right) = ...=\tr(E_j\rho)

Quantum-Information/Measurements/Non-ort.title: Non orthogonal state discrimination
Quantum-Information/Measurements/Non-ort.content:
Potentially, an infinite amount of classical information could be encoded into a qubit (or any quantum system); however, the problem is not the encoding, but rather the decoding. In fact, it can be proven that only orthogonal states can be distinguished through a one-shot quantum measurement process.
Consider two non orthogonal Pure states \ket{\psi _1},\ket{\psi _2}
\ip{\psi_1}{\psi _2}\neq 0
and a POVM tentatively capable of distinguishing between the two
\exists? \{E_1,E_2\}:
P_{i}(\ket{\psi_j}) = \tr\left(\op{\psi _j}{\psi_j }E_i\right) = \delta _{ij}
From E_1 + E_2 = \id:
\ev{\psi_1}{E_2} = \ev{\psi_1}{1- E_1} = 0
\ev{\psi_1}{E_1} =\tr(E_1\op{\psi _1}{\psi_1})= 1
Since E_i\geq 0, their eigenvalues are non negative.
\left\{\begin{array}{l}\ev{\psi_1}{E_2} \geq 0 \\ \ev{\psi_1}{E_2} = 0\end{array}\right.\quad\Rightarrow \exists\lambda^{(2)}_1 = 0, E_2\ket{\psi_1} = \lambda^{(2)}_1\ket{\psi _1}
At the same time, \ket{\psi _2} is also an eigenvector of E_2, with associated eigenvalue 1. But that would imply that  \ket{\psi _1},\ket{\psi _2} form an eigenbasis, meaning they are orthogonal, therefore this POVM does not exist.

Quantum-Information/Measurements/POVM's.title: POVM's
Quantum-Information/Measurements/POVM's.content:
Measurement processes in quantum mechanics are generalized by the POVM (Positive Operator-Valued Measure) formalism

The measurement process goes as follows: the system S in the state \rho _S is coupled with a reference system R in the state \tau _R (ideally, this can be sent to a pure state often denoted with \ket{0}), which interacts with S through a global unitary V_{SR} (see Open systems, Quantum channel representations). The evolved global state is:
\rho ' _{SR} = V_{SR} \left(\rho _S\tau _R\right)V_{SR}^\dagger
Then we can perform a projective measurement on the reduced density matrix in R
\tau ' _R = \tr _S\rho ' _{SR} =\tr_S\left( V_{SR} \left(\rho _S\tau _R\right)V_{SR}^\dagger\right)
The rate for each measurement outcome is computed through the Born rule:
P_j (\rho) = \prescript{}{R}{\ev{j}{\tau ' _R}}_R = \tr_S\left(\prescript{}{R}{\ev{j}{V_{SR} \left(\rho _S\tau _R\right)V_{SR}^\dagger}}_R \right)
Using a spectral decomposition for \tau _R
\tau _r = \sum _k q_k \ket{k}_R\bra{k}
P_j (\rho) = \tr_S\left(\sum _k q_k\,\prescript{}{R}{\matel{j}{V_{SR}}{k}}_R \,\rho _S\,\prescript{}{R}{\matel{k}{V_{SR}^\dagger }{j}}_R\right)
We define a set of operators:
E_j \equiv\sum _k q_k\, \prescript{}{R}{\matel{k}{V_{SR}^\dagger }{j}}_R\,\,\prescript{}{R}{\matel{j}{V_{SR}}{k}}_R
For all j; these operators act on the system S so that the Born rule becomes:
P_j (\rho) =\tr (E_j \rho)
Axiomatic definition
A POVM is given by a set of operators \{E_j\}_j that satisfy the following properties:

E_j \geq 0\qquad \forall j
\sum _j E_j = \id, which is needed for \sum _j P_j =1

Projective measurements
Projective measurements are a special case of POVM’s:
E_j = \op{j}{j}
\tr(E_j\rho) = \ev{j}{\rho}
which reproduces the Born rule
Evolution under measurement
Using the most general evolution during the measurement process, found explicitly in Naimark’s theorem:
V_{SR} \ket{\psi}_S\ket{0}_R\equiv\sum _j \left(V_j ^{(S)}\sqrt{E_j ^{(S)}}\ket{\psi} _S\right)\ket{j}_R
Define:
M_j ^{(S)}\equiv V_j ^{(S)}\sqrt{E_j ^{(S)}}
Compare this with the Kraus representation, where the M_j‘s are the Kraus operators and the \sqrt{E_j ^{(S)}} represent the Polar decomposition of the operators.
Focusing on the system S and assuming to have measured the outcome j:
\ket{\psi }_S \overset{j}{\mapsto}\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}M_j ^{(S)}\ket{\psi} _S
where N is just the normalization, equal to the probability of measuring j:
N=  P_j(\ket{\psi}) = \tr(E_j\op{\psi}{\psi})
This process is clearly non-linear and non-unitary, it becomes such if we assume to have performed the measurement process while not having checked the outcome.
In the general mixed state case:

If we check the outcome:

\rho_S \overset{j}{\mapsto}\frac{1}{N}M_j ^{(S)}\rho_S M^{(S)\dagger}_j

If we don’t:

\rho_S \mapsto \sum _j M_j ^{(S)}\rho_S M^{(S)\dagger}_j
compare this with the Kraus representation of quantum channels
Examples
Qubit population

Optic fiber

Quantum-Information/Measurements/Quantum.title: Quantum state tomography
Quantum-Information/Measurements/Quantum.content:
Reasoning
It can be proven (see Non orthogonal state discrimination) that we can distinguish two pure states through a POVM only when those two states are orthogonal. When that is not the case, however, we may still be able to discriminate those states by using many copies of them:
0<\abs{\ip{\psi _1}{\psi _2}}< 1 
\Downarrow
\abs{\left(\bra{\psi _1}^{\otimes N}\right)\left(\ket{\psi _2}^{\otimes N}\right)} = \abs{\ip{\psi _1}{\psi _2}}^N \overset{N\rightarrow\infty}{\rightarrow} 0
Main take: statistics used to recover information.
Tomography

Given a state preparation device producing an ensemble, we run the state preparation process N times and we perform measurements on the states produced in order to characterize the ensemble.
Qubit example
Recall the Bloch representation; a qubit is completely characterized by a vector in \mathbb{R}^3 with norm less than 1. Qubit tomography aims to measure this vector
\rho =\frac{1}{2}\left(\id + \vec{r}\cdot\vec{\sigma}\right)
How to measure \vec{r}? A useful property:
\sigma _i \sigma _j = \delta _{ij} + i\varepsilon _{ijk}\sigma _k
\tr\left(\sigma_i\sigma_j\right) = 2\delta _{ij}
\Downarrow
\tr \rho \sigma _j = r_j
Therefore, we perform projective measurements on the eigenbases of the Pauli operators.
