Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Dep.title: Dephasing channel
Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Dep.content:
Qubit
The dephasing channel \mathcal{D} (or phase flip channel) is a Pauli channel; its action on a qubit \rho is given by:
\mathcal{D}(\rho) = (1-p)\rho +p Z\rho Z, \quad p\in[0,1]
Note that:
Z\ket{+} = \ket{-}
Z\ket{-} = \ket{+}
So this channel introduces a probability of swapping the eigenvectors of the X operator (see Pauli operators)
The dephasing channel can be mapped into a Bit-flip channel through a Hadamard Gate

Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Dep.title: Depolarizing channel
Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Dep.content:
The depolarizing channel \Phi is a qubit channel. Its action on a linear operator \theta acting on \mathcal{H}_2 is given by
\Phi(\theta) =  p \theta +(1-p) (\id/2)(\tr\theta)
The last term is needed for explicit linearity in the qubit case. Applying this transformation on the Bloch sphere generates a movement along the radius towards the center of the sphere.
Depolarizing noise (resistance) is often used as benchmark for quantum devices, as it approximates the combination of all possible noises.
Note that the depolarizing channel is a Pauli channel.

Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Pau.title: Pauli channels
Quantum-Information/Notable-channels/Pau.content:
Qubit
Pauli channels are a generalization of dephasing channels and bit-flip channels. They correspond to applying a random Pauli operator according to a probability distribution:
\rho \mapsto \sum _{i,j=0} ^1 p_{ij} Z^i X^j \rho X^j Z^i
Qudit
The qudit equivalent to Pauli channels is obtained by replacing the Pauli operators in the map above with the corresponding Heisenberg-Weyl operators:
\rho \mapsto \sum _{i,j=0} ^{d-1}p_{ij} Z(i) X(j) \rho X^\dagger (j) Z^\dagger (i)

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Channel representations equivalence
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
Stinespring to Kraus
Given a channel in Stinespring representation (see Quantum channel representations)
\Phi \left(\rho _A\right) = \tr _E \left[U_{BE\leftarrow AE}\left(\rho _A \ket{0}_E\bra{0}\right)U^\dagger _{BE\leftarrow AE}\right]
We can derive its Kraus representation by carrying out the partial trace explicitly
\Phi \left(\rho _A\right) = \sum_l \prescript{}{E}{\bra{l}}U_{BE\leftarrow AE}\ket{0}_E\rho _A \,\prescript{}{E}{\bra{0}}U^\dagger _{BE\leftarrow AE}\ket{l}_E
Then, we define a Kraus element:
K_l \equiv \prescript{}{E}{\bra{l}}U_{BE\leftarrow AE}\ket{0}_E
K_l :\mathcal{H_A}\mapsto\mathcal{H}_B
The resulting Kraus set clearly satisfies
\sum_i K_i ^\dagger K_i =\id _A
and finally
\Phi\left(\rho_A\right) = \sum _i K_i \rho_A K _i ^{\dagger}

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Choi theorem
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
The complete positiveness of a superoperator \Psi can be verified by checking the positivity of the associated Choi matrix \Psi. This is a consequence of Choi’s theorem:
\Psi \textrm{ is completely positive}\Leftrightarrow \rho _{\Psi} \textrm{ is positive}.

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
The Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism identifies a one-to-one relation between Quantum channels and a special class of states in a composite system. Given a system S and a reference system R with the same dimension d, We define the space of density matrices whose Partial trace on S reduces to the completely chaotic state:
\sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}) = \left\{\rho_{SR}: \tr_S\rho _{SR} = \id_R/d\right\}
Then, any element of \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}) is the Choi state of a quantum channel acting on S and any channel acting on S can be described by an element of \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}):
\rho _{SR} \in \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}) \leftrightarrow \Phi\, LCPT
Since quantum channels are closed under Convex combinations, \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}) is a convex space itself.
Proof
\leftarrow
We need to prove that given the channel \Phi and its Choi state \rho ^\Phi _{SR} in SR, the action of the channel is described by
\Phi \left(\ket{\psi}_S\bra{\psi}\right) = d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\ket{\psi ^*}_R=d\,\tr _R \left(\ket{\psi}_R\bra{\psi} \left(\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\right)^{T_R}\right)
Once we achieve this, we only need to prove that \rho ^\Phi _{SR} \in \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}), but this trivially comes from the definition of Choi states.
Take a generic pure state in S:
\ket{\psi}_S =\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\alpha _i \ket{i}_S
and define its conjugate state:
\ket{\psi ^*}_S =\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\alpha ^* _i \ket{i}_S
Then we can prove that:
\Phi \left(\ket{\psi}_S\bra{\psi}\right) = d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\ket{\psi ^*}_R
in fact:
d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\ket{\psi ^*}_R = \sum_{kl}\Phi\left(\ket{k}_S\bra{l}\right)\alpha_k\alpha ^*_{l} = \Phi \left(\ket{\psi}_S\bra{\psi}\right)
As for the second equality, the left hand side is the expectation value of the Choi state on a vector of R, which can be expressed in trace form:
d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\ket{\psi ^*}_R =d\,\tr_R\left(\rho ^\Phi _{SR} \,\ket{\psi ^*}_R\bra{\psi ^*}\right)
Now we recognize that:

Since \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi} is hermitian, \ket{\psi^*}\bra{\psi^*} = (\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi})^T, where T is the Partial transpose operation
The trace is invariant under transpose
So that

d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\ket{\psi ^*}_R =d\,\tr_R\left(\rho ^\Phi _{SR} \,(\ket{\psi}_R\bra{\psi})^{T_R}\right) =d\,\tr _R \left(\ket{\psi}_R\bra{\psi} \left(\rho ^\Phi _{SR}\right)^{T_R}\right) 
\rightarrow
Take a state \rho _{SR} \in \sigma_{1_R}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}) and consider one of its purifications using an auxiliary system A
\ket{\psi}_{SRA}:\tr_A(\ket{\psi}_{SRA}\bra{\psi}) = \rho _{SR}
We can use Schmidt decomposition to write:
\ket{\psi}_{SRA} = \sum _l \lambda _l \ket{\varphi _l}_{SA}\ket{l}_R
where \{\ket{\varphi _l}_{SA}\} is a basis for SA. The requirement
\tr_{SA}(\ket{\psi}_{SRA}\bra{\psi}) = \id_R/d
sets a constraint on the \lambda _l: they all need to be equal to 1/\sqrt{d}
\ket{\psi}_{SRA} = \sum _l \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \ket{\varphi _l}_{SA}\ket{l}_R
Now we explicitly take the partial trace wrt A
\tr_A(\ket{\psi}_{SRA}\bra{\psi}) = \frac{1}{d}\sum _{ijk}\prescript{}{A}{\ip{k}{\varphi _i}}_{SA}\,\prescript{}{SA}{\ip{\varphi _j}{k}}_{A} \otimes\ket{i}_R\bra{j}
In order to prove that the right-hand side is a Choi state, we try to explicitly build the Kraus set for the associated channel:
K_ l \equiv \sum_m \prescript{}{A}{\ip{l}{\varphi _m}}_{SA}\,\,\prescript{}{S}{\bra{m}}
\sum_l K^\dagger _l K_l = \id_S
Then:
\tr_A(\ket{\psi}_{SRA}\bra{\psi}) = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{ijl} K_l \ket{i}_S\bra{j} K_l^\dagger\otimes\ket{i}_R\bra{j}
which is exactly the Choi state associated to the channel.

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Kraus from Choi
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
If one only has the output of a superoperator acting on a generic input state, determining whether the corresponding map is a channel could be a bit of a challenge. Specifically, while checking the trace conservation and the linearity is usually trivial, confirming the complete positivity is not so easy. One possible recipe to do so is the following:


                  
                  Check if a map is completely positive 
                  
                


Find the Choi matrix associated to the map \Phi:

\Phi \mapsto C_\Phi \equiv\frac{1}{d}\sum _{ij}\Phi \left(\ket{i}_A\bra{j}\right)\otimes \ket{i}_R\bra{j}

Compute the eigenvalues of C_\Phi
If all the eigenvalues are non-negative, the map is completely positive (see Choi theorem).



This procedure might work fine for qubits or even qutrits, but increasing the dimensionality could make the eigenvalue problem very hard to solve, especially when we want to solve it analytically (for example, for channels with dependency on a number of parameters or for arbitrary dimensionality).
An alternative procedure could consist in finding the Kraus operators from the Choi matrix and checking whether they satisfy the required conditions. How do we do that?


                  
                  Get Kraus operators from Choi matrix 
                  
                

Consider the Kraus operators K_l of a channel \Phi, their matrix expression being:
K_l = \sum_{mn}K_{mn} ^{(l)} \op{m}{n}
The Vectorization of this objects is:
\ketvec{K_l} = \sum_{mn}K_{mn} ^{(l)} \ket{m}\ket{n}
Computing the Choi matrix using the Kraus representation of \Phi, it can be seen that:
C_\Phi =\frac{1}{d}\sum_l\ketvec{K_l}\bravec{K_l}
Basically, the vectorization of a Kraus operator is an eigenvector of the Choi matrix.
Therefore, the procedure to find the Kraus operators from the Choi matrix works as follows:

Compute the Choi matrix C_\Phi
Try to rewrite the Choi matrix so that it is in the form

C_\Phi =\frac{1}{d}\sum_l\ketvec{K_l}\bravec{K_l}

From \ketvec{K_l},  apply a reshaping operator \mathrm{mat}() which from a d^2-dimensional vector outputs a d\times d matrix whose elements are:

(K_l)_{ij} = \left(\mathrm{mat}\left(\ketvec{K_l}\right)\right)_{ij} = \left(\ketvec{K_l}\right)_{i d + j}
Example implementation in python:
python 	  import numpy as np 	  v = np.array([v0, v1, v2, v3]) 	  d = 2 # Dimension of the subsystem  	  V = v.reshape((d, d))

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Kraus representation equivalence
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
Given the Kraus sets \mathcal{K} =\left\{K_i\right\}_i and \mathcal{K}^\prime=\left\{K ^\prime_i\right\}_i, they represent the same channel if and only if:
K ^\prime_i = \sum _j \mathcal{U}_{ij}K_j
where the \mathcal{U}_{ij} are the matrix elements of an isometry and they satisfy the orthogonality relations

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: LOCC protocols
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
Local Operations and Classical Communications (LOCC) are a class of Quantum channels which respond to a specific protocol: suppose the existence of two parties, Alice and Bob, who share a state in their composite system AB and classical line of communication. Then, they perform a LOCC process if they restrict themselves to doing an arbitrary combination of the following operations:

Perform local operations on their respective systems A and B
Use the classical communication line to exchange bit of information (e.g. outcomes of measurements)
LOCC protocols send separable states into separable states (see Density matrix operators), i.e. they do not generate Entangled states.

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Minimal Kraus representation
Quantum channel representations
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
Axiomatic representation - LCPT
Quantum channels are also called LCPT maps, from the requirements that a superoperator needs to satisfy in order to be considered a physical transformation:

Linearity
Complete Positivity: in general, a positive superoperator is an object that maps positive operators into positive operators; here the requirement is stricter: in fact, given a positive operator in a composite system \theta _{SR}\geq 0, \theta _{SR}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{SR}), we say that a superoperator \Phi _S acting on S is completely positive if the operator
\Phi_S\otimes\chid_R
is positive for any choice of R.
\Phi \,\textrm{ is CP}\Leftrightarrow \Phi \otimes \chid _R \,\textrm{ is P} \quad\forall R
An example of map which is positive but not completely positive can be found in the Partial transpose operation, which can be useful to characterize the Entangled states of a Composite systems, see PPT criterion.
Trace preservation, meaning that the action of quantum channels leave the trace of the input operator unchanged

Stinespring representation
This representation is the most physically intuitive one and the one described in Quantum channels. It is based on the action of a Stinespring dilation, for an operator \theta _A\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_A):
\mathfrak{U}_{A\mapsto BE}:\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_A)\mapsto \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{BE})
\theta_{A}\xmapsto{\mathfrak{U}_{A\mapsto BE}} U_{BE\leftarrow AE} \left(\theta_{A} \otimes \ket{0}_E\bra{0}\right)U_{BE\leftarrow AE}^{\dagger}
The channel, let us call it \Phi, is then found by taking the Partial trace w.r.t. the environment:
\Phi =\tr_E\circ\mathfrak{U}_{A\mapsto BE}
\Phi : \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_A)\mapsto \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{B})
Kraus representation
The Kraus representation is characterized by a set of operators \mathcal{K} = \left\{K_i\right\}_i on \mathcal{H} such that:
\sum _i K^{\dagger}_i K_i = \id
The set \mathcal{K} describes a quantum channel \Phi, defined by:
\Phi\left(\rho\right) = \sum _i K_i \rho K _i ^{\dagger}
The set \mathcal{K} is called Kraus set, while the K_i‘s are called Kraus operators.
Choi-Jamiołkowski representation
The action of a channel \Phi can be described by its Choi state \rho _\Phi:
\rho _\Phi = \frac{1}{d}\sum _{ij}\Phi \left(\ket{i}_A\bra{j}\right)\otimes \ket{i}_R\bra{j}
where d is the dimension of the input system A, through the relation:
\Phi \left(\ket{\psi}_A\bra{\psi}\right) = d\,\prescript{}{R}{\bra{\psi ^*}}\rho_\Phi\ket{\psi ^*}_R=d\,\tr _R \left(\ket{\psi}_R\bra{\psi} \left(\rho _\Phi\right)^{T_R}\right)
where
\ket{\psi} =\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\alpha _i \ket{i} \Rightarrow\ket{\psi ^*} \equiv \sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\alpha^{*} _i \ket{i}
and T_A is the Partial transpose acting on A. This is proven in Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism.
Linearity guarantees that this relation works for any input state

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Quantum channels
Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.content:
The idea of a quantum channel refers to a process which takes a quantum state as an input and outputs a different (evolved) quantum state.
In traditional quantum mechanics, this process is described by unitary transformations; however, this only works for Closed systems, while a more general approach is needed in the case of Open systems.
The main idea behind quantum channels consists in coupling the open system that undergoes evolution (let us call it S) with an external system, called environment (E). We can safely assume that the evolution of the composite system SE is going to be unitary, as we could inglobate in E anything that is not S, making SE a closed system. Then we can evolve the system SE following an appropriate unitary transformation. Finally, performing a partial trace on SE w.r.t. E we can discard all the information related to the environment, which leaves us with the evolved state in the system S.
This picture reflects the Stinespring representation of quantum channels, seen in Quantum channel representations.
Space of quantum channels
LCPT channels are closed under Convex combinations
\Phi _x \,\textrm{ LCPT}\Rightarrow\sum_x p_x\Phi _x\,\textrm{ LCPT}
The space of LCPT maps is a convex space whose border are identified by unitary transformations.

Quantum-Information/Open-system-dynamics.title: Stinespring dilation

Quantum-Information/Protocols/Entangleme.title: Entanglement swapping
Quantum-Information/Protocols/Entangleme.content:
Consider n labs, that present connections through entanglement. Entanglement swapping tries to compensate for the noise generated by distances between labs, which degrade entanglement. Focus on n=3 example
\rho _{ABC}=\frac{1}{2} \ket{0}_C\bra{0}\,\ket{\phi_+}_{AB}\bra{\phi _+}+\frac{1}{2} \ket{1}_C\bra{1}\,\ket{\phi_-}_{AB}\bra{\phi _-}
turns out that AB are separable
\rho _{AB} = ... = \frac{1}{2}\left(\ket{0}_A\bra{0}\,\ket{0}_B\bra{0}+\ket{1}_A\bra{1}\,\ket{1}_B\bra{1}\right)
The PPT criterion tells us that ABC is entangled. Suppose C measures their qubit in the Computational basis. After the measurement, AB will be maximally entangled. C can send outcome (classically) to AB who now know which Bell pair they share.
This is basically the Quantum teleportation protocol, Charlie teleports the qubit C1 to Bob

Quantum-Information/Protocols/Impossible.title: Impossible machines
Quantum-Information/Protocols/Impossible.content:
The following is a collection of protocols/machines which are forbidden due to the laws of quantum mechanics

Bell telephone
Quantum cloner
Classical teleportation machine
Joint measurement of incompatible observables
Universal NOT gate
Many of these machines are impossible due to the impossibility of building a Bell telephone

Approximate impossible machines

Quantum-Information/Protocols/Quantum-te.title: Quantum teleportation
Quantum-Information/Protocols/Quantum-te.content:
Alice wants to send a qudit state \ket{\varphi}_{A^\prime} in her lab in the system A^\prime to Bob. Alice and Bob share a previously prepared maximally entangled qudit pair \ket{\psi_{0,0}}_{AB} in their respective systems A,B.
\ket{\varphi} = \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} \alpha _i \ket{i},
\ket{\psi_{0,0}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\ket{k}\ket{k}.
Protocol:

The total state at the beginning of the process is:

\ket{\psi _{0,0}}_{AB}\ket{\varphi}_{A^\prime} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{ij}\alpha _i\ket{j}_A\ket{j}_B\ket{i}_{A^\prime}.

Alice performs a projective measurement on the Bell basis on her systems A,A^\prime:
\ket{\psi _{a,b}}_{AA^\prime}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\left(\mathrm{Id}^{(A)}\otimes W_{a,b}^{(A^\prime)}\right)\ket{j}_A\ket{j}_{A^\prime}
It’s useful to note here that:
\sum_k \prescript{}{A}{\bra{k}}U_A\ket{\psi}_A\ket{k}_B=U_B\ket{\psi}_B
Contracting this state \ket{\psi _{a,b}}_{AA^\prime} with \ket{\psi _{0,0}}_{AB}\ket{\varphi}_{A^\prime} we obtain, up to a global phase:
\frac{1}{d}X(-b)Z(-a)\ket{\varphi}_B.
which means that each outcome (a,b) can happen with the same probability 1/d^2 and the corresponding output state on Bob’s system is Z(-a)X(-b)\ket{\varphi}_B.
Alice sends the outcome (a,b) of the experiment to Bob through a classical communication line.
Bob reads the outcome and performs a unitary transformation Z(a)X(b) on his system, obtaining \ket{\varphi}_B.

Quantum-Information/Protocols/Super-dens.title: Super-dense coding
Quantum-Information/Protocols/Super-dens.content:
Alice chooses the Qubits she wants to send. In this scenario 1\mathrm{qbit}= 1\mathrm{bit}. If we add a maximally entangled state, 1\mathrm{qbit} +1\mathrm{ebit}= 2\mathrm{bit}. Suppose Alice and Bob share a pair of qubits \ket{\phi ^+}_{AB} prepared by a third party. This additional resource can be exploited by Alice to send 2 bits of classical info. In fact, Alice can decide to change the pair locally to send it in another Bell state. Then, Alice sends the qubit A to Bob, who now has the whole pair ⇒ he performs projective measurement on Bell basis ⇒ 2 bits of info.
If channel is not perfect, performance gain is much higher than 2.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Consider the functions:
f_a(x) = x\cdot a = \mathrm{mod}_2\left[\sum _j x_ja_j\right]
The Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm is a quantum algorithm capable of determining the target bit string a in just one interrogation. Classically, we would need n interrogations.

The functioning of this algorithm is basically the same as Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm’s. The output in A reads:
\sum _{x,y}\frac{(-1)^{f_a(x)+x\cdot y}\ket{y}}{N}
This is exactly \ket{a}, which is evident when projecting onto that vector.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Consider binary functions:
f:\{0,1\}\mapsto\{0,1\}
there are 4 possible functions of this type:
f_1(x) = x
f_2(x) = \bar{x}
f_3(x) = 0
f_4(x) = 1
f_1,f_2 are called balanced functions, while the other are called constant functions.
Consider a situation where you are given a black box, which applies one of the four binary functions above. How many times do we need to apply the black box in order to understand whether the function inside is balanced or constant? Classically, we would need 2 interrogations, in the quantum case one is enough, through the Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm.
Implementation

We use a Uf gate and a few Hadamard gates as seen in the picture. We are just interested in the A register, the B register can be discarded.
The the algorithm follows the steps below:

Initialize qubits in \ket{0}_A\ket{1}_B
Apply Hadamard gates to both registries
Apply U_f gate, of which we want to find to which category the f belongs
Apply Hadamard gate to the A registry
Measurement
The induced transformation is:

\ket{0}_A\ket{1}_B \mapsto\ket{+}_A\ket{-}_B\mapsto\left(\frac{(-1)^{f(0)}\ket{0}_A+(-1)^{f(1)}\ket{1}_A}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\ket{-}_B 
aside a global phase, in the A registry we find \ket{+} if f is constant and \ket{-} if f is balanced; applying the last Hadamard, we transform those two configurations, respectively, into \ket{0}, \ket{1}
Generalization
For boolean functions of the type:
f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}
the division balanced/constant functions is not exhaustive (some functions are neither). There are
N=\left(\begin{array}{c}2^n\\2^{n-1}\end{array}\right)
balanced functions (list all inputs, which are 2^n, all balanced functions are obtained from permutations of the output of a single balance function, which has 2^n/2 1’s and 2^n/2 0’s). If we know that either a constant or balanced function is selected, classically, we would need
\frac{N}{2} +1 \sim \exp (n)
interrogations; in the quantum case just one interrogation is enough.
Algorithm

The algorithm works the same way as the standard one, substituting Hadamard gates with global Hadamard gates in the A registry.
The final measurement is a projective measurement onto \ket{0}_A^{\otimes n}. Given \Omega = 2^n:
\ket{+}\equiv \sum_x\frac{\ket{x}}{\sqrt{\Omega}}
\ket{0}_A ^{\otimes n}\ket{1}_B\mapsto\ket{+}_A\ket{-}_B\mapsto \frac{1}{\Omega}\sum_{x,y}(-1)^{f(x)+x\cdot y}\ket{y}_A
The probability of getting \ket{0}^{\otimes n}_A as the output in A is
\abs{\frac{\sum_x(-1)^{f(x)}}{\Omega}}^2
Therefore, if f is constant, the probability is 1, while if f is balanced, the probability is 0. This is not proof of quantum advantage because a Probabilistic Turing Machine (PTM) is able to solve this problem in poly(n), not \exp (n). The kind of reduction in complexity that we are looking for in order to claim quantum advantage is exponential to polynomial.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Factoring algorithm (Shor's algorithm)
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Problem
Given a big integer N such that its prime composition is:
N = p_1p_2,
where p_1, p_2 are primes. We want to find these primes. Classically, this problem has a complexity of \exp (n^{1/3}\log ^{2/3} n), where N\sim 2^n.
Using a quantum algorithm, which exploits period finding, this problem can be solved in \mathrm{poly}(n).
Classically, the best strategy consist in the random extraction of an integer M; two possible outcomes:

M,N share a divisor: in this case, finding the primes is easy
M,N are coprime, here classically we can do nothing, while in the quantum case M can be used to generate a new number, which will be useful for finding the primes.

Modular exponential
This is related to the order. Consider two integers N,M; define:
f_M(a) = \mod{N}{M^a}
where a\in\{0,1,...,N-1\}; note that f_M(0) =1. f_M is periodic, let us call the period r the smallest integer >0 such that.
f_M(r) = 1
Finding r in this problem specifically is called order finding. The Period finding algorithm allows us to find it easily.
Algorithm

Extract M
Find the period r of f_M(a), so that \mod{N}{M^r -1}= 0
If r is odd, go back to step 1. If r is even, then, by definition
\left(M^{r/2} -1\right)\left(M^{r/2} +1\right)= kN
for some k integer. Call M^{r/2} -1 \equiv M_1 and M^{r/2} +1\equiv M_2. Now, we have two possible situations:

Either M_1 or M_2 are individually proportional to N, meaning M_{1(2)} = k' p_1p_2. This does not tell us anything, restart algorithm
If the case above does not apply, suppose without loss of generality that M_1\propto p_1 and M_2 \propto p_2. Now either of those numbers can be used in the classical algorithm (Compute GCD).

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Grover algorithm
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The Grover algorithm solves a data search problem. The quantum advantage is not of the type
\exp(n)\mapsto\mathrm{poly}(n)
(see Quantum algorithms) but it’s still there
Problem
Suppose we have an unstructured database with N entries N = 2^n and we want to find an integer x_0 in this database. We have an oracle which tells us if an extraction is the correct one:
f(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{l}0 \quad x\neq x_0\\ 1 \quad x = x_0\end{array}\right.
How many interrogations are needed to find x_0 with good probability? Classically, o(2^n). Using the quantum Grover algorithm, this becomes o(2^{n/2}).
Algorithm

From now on, use vector binary notation (see Computational basis). Define a Grover gate which behaves more or less like the oracle:
G\ket{\vec{x}} = \left\{\begin{array}{l}\ket{\vec{x}} \quad x\neq x_0\\ -\ket{\vec{x}} \quad x = x_0\end{array}\right.
These gates present the structure depicted above, where f is the oracle.
Note that G is a unitary and
G = \mathrm{Id} -2\op{\vec{x}_0}{\vec{x}_0}
This unitary can be generalized for any target state:
D_v \equiv \mathrm{Id} -2\op{v}{v}
so that \ket{v} \mapsto -\ket{v} and \ket{v_\perp} \mapsto\ket{v_\perp}. Take \ket{v} to be \ket{s}, the superposition of all the elements of the computational basis:
\ket{s}\equiv \sum_{\vec{x}}\frac{\ket{\vec{x}}}{\sqrt{N}} = H \ket{0}
where H is the global Hadamard.
D_s \equiv D
We want to build the gate associated to D. Take G_0\equiv\mathrm{Id} -2\op{\vec{0}}{\vec{0}}, then:
D = H^{\otimes n} G_0 H^{\otimes n}
Now we only need to build G_0, as seen in the picture below, the rest is easy.

The main feature of the algorithm consists in applying a sequence of DG gates to an initial state \ket{s} a number of times of order \sqrt{N}. When doing this, we can prove that the probability of getting \ket{\vec{x}_0} at the end is close to 1.
Consider the state
\ket{r} = \sum_{x\neq x_0} \frac{\ket{\vec{x}}}{\sqrt{N-1}}
and note that
\ket{s} = \sqrt{\frac{N-1}{N}}\ket{r}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\ket{\vec{x}_0}
Now, take \ket{r},\ket{\vec{x}_0}; these two states are orthogonal:
\ip{r}{\vec{x}_0} =0
Consider the 2-dimensional Hilbert space spanned by them:
\mathcal{H}_G \equiv \mathrm{span}\left\{\ket{r},\ket{\vec{x}_0}\right\}
Obviously:
\ket{s}\in\mathcal{H}_G
It turns out that \mathcal{H}_G is an eigenspace of D and G. For G this is trivial, while for D, it sends \ket{s}\mapsto-\ket{s} while \ket{s ^\perp}\mapsto\ket{s^\perp}.
We apply DG K times:
(DG)^K\ket{s}\in\mathcal{H}_G
Using a representation where \ket{r} is the y vector and \ket{\vec{x}_0} is the x vector, DG in matrix form becomes:
DG \sim \begin{pmatrix}1-\frac{2}{N} & -2\frac{\sqrt{N-1}}{N}\\ 2\frac{\sqrt{N-1}}{N} & 1-\frac{2}{N}\end{pmatrix}
which is clearly a rotation in \mathcal{H}_G:
\sin \theta \equiv 2\frac{\sqrt{N-1}}{N}
For large N:
\theta \sim \frac{2}{\sqrt{N}}
Since the angle between \ket{s} and \ket{r} is very small, approximately we need to apply this transformation as many times K as it takes in order to have:
K\sim \pi/(2\theta)\sim\sqrt{N}
It is possible to prove that this is the best we can do in the quantum case.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Period finding
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
We can use the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) to find the period of a function in a polynomial number of steps:
f:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto \{0,1\}^m
f\left(\mod{2^n}{x+r}\right) = f(x) \qquad \forall \vec{x}
where {r}, 0< r< N-1, is the smallest period, which we want to find, and we are working in the Computational basis switching from binary form to integers:
x= x_0 2^0 + ... +x_{n-1}2^{n-1}
For the sake of simplicity we will make a number of assumptions:

r is a divisor of N=2^n, which means r=2^t and t\leq \log _2 N = n.
No accidental periodicity
Basically, we are restricting ourselves to functions that are monotonous at fixed intervals:


Implementation
The first step in the procedure goes as illustrated below, using the Hadamard Gate, the Function Gate and the QFT gate:

Performing the measurement on B before or after the QFT on A is equivalent, so it’s usually convenient to perform the measurement first.
We can rewrite the state before the QFT as a superposition based on the state in the B registry, so that we can group together states associated to the same value of f; performing the measurement on B first, and supposing the outcome is f(x'), 0 \leq x' \leq r-1, then the state before the QFT is:
\frac{\sum _{k=0} ^{N/r -1} \ket{x'+kr}_A\ket{f(x')}_B}{\sqrt{N/r}}
Obtaining a specific value f(x') has probability 1/r (uniform distribution). Now discard the B registry, applying the QFT on A returns:
\ket{\psi}_A = \sqrt{\frac{r}{N}}\sum _{k=0} ^{N/r -1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum _{y=0} ^{N-1} e^{2\pi i y (x'+kr)/N}\ket{y}_A
It is useful to note here that:
\sum _{k=0} ^{N/r-1} e^{2\pi i y kr/N}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}0 &\quad\forall y\neq lN/r, \,l\in\mathbb{N}\\ N/r &\quad\forall y = lN/r, \,l\in\mathbb{N}\end{array}\right.
So that only some y‘s survive the sum, with the maximum possible value being y=N
\ket{\psi}_A= \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}\sum _{l=0} ^{r-1} e^{2\pi i y x'/N}\ket{y}_A\delta (y-lN/r)
If we repeat the protocol a few times and measure the A register, we find a list of y_i:
y_i = l_i N/r
N/y_i = r/l_i
In \mathrm{poly}(n) repetitions, there exists an efficient classical algorithm for finding r from the r/l_i fractions. Broadly speaking, what we need to do is the following:

For each N,y_i, compute the greatest common divisor, with an existing efficient algorithm \rightarrow GCD(N,y_i) \equiv G_i, so that
N= q_i G_i\qquad y_i = q'_i G_i
where q_i,q'_i are coprime
Here we have
N/y_i = q_i/q'_i = r/l_i
We have two possibility:

r=q_i, l_i=q'_i, which means that r,l_i are coprime
r is a multiple of q_i, and so r and l_i share a divisor. This means that q_i is a lower bound for r


Estimate:
\tilde{r} = \max \{q_i\}
what is the probability that \tilde{r} = r? Once y_i is extracted, the q_i,q'_i are fixed and so is l_i. The probability that \tilde{r} = r is equivalent to the probability of extracting a y_i such that l_i and r are coprime after k repetitions. Since extracting y_i follows a flat distribution, the problem is equivalent to randomly extracting a number between 0 and r and hoping for it to be coprime with r. After k extractions, we get a lower bound

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT)
Quantum algorithms
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Using Quantum computation, we can build algorithms capable of solving problems much faster then Classical computation algorithms. The kind of improvement we are looking for is:
\exp(n)\mapsto\mathrm{poly}(n)
see Computational complexity classes.
Some notable quantum algorithms include:

Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm
Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm
Simon algorithm
Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT)
Quantum order finding algorithm
Period finding
Factoring algorithm (Shor’s algorithm)
Grover algorithm

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Quantum order finding algorithm
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Order definition
Take two positive integers x, N with no common factors. The order of x modulo N is the least positive integer r such that:
\mod{N}{x^r} = 1

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Simon algorithm
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Consider the function:
f_b:\{0,1\}^n\mapsto\{0,1\}^n
where b is not the null string, such that it presents a kind of periodicity:
f_b(x) =f_b(y)\Leftrightarrow x=y\oplus b
Meaning that the inputs can be grouped into couples that share the same output.
Algorithm
If we find two inputs belonging to the same output class, it’s easy to find b, as we can just XOR sum them.
Classically, we need to do a random search on the inputs, which has complexity \exp(n).
In the quantum case:


We have two registers A and B, containing n qubits each, initialized in \ket{0}^{\otimes n}_A\ket{0}^{\otimes n}_B
Apply a global Hadamard gate on A
Apply a Uf gate on A and B
Apply a global Hadamard gate on A
Measure everything
After the U_f gate, the state reads:

\sum_x\frac{\ket{x}_A\ket{f_b(x)}_B}{\sqrt{N}}
The last Hadamard on A and the measurement on B commute.
We perform the measurement first, so if we label the output classes in B f_j, for each f_j we would have two states in A corresponding to the input associated to f_j, i.e. \ket{x_{f_j}}_A,\ket{x_{f_j}\oplus b}_A. Before the measurement:
\frac{1}{\sqrt{N/2}}\sum _{j}\left(\frac{\ket{x_{f_j}}_A+\ket{x_{f_j}\oplus b}_A}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{f_j}_B\right)
So when we perform a projective measurement onto \ket{f_j}_B, each output is equiprobable with probability 2/N.
After the measurement, on registry A:
\frac{\ket{x_{f_j}}+\ket{x_{f_j}\oplus b}}{\sqrt{2}}
We apply the Hadamard:
\frac{\ket{x_{f_j}}+\ket{x_{f_j}\oplus b}}{\sqrt{2}}\mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{C}{\sqrt{N}}\sum _y (-1)^{x_{f_j}\cdot y}\left(1+(-1)^{b\cdot y}\right)\ket{y}
where C is a normalization constant (possibly 1 but not sure and it’s not important to the functioning of the algorithm). The only remaining states y in the output of A are those orthogonal to b:
y\cdot b =0
If we run the protocol k times, it’s very unlikely to extract the same y, therefore after k runs of the protocol we have k different values of y all orthogonal to b. This induces a set of k linear equations.
\left\{\begin{array}{l}b\cdot y_1 =0\\ b\cdot y_2 =0\\ \vdots\\ b\cdot y_k =0\end{array}\right.
Which k is enough to find b? It scales \sim O(n).

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: CNOT gate
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The CNOT gate is a controlled gate which induces the X transformation (NOT, see Pauli operators) on one qubit when the other is in the \ket{1} state:
CNOT\ket{0}_A\ket{\psi}_B = \ket{0}_A\ket{\psi}_B
CNOT\ket{1}_A\ket{\psi}_B = \ket{1}_AX_B\ket{\psi}_B
CNOT gates generate entanglement and they can be used to generate Bell states.
On elements of the Computational basis:
\ket{x_0}_A\ket{x_1}_B \overset{CNOT}{\mapsto} \ket{x_0}_A\ket{x_0\oplus x_1}_B
Action on Pauli’s
The CNOT gate (controlled by the first qubit here) acts on Pauli operators as follows:
X\otimes \id\overset{CNOT}{\mapsto}X\otimes X,\quad \id\otimes X\overset{CNOT}{\mapsto}\id\otimes X
Z\otimes \id\overset{CNOT}{\mapsto}Z\otimes \id,\quad \id\otimes Z\overset{CNOT}{\mapsto}Z\otimes Z
We can also summarize these relations graphically:


Apparent asymmetry
There is an apparent asymmetry inherent to the CNOT, which is solved by looking at the gate’s action upon +,-:
CNOT \ket{\pm }_A\ket{+}_B=\ket{\pm }_A\ket{+}_B
CNOT\ket{\pm }_A\ket{-}_B = \ket{\mp }_A\ket{-}_B
The CNOT applied on the basis of X induces a transformation on the “controlling” qubit. This is further exacerbated when applying Hadamard gates before and after the CNOT:

Operations built from CNOT
Using CNOT gates and One qubit gates, a number of operations can be constructed:

Controlled unitaries
Swap gates

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Church-Turing Thesis
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
If a function f is computable in any computational model, then there exist a Turing machine that can compute f.
This means that the notion of computability by a Turing machine is the fundamental one.
Quantum computation obeys the CT thesis (functions that are not computable by a Turing machine remain not computable by a quantum computer).
Strong Church-Turing Thesis
Statement:
Any model of computation can be simulated by a Probabilistic Turing Machine (PTM) within a computational time that is polynomial in the computational time of the original model.
Quantum computation may break the SCT thesis.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Classical computation
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Models
There exists two main models for classical computation

Turing machine model
Gate array model (classical)

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Computational complexity classes
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
In the following, by t_{M}(x) we denote the time it takes for a Turing machine M to solve a given problem, and by n we denote the number of digits needed to express the input x.
Decision problems
Decision problems (basically binary functions, see Gate array model (classical)) are used to categorize the computational complexity of a given problem
Terminology

Language: a language L is a subset of an alphabet \Gamma whose elements are all finite
A language L is decided by a Turing machine M if
M(x) = 0,1 \quad\forall x\in L

For a decided language L by the machine M,
x\in L \Rightarrow M(x) =1 


meaning that x is accepted by M

For a decided language L by the machine M,
x\notin L \Rightarrow M(x) =0
meaning that x is rejected by M

P class
Poly time
A problem f belongs to the P class if \exists M: t_M(x) = \mathrm{poly}(n).
BPP class
Bounded-error Probabilistic Polynomial time
Given a language L, L\in BPP if there exists a Probabilistic Turing Machine (PTM) PM such that
x\in L \Rightarrow PM (x) =1 \quad\textrm{at least 50\% of the time}
BQP class
Bounded-error Quantum Polynomial time
Quantum equivalent of the BPP class. Factoring problem belongs in BQP for now, as no classical algorithm exists to solve this problem in poly time. If factoring is in BQP but not in BPP, then the SCT thesis is false.
NP class
Non deterministic Poly time
A problem f belongs to the NP class if \nexists M: t_M(x) = \mathrm{poly}(n).
However, once M(x) has been produced, it is easy (P class) to check whether
M(x) = f(x)
For sure, \mathrm{NP}\supseteq\mathrm{P}, however, a big issue here is
\mathrm{NP}\overset{?}{=}\mathrm{P}
No one knows.
More precisely, suppose a language L\in NP, then \exists M such that:

If x\in L then \exists w: M(x,w) = 1 in poly time
If x\notin L then \forall w, M(x,w) = 0 in poly time
All NP problems can be mapped into NP complete problems in poly time.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Gate array model (classical)
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The gate array model is equivalent to the Turing machine model, i.e. one can be mapped into the other in poly time
The model works by encoding the input into strings of bits, so that any function we may want to compute reduces to a binary function:
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\quad f(x)\in \{0,1\}^{m}
The universality of the gate array model is guaranteed through the existence of Universal Gate sets

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Halting problem
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The halting problem is a not computable problem (see Church-Turing Thesis)
For a given Turing machine M, identified by the Turing number T_M, for a given input \vec{x}, one of two things can happen: either the machine reaches the end of the computation or it does not. We want to build a Turing machine capable of predicting which of these two outcomes will happen:
H(T_M,\vec{x}) = \left\{\begin{array}{l}0\quad \textrm{if } M\textrm{ does not halt with input }\vec{x}\\ 1\quad \textrm{if } M\textrm{ halts with input }\vec{x}\end{array}\right.
But, if such a machine existed, a new one called IM could be built that works as follows:

Take an input \vec{x}
Assign y = H(T_{IM},\vec{x})
If y=0 then halt
If y=1, then loop forever
This machine is self-contradictory, so H cannot exist

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Hamming Distance
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Given two bit strings, their Hamming distance is the total amount of different bits between the two strings
In the figure, a new set of strings, at Hamming distance one, is generated by changing the value of the left-most string in the original set.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Landauer Principle
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Is logical irreversibility necessary for Classical computation?
The Landauer principle is in a one to one relationship with the second principle of thermodynamics.
Connection between physics and information theory; suppose there is a machine performing operation in equilibrium with a thermal bath.

Suppose we perform a logically irreversible operation, e.g. erase a bit of information; this costs a certain amount of heat:
\Delta Q \geq k_B T\log 2
We might ask ourselves whether classical computation is only possible if we assume logical irreversibility.
The Toffoli gate is universal and reversible, so the answer is NO, however, what requires dissipation is the erasure of memory

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Maxwell paradox
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The Maxwell paradox provides a rudimentary proof for the Landauer Principle.
Rules of the game: we have a chamber with two internal rooms submerged in a thermal bath at temperature T, see figure. The right wall is frictionless, same as a door between the two rooms.
The Maxwell paradox is a protocol that allows to extract work from the “thermal machine” described in the previous configuration, which is thermodinamically impossible (single thermal bath): there is a “demon” capable of controlling the middle door, which they open when and only when they see a particle moving from right to left, so that they can map whichever starting configuration to the 0 configuration with apparently 0 work. Afterwards, attach middle wall to mechanical engine (e.g. pulley) and let the gas expand ⇒ free energy. However, this process is not a cycle, the demon has acquired memory, which they need to erase ⇒ Landauer principle compensates the energy “produced”.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Probabilistic Turing Machine (PTM)
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
A PTM is a regular Turing machine that integrates a random number generator (RNG), so that steps in the computational process can be decided following a probability distribution.
By construction
PTM \supseteq TM
We say that a function f is computable by a PTM if for every input \vec{x}, we have
PM(\vec{x}) = f(\vec{x})
with probability of at least 1/2, so that the computation can be repeated many times to increase the probability.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Toffoli gate
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The Toffoli gate forms by itself a universal set for Classical computation. It is basically a NOT gate controlled by the value of two external bits (see Controlled gates).
The operation induced by this gate is logically reversible.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Turing machine
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
A Turing machine contains 4 main elements:

Program, the set of internal instructions
Finite state control, the set of internal states of the machine, denoted by
q_1,...,q_m
where m can be considered a constant without loss of generality. In addition to these states, there are also q_s,q_h, the starting and halting states respectively. q_s is the state of the machine at the start of the computation, during which the state will be altered; the computation will reach its end if and when the state of the machine becomes q_h.
Tape, which acts like the memory of a computer and is represented by a one dimensional object whose entries form an “alphabet”, which is the finite set of symbols. The alphabet can be whatever, but it is convenient to take the sample alphabet \Gamma =\left\{0,1,\mathrm{NULL},\triangleright\right\}. \triangleright marks the starting entry of the tape (think of the left-most entry). Initially, the tape will contain the \triangleright symbol, a finite number of 0,1’s, and the rest of the tape will present NULL entries.
Read-write tape-head, pointing to the position of the tape that is currently readable or writable.
The program is a finite ordered list of program lines, which take the form

\langle q,x,q',x',s\rangle

q is the state the machine must be in for the line to be executed
x is the symbol that needs to be read by the tape-head for the line to be executed; all the non NULL entries form an array \vec{x}.
The program searches its program lines in order to find a line that can be executed; if no such lines are found, q \mapsto q_h.
After executing a line, the state of the machine is changed to q' and x is overwritten to x'
The tape-head moves left, right or stands still depending on s = \pm 1,0.
The output of the program is composed of the non NULL entries in the tape
A function f is said to be computable by a Turing machine if there exists a Turing machine that, for any input \vec{x}, reaches q_h in finite time and the final output on the tape reads f(\vec{x}).

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Universal Gate sets
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
A universal gate set is composed of gates whose combinations can compute any computable function (see Turing machine)
An example of universal set of gates is
\{AND,OR,COPY,NOT\}
Any function f can be expressed by a collection of functions:
f:\{0,1\}^{n}\mapsto\{0,1\}^{m}
f(x) = \left(f_1 (x),f_2 (x) ,...,f_m(x) \right)
f_j : \{0,1\}^{n}\mapsto\{0,1\}
This is possible thanks to the feasibility of the COPY operation, see picture below

What kind of functions are the f_j‘s? They are sort of characteristic functions, we can define the supports of the inputs leading to the outputs 0,1:
S_0 \equiv \left\{x:f_j(x) = 0\right\}
S_1 \equiv \left\{x:f_j(x) = 1\right\}
Suppose that \{x_1,...,x_d\} = S_1, then we can write f_j as a composition of projectors onto the elements of the support, combined with OR operations:

f_j (x)= \Pi _{x_1} (x)\lor\Pi _{x_2} (x)\lor...\lor\Pi _{x_d} (x)
\Pi _{z} (x)\equiv \left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \quad \textrm{if }x=z\\0 \quad \textrm{if }x\neq z\end{array}\right.
Can the projectors be represented via the universal set defined above?
Yes: they are a composition of AND gates, where the inputs are the elements of x which can be modified by a NOT gate for each position where the reference vector has a 0, e.g.:

The output is 1 if the input is the same as the reference vector
Minimal universal gate set

OR gate can be replaced by AND and NOT 
AND and NOT gates can be replaced by NAND  
NAND and copy can be replaced by: Taking y=1, both the outputs are \bar{x}.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Universal Turing Machine (UTM)
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Since every element for a fixed Turing machine is finite, we can associate said Turing machine to a specific natural number through a bijective function. This numbers are called Turing numbers T_M. Then, we can build a Universal Turing machine which can compute any kind of computable function f by feeding it the Turing number T_M of the machine M capable of computing f, which identifies a specific set of program lines in the program (i.e. those associated with M) and a generic input \vec{x} separated from T_M by a NULL entry
UTM(T_M,\vec{x}) = M(\vec{x})
An UTM can be built out of an alphabet composed of 8 symbols and an finite state control composed of 23 states.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Clifford hierarchy
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Clifford operations are the normalizers of the n-qubit Pauli group:
GPG ^\dagger = \pm Q
where G is a n-qubit Clifford operation and P,Q are Pauli operators.
This concept can be expanded by introducing the n-qubit Clifford hierarchy (\mathcal{P}_j)_{j\geq 1} being the family of sets of unitaries defined by induction as follows:

The first element \mathcal{P}_1 is the n-qubit Pauli group.
The j-th element \mathcal{P}_j is the set of n-qubit unitaries U such that U \mathcal{P}_1 U^{\dagger} \subseteq \mathcal{P}_{j-1}.
In this context, \mathcal{P}_2 is the Clifford group.

Universality
Upon reaching \mathcal{P}_3, we obtain a Universal Quantum Gate set as the quantum Toffoli and the T phase gate are contained in this set:
T,CCNOT\in\mathcal{P}_3
More generally, we have that:
P\left(\frac{\pi}{2^{j-1}}\right), C^{(j)}NOT\in\mathcal{P}_j
check maximal non dense subgroup of unitaries

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Clifford operations
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Clifford operations generate a subset of all possible operations in Quantum computation, see Universal Quantum Gate set for more information. They are unitary, act on any number of qubits and are generated by Hadamard gates H, a specific kind of phase gate and CNOT gates:
\textrm{Clifford set}=\left\{H, P(\pi/2), CNOT\right\}\equiv \left\{H, S, CNOT\right\}
Note that Toffoli gates can’t be generated using these gates, however Pauli gates can be, as seen below
Pauli operations from Clifford
Trivially:
S^2 = Z
And:
HZH = X
Then combining those we can build the whole Pauli group.
Clifford operations as Pauli normalizers
Clifford operations generate the Normalizer for the n-qubit Pauli group (which are local operations). In fact, given any n-qubit Clifford operation G and two Pauli operations P,Q, we have that:
GPG ^\dagger = \pm Q
Note that phases other than \pm 1 can’t be admitted, as both sides are hermitian.


                  
                  Proof 
                  
                

The relationship is easily shown for Hadamards and S gates:
\begin{array}{ccc}
HXH^\dagger = Z & HYH^\dagger = -Y & HZH^\dagger = X
\end{array}
\begin{array}{ccc}
SXS^\dagger = Y & SYS^\dagger = -X & SZS^\dagger = Z
\end{array}
For CNOT’s, a the commutations with the Pauli group are summarized using the gate array diagrams below




This also holds the other way around: any G satisfying the property above must be a Clifford operation (harder to prove).

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Computational basis
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The computational basis is the conventional basis used in Quantum computation, composed by the eigenvectors of the Pauli operator Z for computation based on qubits. In the qudit case, we take the eigenvectors of the Heisenberg-Weyl operators Z(a).
Vector form
Usually, the elements of the basis are denoted by
\ket{x}
We can apply multiplication and addition on the object x in the form of the logical operations AND and XOR:
x_1x_2 \equiv AND(x_1,x_2)
x_1 + x_2 \equiv XOR(x_1,x_2)
When we are considering registers of more than one qubit, we denote the computational basis in the compact form
\ket{\vec{x}}
where each component of \vec{x} represents the state of a single qubit.
The AND operation translates to a scalar product where the sum is performed modulus 2. The XOR is taken element-wise.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Controlled gates
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content: Controlled gates are a class of Two qubit gates which act on one of the qubits as a unitary only when the other qubit is in a specific state, conventionally \ket{1}, however this can be changed by one qubit gates.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Controlled unitaries
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Controlled unitaries are Controlled gates that induce a unitary transformation on one qubit when the other is in a specific state.
Using a lemma of Euler rotations, which states that any unitary acting on qubits can be written as:
U = (\textrm{global phase}) AXBXC
where A,B,C are unitaries such that ABC=\mathrm{Id}, we can build any controlled unitary using CNOT gates and One qubit gates:

nC-U generalization
Is it possible to build a unitary transformation, controlled by n qubits, acting on another qubit using only 2 qubit gates? We need auxiliary qubits but it is possible:

Arbitrary coupling
In the Computational basis, using nC-U operations, we are able to couple (i.e. the initial state and the final state are coupled through a unitary operation) two states which have Hamming Distance of at most 1 between themselves:
\ket{y}_A\ket{\psi}_B\mapsto\left\{\begin{array}{l}\ket{y}_A\ket{\psi}_B\quad\quad\forall y\neq x \\ \ket{x}_AU\ket{\psi}_B \quad\textrm{ if }y=x\end{array}\right.
However, we are still not able to couple two states with arbitrary Hamming distance.
We try to build a protocol capable of doing that; we are trying to couple the initial bit string x_1 with the bit string x_2, with x_2 being a target bit string, by sending the qubits in the A register of x_1 to the same state as those of x_2 so that we are in the same situation above; however, we need to be careful to build a circuit that only does this for x_1 (basically, we want to prepare the A register so that its qubits are the same as those in x_2 and then apply the controlled unitary, so that the circuit as a whole is a circuit such is a controlled operation that, if the A register is the same as that of x_1, it gets sent to the A register of x_2 plus a unitary on the B register).

If two bit strings differ in at least two positions, we can apply a CCNOT operation that only activates for one of the two strings
We build a sequence of CCNOT gates that send x_1 to x'_1, which shares the bits in the A registry with x_2
Now we apply the nC-unitary
Finally, we apply the preparation protocol in reverse
Using an appropriate sequence of CC-NOT operations we can selectively allow for the coupling of any 2 elements of the computational basis through a nC-U operation. Effectively, the unitary acts non trivially only on 2 elements of the computational basis

Generic unitary
We can use the previous result to build generic unitaries acting on n Qubits.
Theorem
Let \mathcal{U} be a generic unitary operation acting on n qubits, so that \mathcal{U} is a 2^n\times 2^n matrix. Then, \exists \{W_j\} sequence of gates coupling only 2 strings in the computational basis such that
\mathcal{U} = W _t ... W_1
where t is generally a big number t\sim (2^n)^2.
Proof
We start by building the inverse of the last gate, W_t^\dagger, which is the identity everywhere aside from the first 2 elements of the computational basis
\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\mathcal{U} ^\dagger_{11}}{\gamma} & \frac{\mathcal{U} ^\dagger_{21}}{\gamma}\\ \frac{\mathcal{U}_{21}}{\gamma} & \frac{\mathcal{U}_{22}}{\gamma} \end{pmatrix}
By choosing
\gamma \equiv \sqrt{\abs{\mathcal{U}_{11}}^2+\abs{\mathcal{U}_{21}}^2}
we can verify that this matrix is unitary
By carrying out the matrix multiplication W_t ^\dagger \mathcal{U}, it turns out that the matrix in the 21 position is 0. The other elements are non trivial. Let us call the new elements in the positions 11,31,13,33 as \mathcal{U}_{ij} ^\prime; then, we can do the same thing with this element, obtaining that the 31 element of W_{t-1}W_t \mathcal{U} is 0. And so on and so on.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Function Gate
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The U_f gate allows for the computation of binary functions on the Computational basis.

The target functions take on the form:
f:\{0,1\}^{n}\mapsto \{0,1\}^{m}
Consider two registries of Qubits, A and B. The qubits in A will take on the role of inputs, while the output will be stored in B after the gate. We want to build a unitary gate such that:
U_f\left(\ket{x}_A\ket{0}_B\right) = \ket{x}_A\ket{f(x)}_B
Focus on the particular case of m=1
f:\{0,1\}^{n}\mapsto \{0,1\}
If input on B register is \ket{1}, the output needs to be orthogonal to the one above
U_f\left(\ket{x}_A\ket{1}_B\right) = \ket{x}_A\ket{f(x)\oplus 1}_B
Consider a linear combination of elements of the computational basis in B:
\frac{\ket{0}_B-\ket{1}_B}{\sqrt{2}}=\ket{\psi _-}_B
Using linearity, this state is mapped into:
\ket{x}_A \ket{\psi _-}_B\overset{U_f}{\mapsto} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ket{x}_A\left(\ket{f(x)}_B-\ket{f(x)\oplus1}\right)=\left\{\begin{array}{l}\ket{x}_A\ket{\psi _-}_B\quad \textrm{if }f(x)=0\\
-\ket{x}_A\ket{\psi _-}_B\quad \textrm{if }f(x)=1\end{array}\right.
Or, in a more compact form

We started from a definition where, apparently, the A register controls the B register. However, selecting a specific input for B, we wind up in a situation where the A register is controlled by B.
\left(\sum_x \alpha _x \ket{x}_A\right)\ket{\psi_-}_B\mapsto\left(\sum_x (-1)^{f(x)} \alpha _x \ket{x}_A\right)\ket{\psi_-}_B
This is important as this means that we are able to encode f(x) into the relative phases of the A register. See Quantum algorithms.

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Gottesman-Knill theorem
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Any quantum computer containing only the gates (see One qubit gates, Two qubit gates) \{H,P(\pi/2),CNOT\} can be efficiently classically simulated. Note that this gate set is exactly the Clifford set.
In this context, the difference between quantum and Classical computation is just one gate:
P(\pi/2) \leftrightarrow P(\pi/4)
Notice that these simulable machines can still generate Entangled states (see Bell states)

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Hadamard Gate
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The Hadamard gate is a transformation induced on Qubits carried out by the operator:
H \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix}1 &1 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}
In terms of one qubit unitaries:
H=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}{cc}1 & 1\\
1 & -1\end{array}\right) = e^{i\pi}U_{\hat{m}}(\pi)
\hat{m} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,0,1)
The corresponding angle is depicted in the figure above.
Practically, this transformation sends eigenvectors of the Z operator into eigenvectors of the X operator and viceversa (see Pauli operators):

H\ket{0} =\ket{+}
H\ket{1} =\ket{-}
H^2 = \id_2
In terms of Computational basis:
\ket{x}\overset{H}{\mapsto}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\ket{0} + (-1)^{x}\ket{1}\right)
Action on Pauli’s
The action of the Hadamard gate acting on Pauli operators is summarized by:
X\overset{H}{\leftrightarrow}Z
Global Hadamard gate

We are working in the Computational basis
It produces superpositions of all elements of the computational basis, whatever the inputs, given N\equiv 2^n
\ket{x}\mapsto\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_y(-1)^{x\cdot y}\ket{y}
\ket{0}^{\otimes n} \mapsto \sum_y\frac{\ket{y}}{\sqrt{N}}
Qudit Hadamard
\begin{gathered}
H_d|j\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum_{i=0}^{d-1} \omega^{i j}|i\rangle, j \in\{0,1,2, \ldots, d-1\}, \\
\omega:=\mathrm{e}^{2 \pi \mathrm{i} / d} .
\end{gathered}
Transformation acting on two memory registers

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: One qubit gates
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
Given the Pauli operators \sigma = \{\sigma_x ,\sigma_y,\sigma_z\}, a generic qubit unitary U can be written as
U = e ^{i\phi} U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)
where U_{\hat{n}}(\theta) is a rotation of angle \theta around the unit vector \hat{n}:
U_{\hat{n}}(\theta) = e^{-i\frac{\theta}{2} \hat{n}\sigma}
U^\dagger_{\hat{n}}(\theta)\sigma U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)= R(\theta)_{\hat{n}}\sigma
U^\dagger_{\hat{n}}(\theta)\sigma _i U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)= \sum_j\left(R(\theta)_{\hat{n}}\right)_{ij}\sigma_j
U_{\hat{n}}(\theta) = \cos \frac{\theta}{2}\mathrm{Id}-i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}n_i\sigma_i
Using these unitaries, all 1 qubit gates for Quantum computation are built:

Phase gate
Hadamard Gate
See One qubit minimal gate set

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.filePath: ../PhysicsVault/Quantum Information/Quantum Computation/One qubit minimal gate set.md
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: One qubit minimal gate set
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
We want to prove that the set:
\left\{\{P(\phi)\}_\phi,H \right\}
where P(\phi) is a Phase gate and H is a Hadamard Gate, can reproduce all One qubit gates.
Some useful identities:
HZH = X
HP(\phi)H = ...= e^{i\phi/2}U_{\hat{x}}(\phi)
So that we can substitute Hadamard gates and phase gates into the Euler rotations:
U_{\hat{n}} (\theta) = P(\alpha _1)HP(\alpha _2)HP(\alpha _3)
So that any unitary on single qubits is built from these two gates
More practical set
Another more practical, yet approximate, universal set is:
\{P(\pi/4),H\}
we must set a target for accuracy:
U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)\mapsto U^\prime:\norm{U^\prime - U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)}<\epsilon
This can be done through the generalized Euler theorem. In order to do so, we need to generate generic rotations around two different axes using the two gates above.
We define the first rotation:
P(\pi/4)HP(\pi/4)H = e^{i\pi/4}U_{\hat{n}}(\theta)
where:
n\propto\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{8},\sin\frac{\pi}{8},\cos\frac{\pi}{8}\right)
\theta:\cos\frac{\theta}{2} = \cos^2\frac{\pi}{8}
It turns out that \theta/\pi is irrational, so it generates aperiodic rotations if applied multiple times
\left(P(\pi/4)HP(\pi/4)H\right)^N = e^{i\pi/4}U_{\hat{n}}(\tilde{\theta})
The other rotations are found through:
HP(\pi/4)HP(\pi/4) = e^{i\pi/4}U_{\hat{m}}(\theta)
where:
m\propto\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{8},-\sin\frac{\pi}{8},\cos\frac{\pi}{8}\right)

Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.title: Phase gate
Quantum-Information/Quantum-Computation/.content:
The phase gate is identified by the unitary:
P(\phi) =\left(
\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0\\
0 & e^{i\phi}
\end{array}
\right) = e ^{i\phi/2}U_{\hat{z}}(\phi)
It acts on the Computational basis as:
\ket{0}\mapsto \ket{0}
\ket{1}\mapsto e^{i\phi}\ket{1}
So, it induces a relative phase between elements of the basis
\ket{x}\overset{P(\phi)}{\mapsto}e^{i\phi x}\ket{x}
Controlled version
The controlled version of the phase gate induces the following transformation
\ket{x_0}_A\ket{x_1}_B\overset{CP(\phi)}{\mapsto}\ket{x_0}_Ae^{i\phi x_0x_1}\ket{x_1}_B
Important phase gates
An important role in Quantum computation is played by the gate P(\pi/4), also called T gate, see One qubit minimal gate set.
T gates
We define the T gates with:
T\equiv P(\pi/4) =\left(
\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0\\
0 & e^{i\pi/4}
\end{array}
\right)
Action on Pauli’s
The T gate transforms Pauli operators according to:
X\overset{T}{\mapsto}e^{-i\pi/4}SX,\quad Z\overset{T}{\mapsto}Z
X\overset{T^\dagger}{\mapsto}e^{i\pi/4}S^\dagger X,\quad Z\overset{T^\dagger}{\mapsto}Z
where S is defined below
S gates
We define the S gates with:
S\equiv P(\pi/2) = T^2 =\left(
\begin{array}{cc}1 & 0\\
0 & i
\end{array}
\right)
Action on Pauli’s
The S gate transforms Pauli operators according to:
X\overset{S}{\mapsto}Y,\quad Z\overset{S}{\mapsto}Z
X\overset{S^\dagger}{\mapsto}-Y,\quad Z\overset{S^\dagger}{\mapsto}Z
CNOT gates
The CNOT logical can be implemented trivially by connecting corresponding qubits in two different code blocks.
Non-Clifford gates
This is a more general result, but it is not possible to implement non-Clifford gates on 2D codes
